Every time we make a sequel, there are always people who ask us to make the world even bigger. We all know that the scale of the game needs to expand further, but at the time, we hadn’t really figured out what that actually meant.Of course, it’s easy to narrowly interpret “bigger” as playtime corresponding to map size—we even considered reimagining the series as a live-service game.This was a direction we explored early in the project—not to turn it into a service-based game, but to find a gameplay framework that would allow *Subnautica* to function as an endlessly playable game, without even needing a complete story-driven campaign.
On top of that, there’s a drive to make disruptive changes—a force that often comes from team members who have long been responsible for developing the series and have grown weary of it.By the time we were creating *Subnautica: Below Zero*, this group had been in the industry for nearly twelve years, and this time we had complete freedom to use any aspect of the IP we wanted, without having to worry about any parts we didn’t need.If we’d wanted to, we could have even scrapped all story-related content entirely. There were absolutely no rules at the time, since we were the only stakeholders—which allowed us to pivot in a new direction very early on.You can see the freedom to experiment with the IP in these early concepts—flying vehicles, ground bases, and more land-based areas. Some of these elements were already introduced in *Below Zero* and did indeed receive quite harsh criticism; all of them strayed significantly from the core premise of the original *Deep Sea* game.
We initially came up with an idea that really got us excited.We threw ourselves into it with everything we had. It was as if the entire team was diving headfirst into the project. At first, we wondered how this would shape the game’s direction, but we eventually realized it simply wouldn’t work—or that it would completely derail the core experience the game was meant to deliver.I think this situation could have been avoided. We really should have spent more time delving into the game’s core essence—starting with identifying that common core element I mentioned earlier. But trying out these new ideas was just so exciting. Plus, we were still a new team that was just finding our footing.
04
Exploration and Trade-offs
Next, I’d like to take a look back at some of the early prototypes we created while exploring the “one-third new approach.” As far as I know, no one has ever seen these before. And I think it’s valuable to reflect on why we chose these approaches in the first place—and why, ultimately, they weren’t a good fit for this project.
So, let’s start with the first one—this is a project we worked on very early on that centered around ecosystems. We explored the following concept: building and maintaining a fully simulated real-world ecosystem within the game, where players would manage various animal and plant populations.In this scenario, you can see a kelp forest. Once the kelp matures, it releases seeds, which then grow into more kelp forests. At the same time, there are sea urchins in the world that actively search for edible mature and juvenile kelp, and subsequently reproduce to produce more offspring.Subsequently, as sea urchins and kelp compete with one another for survival, the entire system enters a state of equilibrium. We later developed several versions of this project and even introduced predator characters specifically to control the populations of species that were growing too large. We all found the scene before us truly breathtaking and deeply inspiring.
In the early prototype versions, we realized we didn’t want to make a simulation game; instead, we wanted players to truly understand what was going on while playing. The only way to achieve this was to overlay numerous UI layers and use progress bars and charts to visually present the relevant information.We eventually clarified our direction: we wanted to create a game centered on repairing, healing, or harmonizing the environment—one that would allow players to genuinely feel that the world undergoes tangible changes as a result of their healing actions.
You can see this in the way the damaged roots in the world function: healing these roots will bring new life to the area.
I also think this prototype was very helpful in steering us toward simplifying our new product concept. It was truly a groundbreaking breakthrough for the series; although the prototype’s appearance was rather unremarkable, we had originally thought it would be a natural addition to the product line, but in the end, it didn’t quite come to fruition.
We also have another early prototype centered around the concept of “Void Expedition.” So this is the core idea behind cooperative gameplay set in the Void—something we hadn’t fully fleshed out before. We always hear fans say, “I want to go to the Void.”” In the first game, the Void was merely the edge of the world—there was nothing beyond it. To put it bluntly, it was essentially a slaughterhouse designed just for you. But they said that it was still the place they truly wanted to explore. So we took that to mean: they wanted us to fill that void and put enough content in there for them to explore.
Therefore, in these early prototype versions, we experimented with a design concept where the entire game revolved around expeditions into the Void.Someone once proposed the idea that it would be like a game you could play forever. So we began to wonder: Could players simply keep traveling to the Void to explore, return to base to rest and recuperate, then set off again on a new journey into the Void, only to return to base once more? But in the end, we concluded that this actually didn’t align with our core game vision.The Void and these expeditions might have their own merits, but we had strayed too far from our core focus. I think it’s a fantastic idea, but it’s simply not the foundation of the *Subnautica* series.
In some of our early exploratory work, we used a submersible like this—I think you may have seen it not long ago—but it couldn’t move.Speaking of this vehicle, the truth is that at the time, we hadn’t yet figured out how to create submarines that could move in coordination with players. In multiplayer mode, it’s quite challenging to synchronize a submarine’s movement with the players on board without letting them get separated or lose track of each other.What we actually did was have players pilot the submarine on a 2D map; when the submarine reached a designated position on that map, the system would load the corresponding area beneath it. And when you wanted to explore a brand-new area within a predefined part of the world, all players would then enter that map.Honestly, you might even catch me briefly lying in wait to ambush someone.
What really resonated with me in this presentation was that we’re exploring the core essence of *Subnautica* through a process of elimination.We established the foundational framework for the survival experience and then began prototyping new content—just like the journeys you’ve seen. Once we mapped out the various impacts this issue had across the entire game, it actually helped us further clarify our core direction and determine which elements absolutely had to remain unchanged.
I still feel that I’d rather spend a little more time first figuring out the right direction based on the core elements, and then supplementing that with new content. But this has definitely been a great way for our team to learn the Unreal Engine and stay passionate about making games together.We’ve invested a tremendous amount of time in prototyping and experimentation. I don’t think it’s been a waste of time. That’s how we developed new systems for the game adaptation, such as the creature mod, as well as many other features that were ultimately incorporated into the final game.
But ultimately, as we explored new content, we came to realize that many ideas that initially seemed highly disruptive were actually unnecessary distractions that would divert us from the core mission of creating a true sequel to *Subnautica*.And as we finalized many of these features one by one, a concern began to loom large: our final product would end up being too similar to what the fans had already created.
At the time, this was the most ordinary thing in the world. I would talk it over with Charlie, the studio’s creative director at the time, and he always said he felt this direction was too similar to our existing work—that players definitely wouldn’t buy into it because the end result would be virtually indistinguishable from our previous game. That brings me to the topic I’m about to discuss:how to strike just the right balance—at least that’s how we approached it back then—and our benchmark was none other than *Subnautica 1*; it served as our guiding light.
05
Focus on the previous installment; return to the main storyline
Ultimately, after creating multiple prototypes and experimenting with various radical approaches for *Subnautica 2*, we realized we needed to delve deeper into that “North Star” we’d long been familiar with.We’ve always known that our goal was to create a game that aligns much more closely with *Subnautica* than *Below Zero* does. But in our quest to explore and find that one-third of innovative content, we truly lost sight of keeping the team aligned on what we wanted to carry forward and refine.
As it turned out, this task proved far more challenging than expected. We have the most outstanding team I’ve ever worked with, but the studio’s staff composition has indeed undergone significant changes as this project has progressed.Since I joined in 2021, our team size has remained at around 40 people. By the time this game reaches 2025, I expect our team to be around 70 people. Currently, however, we’re just shy of 100 people.
These individuals have varying levels of knowledge about *Deep Sea*—ranging from veteran employees who have been involved in development since the first game to newcomers who joined the studio just two months ago.This certainly made it harder for the entire team to reach a clear consensus on the game’s foundational modules, and everyone may have taken it for granted that team members knew how to build the core gameplay experience—after all, some of them had worked on similar projects 12 years ago.So I think at the time, everyone just assumed that we didn’t need to bother with secondary experiences and should instead focus our energy on innovation.
But given that we were constantly bringing in so many new people at the time, that line of reasoning simply didn’t hold water. So, once we stopped focusing on that one-third of new content and shifted our attention back to the familiar, tried-and-true elements of the game, the entire project finally started to get back on track.
This requires us to spend a significant amount of time specifically re-examining the content we’ve released in the past. For example, what should the balance be for large gas tanks? The first thing we do is open *Subnautica* or *Below Zero* and take a close look to figure out exactly how they handled it before.You might think this is obvious, but when you’re constantly bringing in new people like this, this kind of ability needs to be gradually cultivated within the team.
And sometimes, due to improvements in industry standards and operational guidelines—the so-called “one-third improvement”—we may ultimately part ways with older versions of the game. We often find ourselves having to rediscover what exactly makes *Subnautica* so unique. However, this process is certainly not without its challenges.In a team of this size, with a mix of new and veteran members, it’s quite common for people to zone out or get lost in memories of the past. When we asked some of our long-time team members about the full range of features that were once available in *Subnautica 1*, they were all quite surprised.It’s no easy task to keep track of every single detail regarding what should and shouldn’t be included in a game. I fully understand this, especially after all these years since we first started with the original *Subnautica*.
This problem can be solved—provided, of course, that we focus solely on honing our skills with the original game and examine it exclusively from the perspective of its strengths. So we began conducting regular playtests of our previous titles, at a frequency comparable to that of our regular playtests for *Deep Sea Voyage*.
We’ve also started listening to what our veteran employees have to say and learning about the decision-making process behind various decisions, rather than focusing solely on the final outcome. Furthermore, when it comes to balancing the air tanks, they’ve often been saying the same thing for a long time. Or a designer might say, “Okay, I’m going to try this new approach on the air tanks.”But if we ask the veteran employees, they’ll tell us, “We’ve tried that approach, and it didn’t work for various reasons.” This saves us time, since they’ve already learned the hard way.Honestly, if we’d done more research back then, we could have avoided those procedural issues they’d already tried and found didn’t work. But at the time—maybe I was just being foolish—I said I understood Charlie and thought we had it figured out. But in reality, we hadn’t figured it out at all.We should have spent more time seeking advice from our more experienced colleagues.
06
Consideration of Player Feedback
Speaking of getting our thoughts in order regarding the game we’re developing, there’s one more thing I’d like to mention: we fell into a trap—either by listening too much to our fans’ feedback, or at the very least, by failing to interpret their requests correctly.
For many on the team, this was their first Early Access project, and it was undoubtedly the first time they had successfully built such an enthusiastic and loyal audience.After the announcement, everything went very smoothly, especially during our tests with external partners. As the data came in, it was easy for us to overemphasize the opinions of a few parties—simply because those opinions happened to corroborate our own position. Due to the way the information was presented, these opinions were made to seem far more significant than they actually were.
I am well aware that we are very fortunate to have the audience we have today, but this can also become a trap. If we fail to carefully balance it against the core elements of the series—and if there is no clear, unified consensus within the organization regarding those core elements—it will undermine the quality of the game and lead to a significant diversion of resources.
Therefore, while fans and their feedback are crucial to success—and even more so for us—we also recognize that it is essential to evaluate that feedback daily against our core principles.
Game testers told us that they were confused at the time and had absolutely no idea what to do. The instinctive reaction to this would have been to design features like a quest log and flood the game world with all kinds of on-screen prompts, but we knew that this simply wasn’t the right solution for *Subnautica*.
"Deep Sea Adventure 1" is a game that achieved tremendous success with almost no guidance—or rather, with just the right amount of guidance. The developers allowed players to progress through the game in any order they chose, and all of this was deliberately designed.We have never wavered in our creative direction; we want to respect players’ existing understanding while driving the project forward—but we view this as a gradual, measured process.
My take on this is that sometimes you just have to throw players right into the game and challenge them in a way they might initially resist.Think about it: in user research for early-stage games, you’ve surely heard people say these games are too hard and suggest lowering the difficulty or providing more feedback. But I think if we actually made those changes, the game would completely lose its way.Similarly, when we receive this kind of feedback, we must listen to what’s being said and understand that it’s perfectly normal for people to feel frustrated and experience failure within reasonable limits.
This doesn’t mean we completely ignore fan feedback. The key is to fully understand the core of this IP series and distinguish between which elements can be flexibly adjusted to suit the current era and which must be strictly preserved to ensure that the core, distinctive experience remains intact.
So *Deep Sea* made us aware of this shift, and the process of refining *Deep Sea* helped us clarify the essence of the core experience.Playing *Subnautica* and speaking with the project’s veteran developers helped us refocus our direction : we needed to provide players with some guidance while also allowing them to explore and discover content on their own. Throughout the Early Access phase, this balancing act remained constant: our game does not feature a quest log; we’re willing to let you feel temporarily lost, all to give you the freedom to explore on your own terms.
07
A Decent Sequel
So, what makes a sequel worthy of the name? As we get closer to the original release date and refocus on staying true to the core experience of the original *Subnautica*, we’ve realized that the actual requirements for a “major upgrade” are far simpler than we had anticipated.
So for us, the heart of this new game is a brand-new world that players love—the world of *Subnautica 1*, which we love very much ourselves. But to truly make them feel right at home again—we know this is the experience players want from a sequel—we also want them to experience a whole new *Subnautica*.
Unlike some survival games, *Subnautica 2* is a fully finished game that you can complete and see the credits for.We had to focus on crafting a spectacular new story, and I believe our narrative team truly helped us achieve that. This new, self-contained storyline gives *Subnautica* a core identity all its own.
The last one is multiplayer mode, which used to be our most controversial feature. This is because, in the public’s perception, *Subnautica* is a game that emphasizes solitary immersion, yet after introducing the optional multiplayer mode, it actually became one of our standout features.We knew full well that this feature had to be optional, but we also understood at the time that this brand-new feature was crucial for us in making the game feel like a complete and fresh experience.
When it comes to optimization, there are of course visual improvements as well—after all, *Subnautica* was already a visually stunning game to begin with. I still think it looks great, but I recall that the game’s earliest Early Access version was released back in 2014. So, it’s starting to show its age.And I think the final result in *Subnautica 2* is truly stunning. So we know that simply having our existing art team create an entirely new world in *Subnautica 2* will already deliver a significant improvement in the overall experience.
It’s really been ten years since *Subnautica* was released. The gaming industry has changed, and there are now many similar games on the market; playing these titles can provide us with a wealth of insights and inspiration. And that is how the cycle of life in sequel development continues.
I believe another feature that was improved—and has now become a cornerstone of *Deep Sea*—is our base-building system. I still consider this to be the game’s most standout core feature, representing a significant, all-around upgrade compared to previous versions.This is crucial for us because, although many players are drawn to the game’s survival mechanics, a significant portion of our audience plays exclusively in Creative Mode—which came as a surprise to me when I saw the data. This is a classic example of a game system where:We began by conducting in-depth research into the immersive experience of our core players, then explored clever optimization strategies to enhance it. This is also an excellent example of how, in our game design, we prioritize the player experience over realism. We’ve always understood that, for this series, prioritizing fun over realism is the best choice.
Conclusion
Although we’ve said a lot, I believe the most profound lesson here is actually quite simple. We started with the “one-third” principle: one-third reused existing content, one-third was proven content, and one-third was brand-new content. I still strongly believe in this model to this day.During the development of this game, we mistakenly believed we already had a clear understanding of the logical sequence and had reached a consensus on it, but instead, we immediately poured all our energy into creating brand-new content—at the time, there was an excessive emphasis on differentiation, treating it as the core defining feature of our sequel, while overlooking the fact that content familiar to the audience is the foundation.
By “optimization,” we mean enhancing the user experience while preserving designs that allow players to truly feel as though they are making difficult and unique discoveries.By “all-new,” we mean replacing core elements such as the game world and storyline, rather than requiring our game’s underlying architecture to support entirely different game mechanics like ecosystems or permanent systems. For us, sometimes the clearest source of inspiration is simply going back to play those old games and figuring out why those design decisions worked in the first place.So, if there’s one thing I hope you’ll take away from our experience, it’s this: before you start thinking about what new content a sequel needs, first figure out what content you can do without.

In May of this year, the development team behind *Deep Sea Adventure 2* tackled a rather challenging question: With the original game having sold over 10 million copies worldwide, how could a sequel achieve that level of success again?

Their results included a satisfaction rate of over 90 percent, first-day sales exceeding one million, and first-week sales surpassing four million. But behind these achievements lay far more uncertainty and trial and error than the outside world could have imagined.

Established IPs naturally attract more attention early on, but they also come with more complex expectations from players: they must retain the essence of the original while introducing enough new content, all while ensuring quality and commercial success.During this year’s Gamescom, Anthony Gallegos, Creative Director of *Subnautica 2*, reflected on a set of “sequel principles” the team had developed for the follow-up during a developer panel: what must be carried over, what is worth improving, and where to focus their limited innovation.

This line of reasoning is actually more broadly applicable than simply “how to make a sequel.” As Anthony pointed out, in a sense, all game developers are creating “sequels.” Even original works inherit mechanics and draw inspiration from similar titles, then evolve through new designs.Titles he has worked on—such as *Diablo*, *Torchlight*, and *Marvel Heroes*—are prime examples: though they all fall under the loot-based RPG genre, each has its own distinct characteristics, and all draw on the legacy of predecessors like *Diablo II*.

Therefore, this post-mortem discussion of *Subnautica 2* actually addresses a more general issue in game development: when creators build upon proven, successful practices within a genre, what should they keep, and what should they change?

The following is a transcript of the presentation, which has been edited and organized.

01

Before *Subnautica*

Today, I’d like to talk to you all about game sequels. This is something I’ve devoted a significant amount of effort to exploring throughout my career.I believe that, in many ways, we’re all developers working on sequels. All the games we’re currently developing are, to some extent, sequels. While intellectual property may be defined differently, as developers and enthusiasts, we’re constantly learning, practicing, drawing inspiration, and iterating on our ideas based on the content we encounter.

I tend to refer to these types of games as “cousin games.” They aren’t sequels, but if you pay close attention, you can clearly see their influence. Some might call them “spiritual sequels.”I mention this because these games are closely tied to my career. You can even see that this influence extends not only to directly related titles I’ve worked on, such as *Torchlight* and *Diablo*, but also to development teams behind games like *Path of Exile*, which have been deeply influenced by them.

For example, I once worked on the game *Marvel Heroes*; unfortunately, almost no one played it, but it was actually really great—and it was an original creation.Although this game was a brand-new title, in many ways it could be considered a true sequel to *Diablo II*, featuring all the classic action-RPG mechanics of Blizzard’s renowned IP. This is actually not surprising, as roughly half of the Blizzard team was involved in the project as core members at the time.

So someone like David Brevik—who was the lead designer and creator of *Diablo*, as well as the head of that team—basically copied all of his health bars, skill bars, and other such designs directly from *Diablo*. And that was exactly the task we were given: to create a Marvel version of *Diablo*.

But over time, the game changed completely. It’s a service-based game that has been running for several years. And in fact, as a younger generation of developers began taking on more leadership roles, we all started adjusting the game’s direction to appeal to a broader audience.

Throughout this process, we drew heavily on the gameplay mechanics of *Diablo III*. So, as you can see, the interface on the left actually resembles the skill tree design from *Diablo II*. Later, as the veteran *Diablo II* player base gradually dwindled, we set out to adjust the game to appeal to a broader audience.We drew inspiration directly from *Diablo III*. I bring this up because I don’t feel the slightest bit embarrassed about it—it’s only natural to draw inspiration and ideas from other games, and I still do that to this day. The same goes for *Subnautica*.

02

Distinguishing Between Sequels and Spin-offs

"Deep Sea Adventure 2: Alien Waters" is an underwater survival adventure game set on a brand-new alien world. In this game, players can build their own bases, craft various tools, adapt to the environment, and survive underwater.People often refer to it as a survival game, but internally, we tend to position it more as an exploration game that just happens to include some survival elements. Today, I’d like to talk to you all about topics related to the sequel.

I believe that the best designers, artists, and programmers all draw inspiration from the things they see in everyday life—especially from various games—and then adapt and apply that inspiration to meet their own needs. This is exactly how sequel development works in practice; it’s just that, in the case of a direct sequel, there are a few additional steps involved.

So what exactly counts as a sequel? At least when it comes to reaching a consensus, defining what is and isn’t a sequel is no easy task.Does a game automatically qualify as a sequel simply because it’s listed as a sequentially numbered entry in a series? Take *Subnautica: Below Zero*, for example—even though there are some negative reviews of it online, I still think it’s a great game.Moreover, it meets many of the criteria I believe most of us would agree a sequel should have. As a brand-new entry in the franchise, it features a completely new story setting, including new environments, unlockable content, and gameplay systems.

That said, as far as we’re concerned, we’ve never regarded *Subnautica: Below Zero* as a sequel. This is because it was originally just an expansion for *Subnautica*—a standalone spin-off—and was never intended to be a standalone product from the start.Moreover, I think the main reason is that, although it qualifies as a full-fledged game in its own right, most of its setting, narrative framework, and game engine are derived from other works. Therefore, ultimately, this game should be viewed as a spin-off of the original *Subnautica* rather than a direct sequel.

I think many players would agree with this view, because *Below Zero* isn’t any larger in scale than its predecessor, nor does it offer players a brand-new world to explore. It introduces players to a brand-new, original area on the planet, but fundamentally, it bears far too many similarities to the original game.

I have to admit that even when we were first conceptualizing what is now *Subnautica 2*, we had heated debates over whether the game should be called *Subnautica 2* or *Subnautica 3*—and at the time, I personally referred to it as *Subnautica 3*.If you search online, you’ll find that players are clearly discussing *Subnautica 3* rather than *Subnautica 2*. But in the end, the publisher decided to title this game *Subnautica 2*, while *Below Zero* was designated as a spin-off.

We sat down and carefully sorted through our ideas, clarifying the core elements of both the sequel and the spin-off. This discussion was very productive, and I believe it also highlights the general risks we currently face.

We own this IP, so technically speaking, we could create almost any kind of content and call it *Subnautica*; but after *Below Zero*, what players were really hoping for wasn’t another spin-off or a smaller-scale game—they were waiting for a return to the main storyline.And we needed to figure out what this “return” actually meant—both for us and for them.

03

The “One-Third Rule” and “Sequel Syndrome”

So, we’ve derived a formula to help us determine the composition of *Subnautica 2*’s content. We call it the “one-third” rule.

One-third of the content in *Subnautica 2* will remain unchanged, so players should clearly recognize the influence of the original game and feel a sense of familiarity, as if coming home;Another third of *Deep Sea Adventure*’s content will be optimized—a comprehensive overhaul of both mechanics and visuals that will give the game a feel more in line with modern standards; at the same time, one-third of the content will be entirely new, and this is precisely the aspect we’ve found most challenging to manage.

To put it simply, this principle doesn’t actually involve any math at all. It’s just a solid framework—especially for us—but I can’t say with absolute certainty that if we follow this plan, the game we end up with will definitely be a good fit for the *Deep Sea* series.It’s really just a practical model we’ve discovered that helps us evaluate the game at various fixed points to ensure it has the feel of a sequel, without getting bogged down in whether we’ve strictly achieved a larger scale or more innovative content. That’s it.

We believe this is the foundation upon which *Subnautica* was built, and its core lies in determining which aspects of the game to focus on refining, as well as identifying which of these three major areas still poses a significant challenge.

We came up with this three-part framework almost immediately. Using this framework, we’ve identified the core elements of the *Deep Sea Adventure* series, including gameplay on the water, item crafting, and base building, as well as core survival mechanics such as food, water, and oxygen, and a complete, playthroughable storyline.

Right from the start, we asked ourselves what we expected from this sequel and how it would fit into the structure of these three parts. However, I think this may have been a rather significant mistake, because as a result, the team later fell victim to what I call “sequel syndrome.”

I believe “sequel syndrome” is a problem where conflicting interests pull the game in too many different directions. This can make it really hard to stay the course. Sequel syndrome stems from three competing demands: creating something different, making it bigger, while still maintaining a sense of familiarity.This often leads teams to place extra emphasis on certain aspects while paying less attention to others.

We used to hang out on Discord a lot, and people would ask, “Will Peeping Fish be coming back? Will Death Leviathan be coming back?” And we always have to keep in mind that players want to see that classic content—we even seriously considered resetting the game’s setting to the same planet;We also realize that some of our initial ideas for the new game might have been too outlandish, and fans would likely have had a hard time accepting them. This alone took up a significant amount of the team’s energy.

Leviathan, the Grim Reaper

While we were in the early stages of developing this game, we were also learning the Unreal Engine. All previous games in the *Deep Sea* series were developed using the Unity engine.Since we had to learn Unreal Engine while also moving the project forward, the team members familiar with your Coral environment provided a solid option for the team—a space where everyone could develop the project and practice their Unreal Engine skills.

Every time we make a sequel, there are always people who ask us to make the world even bigger. We all know that the scale of the game needs to expand further, but at the time, we hadn’t really figured out what that actually meant.Of course, it’s easy to narrowly interpret “bigger” as playtime corresponding to map size—we even considered reimagining the series as a live-service game.This was a direction we explored early in the project—not to turn it into a service-based game, but to find a gameplay framework that would allow *Subnautica* to function as an endlessly playable game, without even needing a complete story-driven campaign.

On top of that, there’s a drive to make disruptive changes—a force that often comes from team members who have long been responsible for developing the series and have grown weary of it.By the time we were creating *Subnautica: Below Zero*, this group had been in the industry for nearly twelve years, and this time we had complete freedom to use any aspect of the IP we wanted, without having to worry about any parts we didn’t need.If we’d wanted to, we could have even scrapped all story-related content entirely. There were absolutely no rules at the time, since we were the only stakeholders—which allowed us to pivot in a new direction very early on.You can see the freedom to experiment with the IP in these early concepts—flying vehicles, ground bases, and more land-based areas. Some of these elements were already introduced in *Below Zero* and did indeed receive quite harsh criticism; all of them strayed significantly from the core premise of the original *Deep Sea* game.

We initially came up with an idea that really got us excited.We threw ourselves into it with everything we had. It was as if the entire team was diving headfirst into the project. At first, we wondered how this would shape the game’s direction, but we eventually realized it simply wouldn’t work—or that it would completely derail the core experience the game was meant to deliver.I think this situation could have been avoided. We really should have spent more time delving into the game’s core essence—starting with identifying that common core element I mentioned earlier. But trying out these new ideas was just so exciting. Plus, we were still a new team that was just finding our footing.

04

Exploration and Trade-offs

Next, I’d like to take a look back at some of the early prototypes we created while exploring the “one-third new approach.” As far as I know, no one has ever seen these before. And I think it’s valuable to reflect on why we chose these approaches in the first place—and why, ultimately, they weren’t a good fit for this project.

So, let’s start with the first one—this is a project we worked on very early on that centered around ecosystems. We explored the following concept: building and maintaining a fully simulated real-world ecosystem within the game, where players would manage various animal and plant populations.In this scenario, you can see a kelp forest. Once the kelp matures, it releases seeds, which then grow into more kelp forests. At the same time, there are sea urchins in the world that actively search for edible mature and juvenile kelp, and subsequently reproduce to produce more offspring.Subsequently, as sea urchins and kelp compete with one another for survival, the entire system enters a state of equilibrium. We later developed several versions of this project and even introduced predator characters specifically to control the populations of species that were growing too large. We all found the scene before us truly breathtaking and deeply inspiring.

In the early prototype versions, we realized we didn’t want to make a simulation game; instead, we wanted players to truly understand what was going on while playing. The only way to achieve this was to overlay numerous UI layers and use progress bars and charts to visually present the relevant information.We eventually clarified our direction: we wanted to create a game centered on repairing, healing, or harmonizing the environment—one that would allow players to genuinely feel that the world undergoes tangible changes as a result of their healing actions.

You can see this in the way the damaged roots in the world function: healing these roots will bring new life to the area.

I also think this prototype was very helpful in steering us toward simplifying our new product concept. It was truly a groundbreaking breakthrough for the series; although the prototype’s appearance was rather unremarkable, we had originally thought it would be a natural addition to the product line, but in the end, it didn’t quite come to fruition.

We also have another early prototype centered around the concept of “Void Expedition.” So this is the core idea behind cooperative gameplay set in the Void—something we hadn’t fully fleshed out before. We always hear fans say, “I want to go to the Void.”” In the first game, the Void was merely the edge of the world—there was nothing beyond it. To put it bluntly, it was essentially a slaughterhouse designed just for you. But they said that it was still the place they truly wanted to explore. So we took that to mean: they wanted us to fill that void and put enough content in there for them to explore.

Therefore, in these early prototype versions, we experimented with a design concept where the entire game revolved around expeditions into the Void.Someone once proposed the idea that it would be like a game you could play forever. So we began to wonder: Could players simply keep traveling to the Void to explore, return to base to rest and recuperate, then set off again on a new journey into the Void, only to return to base once more? But in the end, we concluded that this actually didn’t align with our core game vision.The Void and these expeditions might have their own merits, but we had strayed too far from our core focus. I think it’s a fantastic idea, but it’s simply not the foundation of the *Subnautica* series.

In some of our early exploratory work, we used a submersible like this—I think you may have seen it not long ago—but it couldn’t move.Speaking of this vehicle, the truth is that at the time, we hadn’t yet figured out how to create submarines that could move in coordination with players. In multiplayer mode, it’s quite challenging to synchronize a submarine’s movement with the players on board without letting them get separated or lose track of each other.What we actually did was have players pilot the submarine on a 2D map; when the submarine reached a designated position on that map, the system would load the corresponding area beneath it. And when you wanted to explore a brand-new area within a predefined part of the world, all players would then enter that map.Honestly, you might even catch me briefly lying in wait to ambush someone.

What really resonated with me in this presentation was that we’re exploring the core essence of *Subnautica* through a process of elimination.We established the foundational framework for the survival experience and then began prototyping new content—just like the journeys you’ve seen. Once we mapped out the various impacts this issue had across the entire game, it actually helped us further clarify our core direction and determine which elements absolutely had to remain unchanged.

I still feel that I’d rather spend a little more time first figuring out the right direction based on the core elements, and then supplementing that with new content. But this has definitely been a great way for our team to learn the Unreal Engine and stay passionate about making games together.We’ve invested a tremendous amount of time in prototyping and experimentation. I don’t think it’s been a waste of time. That’s how we developed new systems for the game adaptation, such as the creature mod, as well as many other features that were ultimately incorporated into the final game.

But ultimately, as we explored new content, we came to realize that many ideas that initially seemed highly disruptive were actually unnecessary distractions that would divert us from the core mission of creating a true sequel to *Subnautica*.And as we finalized many of these features one by one, a concern began to loom large: our final product would end up being too similar to what the fans had already created.

At the time, this was the most ordinary thing in the world. I would talk it over with Charlie, the studio’s creative director at the time, and he always said he felt this direction was too similar to our existing work—that players definitely wouldn’t buy into it because the end result would be virtually indistinguishable from our previous game. That brings me to the topic I’m about to discuss:how to strike just the right balance—at least that’s how we approached it back then—and our benchmark was none other than *Subnautica 1*; it served as our guiding light.

05

Focus on the previous installment; return to the main storyline

Ultimately, after creating multiple prototypes and experimenting with various radical approaches for *Subnautica 2*, we realized we needed to delve deeper into that “North Star” we’d long been familiar with.We’ve always known that our goal was to create a game that aligns much more closely with *Subnautica* than *Below Zero* does. But in our quest to explore and find that one-third of innovative content, we truly lost sight of keeping the team aligned on what we wanted to carry forward and refine.

As it turned out, this task proved far more challenging than expected. We have the most outstanding team I’ve ever worked with, but the studio’s staff composition has indeed undergone significant changes as this project has progressed.Since I joined in 2021, our team size has remained at around 40 people. By the time this game reaches 2025, I expect our team to be around 70 people. Currently, however, we’re just shy of 100 people.

These individuals have varying levels of knowledge about *Deep Sea*—ranging from veteran employees who have been involved in development since the first game to newcomers who joined the studio just two months ago.This certainly made it harder for the entire team to reach a clear consensus on the game’s foundational modules, and everyone may have taken it for granted that team members knew how to build the core gameplay experience—after all, some of them had worked on similar projects 12 years ago.So I think at the time, everyone just assumed that we didn’t need to bother with secondary experiences and should instead focus our energy on innovation.

But given that we were constantly bringing in so many new people at the time, that line of reasoning simply didn’t hold water. So, once we stopped focusing on that one-third of new content and shifted our attention back to the familiar, tried-and-true elements of the game, the entire project finally started to get back on track.

This requires us to spend a significant amount of time specifically re-examining the content we’ve released in the past. For example, what should the balance be for large gas tanks? The first thing we do is open *Subnautica* or *Below Zero* and take a close look to figure out exactly how they handled it before.You might think this is obvious, but when you’re constantly bringing in new people like this, this kind of ability needs to be gradually cultivated within the team.

And sometimes, due to improvements in industry standards and operational guidelines—the so-called “one-third improvement”—we may ultimately part ways with older versions of the game. We often find ourselves having to rediscover what exactly makes *Subnautica* so unique. However, this process is certainly not without its challenges.In a team of this size, with a mix of new and veteran members, it’s quite common for people to zone out or get lost in memories of the past. When we asked some of our long-time team members about the full range of features that were once available in *Subnautica 1*, they were all quite surprised.It’s no easy task to keep track of every single detail regarding what should and shouldn’t be included in a game. I fully understand this, especially after all these years since we first started with the original *Subnautica*.

This problem can be solved—provided, of course, that we focus solely on honing our skills with the original game and examine it exclusively from the perspective of its strengths. So we began conducting regular playtests of our previous titles, at a frequency comparable to that of our regular playtests for *Deep Sea Voyage*.

We’ve also started listening to what our veteran employees have to say and learning about the decision-making process behind various decisions, rather than focusing solely on the final outcome. Furthermore, when it comes to balancing the air tanks, they’ve often been saying the same thing for a long time. Or a designer might say, “Okay, I’m going to try this new approach on the air tanks.”But if we ask the veteran employees, they’ll tell us, “We’ve tried that approach, and it didn’t work for various reasons.” This saves us time, since they’ve already learned the hard way.Honestly, if we’d done more research back then, we could have avoided those procedural issues they’d already tried and found didn’t work. But at the time—maybe I was just being foolish—I said I understood Charlie and thought we had it figured out. But in reality, we hadn’t figured it out at all.We should have spent more time seeking advice from our more experienced colleagues.

06

Consideration of Player Feedback

Speaking of getting our thoughts in order regarding the game we’re developing, there’s one more thing I’d like to mention: we fell into a trap—either by listening too much to our fans’ feedback, or at the very least, by failing to interpret their requests correctly.

For many on the team, this was their first Early Access project, and it was undoubtedly the first time they had successfully built such an enthusiastic and loyal audience.After the announcement, everything went very smoothly, especially during our tests with external partners. As the data came in, it was easy for us to overemphasize the opinions of a few parties—simply because those opinions happened to corroborate our own position. Due to the way the information was presented, these opinions were made to seem far more significant than they actually were.

I am well aware that we are very fortunate to have the audience we have today, but this can also become a trap. If we fail to carefully balance it against the core elements of the series—and if there is no clear, unified consensus within the organization regarding those core elements—it will undermine the quality of the game and lead to a significant diversion of resources.

Therefore, while fans and their feedback are crucial to success—and even more so for us—we also recognize that it is essential to evaluate that feedback daily against our core principles.

Game testers told us that they were confused at the time and had absolutely no idea what to do. The instinctive reaction to this would have been to design features like a quest log and flood the game world with all kinds of on-screen prompts, but we knew that this simply wasn’t the right solution for *Subnautica*.

"Deep Sea Adventure 1" is a game that achieved tremendous success with almost no guidance—or rather, with just the right amount of guidance. The developers allowed players to progress through the game in any order they chose, and all of this was deliberately designed.We have never wavered in our creative direction; we want to respect players’ existing understanding while driving the project forward—but we view this as a gradual, measured process.

My take on this is that sometimes you just have to throw players right into the game and challenge them in a way they might initially resist.Think about it: in user research for early-stage games, you’ve surely heard people say these games are too hard and suggest lowering the difficulty or providing more feedback. But I think if we actually made those changes, the game would completely lose its way.Similarly, when we receive this kind of feedback, we must listen to what’s being said and understand that it’s perfectly normal for people to feel frustrated and experience failure within reasonable limits.

This doesn’t mean we completely ignore fan feedback. The key is to fully understand the core of this IP series and distinguish between which elements can be flexibly adjusted to suit the current era and which must be strictly preserved to ensure that the core, distinctive experience remains intact.

So *Deep Sea* made us aware of this shift, and the process of refining *Deep Sea* helped us clarify the essence of the core experience.Playing *Subnautica* and speaking with the project’s veteran developers helped us refocus our direction: we needed to provide players with some guidance while also allowing them to explore and discover content on their own.Throughout the Early Access phase, this balancing act remained constant: our game does not feature a quest log; we’re willing to let you feel temporarily lost, all to give you the freedom to explore on your own terms.

07

A Decent Sequel

So, what makes a sequel worthy of the name? As we get closer to the original release date and refocus on staying true to the core experience of the original *Subnautica*, we’ve realized that the actual requirements for a “major upgrade” are far simpler than we had anticipated.

So for us, the heart of this new game is a brand-new world that players love—the world of *Subnautica 1*, which we love very much ourselves. But to truly make them feel right at home again—we know this is the experience players want from a sequel—we also want them to experience a whole new *Subnautica*.

Unlike some survival games, *Subnautica 2* is a fully finished game that you can complete and see the credits for.We had to focus on crafting a spectacular new story, and I believe our narrative team truly helped us achieve that. This new, self-contained storyline gives *Subnautica* a core identity all its own.

The last one is multiplayer mode, which used to be our most controversial feature. This is because, in the public’s perception, *Subnautica* is a game that emphasizes solitary immersion, yet after introducing the optional multiplayer mode, it actually became one of our standout features.We knew full well that this feature had to be optional, but we also understood at the time that this brand-new feature was crucial for us in making the game feel like a complete and fresh experience.

When it comes to optimization, there are of course visual improvements as well—after all, *Subnautica* was already a visually stunning game to begin with. I still think it looks great, but I recall that the game’s earliest Early Access version was released back in 2014. So, it’s starting to show its age.And I think the final result in *Subnautica 2* is truly stunning. So we know that simply having our existing art team create an entirely new world in *Subnautica 2* will already deliver a significant improvement in the overall experience.

It’s really been ten years since *Subnautica* was released. The gaming industry has changed, and there are now many similar games on the market; playing these titles can provide us with a wealth of insights and inspiration. And that is how the cycle of life in sequel development continues.

I believe another feature that was improved—and has now become a cornerstone of *Deep Sea*—is our base-building system. I still consider this to be the game’s most standout core feature, representing a significant, all-around upgrade compared to previous versions.This is crucial for us because, although many players are drawn to the game’s survival mechanics, a significant portion of our audience plays exclusively in Creative Mode—which came as a surprise to me when I saw the data. This is a classic example of a game system where:We began by conducting in-depth research into the immersive experience of our core players, then explored clever optimization strategies to enhance it. This is also an excellent example of how, in our game design, we prioritize the player experience over realism. We’ve always understood that, for this series, prioritizing fun over realism is the best choice.

Conclusion

Although we’ve said a lot, I believe the most profound lesson here is actually quite simple. We started with the “one-third” principle: one-third reused existing content, one-third was proven content, and one-third was brand-new content. I still strongly believe in this model to this day.During the development of this game, we mistakenly believed we already had a clear understanding of the logical sequence and had reached a consensus on it, but instead, we immediately poured all our energy into creating brand-new content—at the time, there was an excessive emphasis on differentiation, treating it as the core defining feature of our sequel, while overlooking the fact that content familiar to the audience is the foundation.

By “optimization,” we mean enhancing the user experience while preserving designs that allow players to truly feel as though they are making difficult and unique discoveries.By “all-new,” we mean replacing core elements such as the game world and storyline, rather than requiring our game’s underlying architecture to support entirely different game mechanics like ecosystems or permanent systems. For us, sometimes the clearest source of inspiration is simply going back to play those old games and figuring out why those design decisions worked in the first place.So, if there’s one thing I hope you’ll take away from our experience, it’s this: before you start thinking about what new content a sequel needs, first figure out what content you can do without.

title: Even miHoYo has set up a branch here—can Guangzhou really live up to the hype when it comes to its anime and manga scene?
text:
About two years ago, the topic of “which city ranks second in terms of anime and manga culture” could still spark discussions with over a hundred comments across various social media platforms. Some believed Guangzhou was the second-ranked city, while others argued that Chengdu was the true runner-up; there were also those in the middle who felt that Guangzhou and Chengdu were in the same tier, neck and neck with each other.
Looking at the trend data from Xiaohongshu at the time, the "Chi Gu" trend in Guangzhou had over 55 million views, ranking second nationwide. Chengdu was hot on its heels with over 42 million views, so the outcome remained uncertain until the very end.
Two years later, I don’t think there’s much left to discuss on this topic: Guangzhou is the second-largest city.
In recent years, Guangzhou’s anime and manga content industry has experienced explosive growth on both the consumer and industrial sides, and this momentum is here to stay.
Let’s start with consumer spending. According to reports, the 11 major ACG conventions held in Guangzhou during the first half of 2025 attracted 840,000 visitors. Among them, the Firefly Comic Convention generated 170 million yuan in related spending. During this period, Guangzhou was also the top choice for Japanese voice actors’ meet-and-greets and small-scale live performances in China, with the number of events far exceeding that of other cities.When *Zero Zone* held its first FES event outside of Shanghai, it chose the Canton Fair platform—and tickets sold out in 30 seconds. I believe these figures would be difficult for any city other than Shanghai to achieve.
Now let’s look at the industry. Local companies such as Kuro, Shiyue, and Deep Blue Interactive are continuing to expand; titles like *Mingchao* and *Return to the Future: 1999* have already established their brands, and the new title *Wangyue* is poised for release.After leaving his position as the original producer of *Onmyoji*, Jin Tao founded Jiezi Games in Guangzhou and is reportedly set to receive a license from *Onmyoji* to develop a new title.
But the most crucial signal still comes from miHoYo.
In June of this year, miHoYo established a wholly-owned subsidiary, Canggang Technology, in Guangzhou—marking the first time in its 15-year history that the company has set up a domestic branch. From the "Absolute FES" event at the end of 2025 to the establishment of a physical company, the transition to taking root in Guangzhou was completed in just half a year.
As IPs created by local studios gain traction and mature, they ultimately enrich a city’s cultural atmosphere. This trajectory is similar to that of Shanghai, except this time it’s happening in Guangzhou. How do these changes feel to the people directly affected?
▍Mi Tu, the game designer who works on the second game while wearing flip-flops
I moved back to Guangzhou from Shanghai for work. To say that the climate and food were the deciding factors would be an exaggeration. But my family is here, so if I had a choice, I’d definitely choose Guangzhou—that’s why I came back as soon as I had the chance.
Before I returned to Guangzhou, I felt that second-tier game developers in Guangzhou generally exhibited a regional tendency toward user acquisition—an ecosystem that, when it comes down to it, has been shaped by its surrounding environment.
Many game developers in Guangzhou come from backgrounds in browser games, reskinned games, and user acquisition-driven products. When I have lunch with them, they talk about LTV and ARPU, and they’re always hounding me for data—they never bring up things like which character is sexier or how a particular plot should be written.
There are only a handful of companies in Guangzhou that specialize in second-tier games, and people jump back and forth between them all the time. You might even run into someone from your old company while out to dinner—sometimes it feels like a small town. If you move from Company A to Company B, there’s a good chance your former coworkers will follow you there next month. But right now, there really aren’t many options for game designers in the second-tier sector—they’re all pretty much the same.
I think the biggest difference in product philosophy between Shanghai and Guangzhou developers is that the Guangzhou side believes more in having one standout feature—as long as the core experience is amazing, that’s all that matters.Shanghai developers, on the other hand, aim for a more well-rounded approach—basically, every aspect needs to meet or exceed a certain standard. Development pace? No need to make fun of each other—it’s the same across the whole industry. Every day when we get to the office, we just hit the ground running and work our butts off.
Living in Guangzhou, much of the industry gossip and news about changing trends comes from secondhand information shared in WeChat groups. It’s not like in Shanghai, where you can hear it firsthand from friends just by going out to dinner.
But when you look at it another way, sometimes it’s actually a good thing.
Over in Shanghai, everyone’s keeping a close eye on what the others are doing, so it’s easy to fall into that “if they do it, I have to do it too” mindset; in Guangzhou, because of the physical distance, there’s a bit of a buffer in information flow, so it’s actually harder to get swept up in that. Just quietly work on your own stuff—if you pull it off, people will naturally take notice; if you don’t, well, nobody really cares, haha.
If I had to describe the experience of working in the adult entertainment industry in Guangzhou in one word, I’d say: “a traveler in flip-flops.” It’s that laid-back, carefree look—but deep down, I’m always trying to catch up with the folks in Shanghai.
▍A Night in Shuo, Where I No Longer Miss Shanghai
I used to work in the gaming industry in Shanghai, and later moved to Guangzhou through a friend's referral to work on an app at an internet company.
Shanghai gives me the impression that it forces people into a cycle of competition—a kind of self-driven internal competition—where anyone who can keep going is considered a workhorse; it has a culture that favors the "mainline" faction.
Overall, the work environment in Guangzhou is fairly relaxed, and managers often talk about “getting off work early.” The company doesn’t force employees to work overtime, but when things get busy, you have to put in the extra hours. I feel that the focus here is on actual work output, and there’s a strong aversion to meaningless overtime. Competition is still fierce, so you need to be competent and adapt to your department’s pace; communication is key.
Actually, at the few companies I’ve worked for in Shanghai, there were very few anime fans—sometimes I was the only one in my team. But at this current company, I’ve already spotted five anime fans, and one colleague even has a lenticular photo album of nude characters from *Love and Deep Space* displayed at their desk.The anime and manga scene in Guangzhou is really great, and there’s a high chance of running into fellow anime and manga fans.
Of course, Shanghai is still way ahead when it comes to live performances, comic conventions, and the like; Shanghai is still the undisputed leader—purchasing power determines strength.
Guangzhou's anime and gaming industry still lags significantly behind Shanghai's, and its products aren't as well-known as those in Shanghai. I don't think Mihoyo's Guangzhou branch will go so far as to poach professionals from Shanghai; it would be good enough if they could just recruit local talent.
Furthermore, a high proportion of user acquisition companies are based in Guangzhou, with firms like 37 Games and Tanwan being the major players. So I think Mihoyo’s move to Guangzhou is more about expanding its footprint and addressing the issue that anime-style content was previously limited to Shanghai. After all, the underlying logic still follows the flow of talent, and the local ecosystem remains very important.
But Guangzhou has way more delicious food than Shanghai. Shanghai has everything, but nothing’s authentic. It’s different with the locals here—they’ve preserved the Guangdong flavor better, and everyone’s pretty particular about food.I’m really craving those traditional Cantonese sweet soups and dim sum—Cantonese people can enjoy them from morning till night, which is just so awesome. The first time I tried dim sum, I was blown away by the extensive menu; I wanted to try everything, so I had to ask a local to pick for me.
So if I ever have the chance to return to the gaming industry, I’d definitely choose Guangzhou—there’s just so much food there, I couldn’t possibly eat it all.
▍Duke’s “Special Forces-Style” Exploration of Guangzhou’s Anime and Manga Scene
This New Year’s Day marked my second trip to Guangzhou, and I went mainly to check out the fireflies.I’d heard for a while that Guangzhou has a strong anime and manga culture, so I took this opportunity to really soak it up for a few days. How can I put it? Before I went, I thought I’d see traces of it everywhere, but as I explored, I realized it’s not actually that obvious outside of convention periods—you really need a local to show you the ropes.
Guangzhou’s anime and manga hotspots are mainly concentrated in three areas, and coincidentally, they’re all underground malls—Anime Star City is considered a “traditional” veteran. Diwang Plaza is a hub for otaku dance; people often gather in the open space on the third basement level to dance there. There’s also Fashion Tianhe, where it’s easy to get lost, but it’s also home to quite a few great shops.
On New Year’s Day, the Yuefa Live event also featured a performance by Diou. Although there weren’t many people in the audience, the atmosphere was electric. The fans in the crowd were absolutely on fire. At the end of the show, the idols stepped off the stage, and everyone formed a circle around them, singing and dancing together—the sense of participation was off the charts.
Diou Live
At this year’s New Year’s Day Firefly event, I got the impression that the proportion of cosplayers was significantly higher than at BW.While BW is already a large-scale, comprehensive digital culture and entertainment expo, Firefly feels more like an offline meetup for the anime and manga community. Firefly had plenty of empty booths, but there were still enough people to fill them all—it was incredibly crowded. There’s also a unique outdoor photography culture found nowhere else in the country, with cosplayers and photographers alike gathering outside the venue.
Speaking of the business side of things, I’ve noticed something. Guangzhou’s food is truly tempting, but the climate is a real turn-off. Among the friends I’ve spoken with from the north, quite a few feel that the southernmost they could handle is the Shanghai-Hangzhou area.
For most senior and expert-level positions, it would likely be difficult to accept a relocation from Shanghai to Guangzhou.Kulo even went out of its way to open a Shanghai branch, which continues to grow. So, you’re asking whether companies like Mi Home and Kulo, by establishing branches in Guangzhou, might end up poaching talent from Shanghai? I think, aside from entry-level operational roles where they might be able to pick up some talent, there’s currently no trend of core talent flowing south.
A Night at the Firefly Outdoor Venue
▍Sitting Back and Watching as Companies in Shanghai and Guangzhou Poach Talent from Each Other—Shi Yu
I'm from Guangzhou and grew up there. Later, I moved to Shanghai to work in the secondary game development industry, where I helped build projects from the ground up.
Coming to work in Shanghai actually had little to do with salary and benefits. At the time, the project was just getting started, and opportunities to build a new game from scratch are rare. I also really liked the concept behind our project, so I came without hesitation. After moving to Shanghai, I discovered how convenient it was to travel to Japan to see performances—I could easily make a round trip over the weekend.
I’ve always felt that Guangzhou has a pretty strong anime and manga scene. I started going to comic conventions back in middle school, and the Firefly Comic Convention was already around back then.Back then, the Firefly Convention was mostly made up of individual vendor booths selling merchandise that was either homemade or of unknown origin, and there weren’t any large exhibition booths. As the gaming industry has grown, the Firefly Convention has expanded significantly; more and more game companies are participating, and both its scale and professionalism have improved.
(The first time my phone was stolen was on Firefly.)
I’ve been visiting Anime Star City since middle school, through high school and college, and I still go there often even now that I’m working. The atmosphere has become even more vibrant over the years. In addition to Anime Star City, there are now quite a few fan communities and streets dedicated to anime and manga, and I make a point of checking them out whenever I go home for the holidays.
In the past, everyone thought Guangzhou didn’t have much of a secondary game industry. A few years ago, *War Dual* was pretty much the only game in town, but later *1999* also gained traction, and more and more small and medium-sized studios have been popping up and gradually growing.
Mihoyo is setting up a branch office in Guangzhou, which should attract some professionals from Shanghai to work there. However, Kuro also has a branch office in Shanghai; they started by hiring technical staff, and now they also have positions in publishing and operations. I think the two companies will poach talent from each other.
The gaming industry is a small community, and talent flows freely between companies. When Shanghai-based companies come to Guangzhou, they’re looking to recruit local talent at a lower cost; when Guangzhou-based companies go to Shanghai, they’re poaching highly skilled professionals. In short, both are promoting the flow of talent.
Guangzhou really does offer a lot of opportunities right now, and the cost of living is significantly lower than in Shanghai. If the salary is competitive, and considering my family situation, moving back to Guangzhou would be a good fit for me.
So, what should we eat today?
After a round of conversation, several interviewees all independently came back to the topic of “food.”Although Guangzhou’s anime and manga industry is still catching up, it’s the sweet soups, slow-simmered soups, and dim sum that truly keep people here. Let’s set work aside for a moment—after all, food is the foundation of life, and even those in the anime and manga world need to eat!

title: 米哈遊まで支社を設立するほど、広州のオタク文化の濃度はかなり高いと言えるだろうか？
text:
およそ2年前、「二次元『濃度が2番目に高い都市』」という話題は、各SNSプラットフォームで100件以上のコメントが寄せられるほど盛り上がった。広州が2番目だと考える人もいれば、成都こそが2番目だと主張する人もいた。また、中立的な立場の人々は、広州と成都は同等のレベルにあり、互角だと考えていた。
当時「小紅書」のトピックデータを見ると、広州の「吃谷」トピックは5500万回以上の閲覧数を記録し、全国で2位だった。成都も4200万回以上と迫っており、勝敗の行方は最後まで予断を許さなかった。
2年が経った今、この話題についてこれ以上議論する余地はないと思う。第2の都市といえば、やはり広州だ。
ここ数年、広州の二次元コンテンツ産業は、消費面と産業面の両方で急成長を遂げており、この勢いはもはや無視できないものとなっている。
まず消費面を見てみましょう。報道によると、2025年上半期に広州で開催された11回の大型ACGイベントには、延べ84万人が来場しました。そのうち、「蛍」コミックフェアは1億7000万元の関連消費を牽引しました。この期間、広州は日本の声優のファンミーティングや小規模ライブが中国で開催される際の第一の選択肢となっており、その開催回数は他の地域をはるかに上回っています。『絶区ゼロ』が上海を離れて初めてFESを開催した際、選んだのは広州交易会のプラットフォームであり、チケットは30秒で完売した。こうした数字は、上海以外の都市では達成が難しいだろう。
次に業界の状況を見てみよう。「クロ」、「詩悦」、「深藍互動」といった現地企業が拡大を続けており、『鳴潮』や『重返未来：1999』はすでにブランドを確立し、新作『望月』もリリースに向けて準備を進めている。『陰陽師』の元プロデューサーである金韜氏は退社後、広州で芥子ゲームを設立し、『陰陽師』のライセンスを取得して新作を開発していると伝えられている。
しかし、最も重要な兆候はやはりミホヨだ。
今年6月、米哈遊は広州に完全子会社である蒼剛科技を設立した。これは同社が設立されてから15年間で、初めて国内に支社を設立したことになる。2025年末の「絶FES」から実体のある企業の設立に至るまで、わずか半年で広州に根を下ろすという変貌を遂げた。
地元企業が生み出したIPが成長し、広がっていくにつれて、最終的にはその都市の文化的雰囲気を豊かにすることになる。この流れは上海と似ているが、今回は広州で起きている。こうした変化が、具体的な人々にとってどのような実感をもたらすのだろうか。
▍スリッパを履いてセカンドツアーを企画するミートゥ
私は上海から広州に戻って働いています。気候や食べ物について、それが決定的な要因だと言うのは大げさすぎます。でも、私の実家はここにあるので、もし選べるなら間違いなく広州を選びます。だから、機会があればすぐに戻ってきます。
広州に戻る前、広州のゲーム開発会社の多くには、ユーザー獲得に重点を置くという地域特有の傾向があると感じた。このエコシステムは、結局のところ周囲の環境によって形作られているのだ。
広州のゲーム開発者の多くは、ブラウザゲームやスキン変更ゲーム、ユーザー獲得に注力したゲームの分野から転身してきた人たちだ。彼らと食事をする際、話題はLTVやARPUに集中し、ひたすらデータについて質問してくる。どのキャラクターがセクシーか、このストーリーをどう書くべきかといった話は決して出てこない。
広州でセカンドティアゲームを手がける企業はほんの一握りしかなく、社員はあちこちと移り変わっている。食事に出かけても元職場の同僚にばったり会うことがあり、まるで田舎の村のようだ。A社からB社に移ると、以前の同僚が来月には移ってくることだってあり得る。とはいえ、今のセカンドティアゲームのプランナーには、正直なところ行く先もあまりなく、どこの会社も大差ないのだろう。
上海のメーカーと広州のメーカーの製品開発における考え方の最大の違いは、広州の方が「一芸に秀でる」ことを重視し、中核となる体験が素晴らしければそれでいいと考えている点だと思います。上海のメーカーはより包括性を重視しており、基本的にどの分野でも一定の水準以上を達成することを求めています。開発のペース？兄弟同士で冗談を言い合うようなもので、二次元の世界も皆同じです。毎日会社に来ると、勢いよく仕事に取り組みます（必死に働く）。
広州にいると、さまざまな業界の噂やトレンドの変化は、ほとんどがWeChatのグループチャットで耳にする二次情報だ。上海のように、外食すれば友人から直接話を聞くことができるのとは違って。
しかし、逆に考えれば、時には良いこともある。
上海の方では、皆が相手の動向を注視しているため、「相手がやったから自分もやらなきゃ」という焦りに陥りやすい。一方、広州は物理的に距離があるため、情報の伝達にタイムラグがあり、かえってその流れに巻き込まれにくい。静かに自分の仕事をしていれば、成果が出れば自然と皆の目に留まるし、出なくても誰も気にしない、ハハ。
広州で「二遊」をしている感覚を一言で表すなら、私は「サンダルを履いて急ぐ人」と言うだろう。見た目はだらりと、とてものんびりとした様子だが、心の中ではずっと上海の連中に追いつきたいと願っているのだ。
▍上海を懐かしむ朔夜
以前は上海でゲーム開発をしていましたが、その後、友人の紹介で広州に移り、あるインターネット企業でアプリの制作に携わっています。
上海という街は、人々に過度な競争を強いるような印象を受けます。自発的な「内巻き」が蔓延しており、息をしているだけで働き蜂のように扱われる、いわば「正統派」の文化が色濃く根付いているようです。
広州の職場環境は全体的に比較的ゆったりとしており、上司はよく「早めに退社しよう」と口にしています。会社側は残業を強制しませんが、忙しい時は当然残業も必要です。ここでは実際の業務成果が重視されており、無意味な残業は好まれないと感じます。競争は依然として激しく、十分な能力を持ち、部署のリズムに適応する必要があります。コミュニケーションも非常に重要です。
実は、私が上海で勤めていたいくつかの会社では、オタク系の人がほとんどおらず、時にはチームで私だけがオタクだったこともあります。ところが今の会社では、すでに5人のオタクを見つけました。中には、『恋と深空』のヌードのラスターアルバムを自分のデスクに飾っている同僚さえいます。広州の二次元文化の雰囲気は本当に良く、二次元好きの同僚に出会える可能性もかなり高いですね。
もちろん、上海はライブやコミックイベントなどの面では依然として他を圧倒しており、上海の威信は依然として絶大だ。購買力が実力を決定づけるのだ。
広州の二次元ゲーム産業は、上海に比べて依然として少なからぬ差があり、製品の知名度も上海に後れを取っている。miHoYoの広州支社が、逆に上海の業界関係者を引き抜くとは考えにくく、地元の人材を発掘できればそれで十分だろう。
さらに、広州にはユーザー獲得を専門とする企業が非常に多く、三七や貪玩といった企業が主流のプレイヤーとなっています。ですから、miHoYoが広州に進出したのは、事業領域を拡大し、「二次元コンテンツは上海でしか作れない」という課題を解決するためだと私は考えています。結局のところ、根本的な論理としては人材の流動に従わなければならず、地元のエコシステムは依然として非常に重要だからです。
ただ、広州の方が上海よりも美味しいものがずっと多い。上海には何でも揃っているけど、どれも本場の味じゃない。広州の人たちは違う。広州の味はよりよく守られていて、みんな食べ物にはかなりこだわりがあるんだ。私は広東式の甘いスープや、朝茶が本当に大好きだ。広東の人たちは朝から晩まで朝茶を楽しんでいる。本当に最高だ。初めて朝茶を食べた時、その豊富なメニューに驚かされた。何でも食べたくなってしまい、結局広東の人に選んでもらうしかなかった。
だから、もしまたゲーム業界に戻る機会があれば、間違いなく広州を選びます。食べ物が本当に多すぎて、食べきれないほどですから。
▍特殊部隊スタイルで広州のオタク文化を調査するDuke
今年の元旦、私は2度目の広州を訪れました。主な目的はホタルを見ることでした。以前から広州はオタク文化が盛んだと聞いていたので、今回はついでに数日間じっくりと体験してきました。どう言えばいいでしょうか、行く前は至る所にオタク文化の痕跡が見られると思っていたのですが、実際に歩いてみると、イベント期間以外はそれほど目立たず、地元の人に案内してもらわないとその醍醐味は味わえないことが分かりました。
広州のオタク文化の集積地は主に3か所に集中しており、偶然にもそのすべてが地下広場だ。その中でも「アニメスターシティ」は「伝統的な」老舗と言える。一方、「地王広場」はオタクダンスの拠点となっており、地下3階の広々としたスペースでは、よくオタクダンスが踊られている。もう一つは「ファッション天河」で、迷いやすいが、隠れた名店も数多くある。
元旦の日、粤発ライブではローカルアイドルのパフォーマンスも行われました。会場の観客数はそれほど多くはありませんでしたが、雰囲気は最高でした。会場のファンたちは皆、熱狂の極みでした。パフォーマンスの終盤、アイドルたちがステージを降りると、みんなが輪になって彼女たちを取り囲み、一緒に歌って踊りました。その一体感はまさに爆発的でした。
地偶Live
今年の元旦の「ホタル」では、BWに比べてコスプレイヤーの割合がはるかに高いという印象を受けました。BWはすでに総合的な大規模デジタル文化エンターテインメントイベントとなっているが、ホタルはむしろ二次元のオフライン交流会のような雰囲気だ。ホタルには空きブースが大量にあるにもかかわらず、人で埋め尽くされるほど混雑していた。また、全国でもここだけの屋外撮影文化があり、コスプレイヤーやコスプレイヤーを撮影したい人たちが会場の外にひしめき合っていた。
産業の面について言えば、私なりに気づいたことがあります。広州の食事は本当に魅力的ですが、気候は正直言って敬遠したくなるほどです。私が話を聞いた北方の友人たちのうち、かなりの人が、自分にとって受け入れられる最南端は上海・杭州一帯までだと感じているようです。
ベテランやエキスパートクラスのポジションの場合、上海から広州へ転勤することを受け入れるのは、大半にとってかなり難しいはずだ。クロもわざわざ上海支社を設立し、しかもその規模は拡大し続けている。だから、米家やクロといった企業が広州に支社を設立すれば、逆に上海の人材を引き抜くことになるのではないか、という指摘がある。しかし、基本的な実務職なら多少は確保できるかもしれないが、中核となる人材が南へ流出する傾向は、現時点ではまだ見られないと思う。
ホタルのいる野外での夜
▍上海と広州のメーカーが互いに人材を引き抜く様子を傍観する時雨
私は広州出身で、幼い頃から広州で育ちました。その後、上海へ移り、セカンダリーゲーム開発に携わり、プロジェクトに参画してゼロから始めました。
上海で働くことになったのは、実は給与や待遇とはあまり関係がありませんでした。当時、このプロジェクトは始まったばかりで、ゼロから新しいゲームを作る機会はそう多くありませんでしたし、私自身もこのプロジェクトのコンセプトに惹かれたので、迷わずここに来ることにしました。上海に来てから、日本での公演を観に行くのがとても便利だと気づきました。週末にさっと行けば、日帰りで往復できるほどです。
広州の「二次元」の雰囲気は、昔からかなり濃厚だと感じています。私は中学生の頃からコミケに通い始めましたが、その当時からすでに「蛍」というコミケがありました。当時は「蛍」も主に個人による露店が中心で、販売されていたのは自作のものや出所不明のグッズばかりで、大きなブースなどほとんどありませんでした。オンラインゲーム業界の発展に伴い、現在では「蛍」はますます規模を拡大し、出展するゲームメーカーも増え、規模も専門性も格段に向上しています。
（私のスマホが初めて盗まれたのは、まさに『ホタル』でのことでした）
私も「アニメスターシティ」には、中学時代から高校、大学と通い続け、社会人になってからもよく足を運んでいます。ここ数年、その雰囲気はますます盛り上がりを見せています。「アニメスターシティ」以外にも、今では多くの同人コミュニティやストリートが加わり、休暇で実家に帰った際には、わざわざ立ち寄って回っています。
以前は、広州にはモバイルゲーム開発スタジオがほとんどないと思われていました。数年前までは『戦双』が唯一の存在でしたが、その後『1999』も台頭し、中小のスタジオがますます増えてきて、いずれも着実に成長しています。
miHoYoが広州に支社を設立したことで、上海の業界関係者の一部が広州で働くようになるだろう。とはいえ、Kuroも上海に支社を構えており、当初は技術職を募集していたが、現在ではパブリッシングや運営のポジションも設けられている。両社は互いに人材を引き抜くことになるだろう。
ゲーム業界はそれほど大きくなく、人材は相互に行き来している。上海の企業が広州に進出するのは、低コストで現地の人材を確保するためであり、広州の企業が上海に進出するのは、高度な技術力を持つ人材を引き抜くためだ。いずれにせよ、いずれも人材の流動を促進している。
確かに、今の広州はチャンスに満ちた場所ですし、生活費も上海よりかなり安いです。給料がそれに見合っていれば、家庭の事情も相まって、広州に戻るのは私にとってかなり適していると思います。
じゃあ、今日は何を食べようかな？
一通り話を聞いてみると、数人のインタビュー対象者は、まるで約束でもしていたかのように、皆「食べる」という話題に戻ってきた。広州の二次元産業はまだ追いつきつつある段階だが、甘味、じっくり煮込んだスープ、朝茶といったものは、確かに人々を引き留める力がある。仕事のことはひとまず置いておこう。結局のところ、「食は天なり」であり、二次元の人たちだって食事は欠かせないのだ！
