01
The best of times—when everything falls into place naturally
Teahouse: Back when you decided to strike out on your own and develop a large-scale domestic single-player game, the market wasn’t as thriving as it is today. There weren’t many developers who truly wanted to make single-player games, and opportunities were scarce. Why did you make that decision?
Fu Kun: I think we were just lucky enough to be in the right place at the right time. With *Black Myth: Wukong* having paved the way and stimulated demand in the domestic market, we simply went with the flow—it wasn’t as if we made any special decision. Our team has always been big fans of action-adventure games, so when the opportunity arose, why not go for it?
Fu Kun, Producer of *Tide of Oblivion*
Teahouse: When you launched the project in 2011, the concept of a “domestic AAA game” didn’t exist yet. How did you convince investors to back it? As the main investor, what role did Tencent play?
Fu Kun: Let me clarify something—we actually didn’t officially launch the project until early 2023. Before that, it was just a series of small tasks the company was handling; we gradually built up the team and evolved into a game development company, taking it one step at a time.Our investor, Tencent, has been very accommodating toward us; we have complete autonomy over the project. Tencent has provided us with a great deal of material and technical support, as we’ve discussed before.
Teahouse: You once said that the team consists of creators in their “Zhongdeng years,” and that their core goal is to do things that are worthwhile within a limited amount of time. So what exactly counts as “worthwhile”?
Fu Kun: “Worth it”—for developers, the definition is relatively simpler and more straightforward. After all, as we get older, all we want to do is make the games we love; we just want to do what we’re passionate about as much as possible. If we don’t have that passion, by the time our years are up, all that will be left is regret.Of course, even without passion, you can still support your family—but you won’t have the same passion and drive you have now to take a chance and make the games you love.
Teahouse: *Tide of Oblivion* isn’t set in China. How do you tell a story with a Chinese core in a game framed by a foreign culture?
Fu Kun: To be honest, we didn’t really think too much about using cultural elements as a gimmick at the time. The whole project started out as an action-adventure game; action was the primary focus, and combat was at its core.Our main goal was to see if we could add some flair to the combat and incorporate a bit of our own vision. So we kept exploring in that direction, and eventually developed the Knights’ Combat System.
Our idea was this: as the protagonist battles, other characters would accompany the player through the challenges, eventually forming a group of knights surrounding the protagonist as the central figure. With this concept in place, we asked ourselves what was most closely associated with knights, and ultimately traced it back to the origins of knighthood—the most elegant of which is the myth of the Knights of the Round Table.Whether it’s London or Britain as a whole, it is, after all, the birthplace of the Knights of the Round Table, so the two concepts came together quite naturally. This was our starting point; we never intended to use that culture merely as a veneer—it simply fit perfectly on its own.
Teahouse: It’s like first considering the core combat system, and then developing a suitable theme or backstory around it. As it happens, knights are quite similar to the chivalric culture of Europe, particularly Northern Europe.
Fu Kun: Right. Actually, we didn't draw on any specific cultural elements; we just felt that the myth of King Arthur was better suited to shaping and portraying the image of a knight.
Teahouse: You once quoted Feng Ji, the producer of *Black Myth*, who said, “As long as it’s told by a Chinese person, it’s a Chinese story.” How should we interpret this statement?
Fu Kun: This is how I see it: Our culture stems from our education. We are a generation that grew up under a purely Chinese cultural education system, so the content we present is inevitably influenced by that education, and our stories will certainly differ from how people in Europe and America understand them.We aim to incorporate action sequences typical of the action-adventure genre—such as challenging mighty deities and fighting alongside orders of knights. Therefore, our game is essentially a Chinese team’s interpretation of the King Arthur myth; it is not a direct representation of the original culture.
Teahouse: I’ve noticed that your character designs aren’t quite as Western-influenced as they used to be. So, in what ways do you incorporate elements that better suit Eastern aesthetics?
Fu Kun: You could say that the Eastern cultural interpretations we’ve incorporated are actually everywhere.First, take character design: our top priority was to create an aesthetic that would be appealing to both Eastern and Western audiences, so we blended the two in a comprehensive way. Beyond that, there are elements that our team finds particularly honorable in Chinese culture—such as the Martial Saint, a symbol of Eastern chivalry or a representative of traditional Chinese culture. Characters like this are naturally presented to the audience as Gwen’s mentor.
Teahouse: The topic of “Lord Guan Beating a Japanese Samurai” has been all the rage on Xiao Hei Hei these past couple of days. At first, everyone was complaining about how they gave a dragon to a Japanese character, but it turned out that the Martial Saint subdued him with a single Azure Dragon.
Fu Kun: The Chinese dragon used in *Wusheng* is an authentic Yellow Dragon. The dragon imagery in Japanese characters differs from our Eastern dragons, and we want to subtly convey this distinction.
Teahouse: I noticed that the China Pavilion appeared in the demo’s side quest. How will Chinese culture be represented in the game going forward?
Fu Kun: That’s right. The character of the Martial Saint is closely tied to the protagonist. As for the connection between the Martial Saint and the China Gallery, since the British Museum itself embodies the fusion of Eastern and Western cultures, we thought it was a perfect fit to incorporate the Martial Saint there.We hope that within the game, this character fits seamlessly into the levels and the game’s world. By approaching it in this organic way, we can ensure that future elements of Chinese culture will be integrated naturally into our levels and world—rather than forcing in various elements of traditional Chinese culture in a contrived manner.
02
From “Clumsy Hands” to the Knights’ Order System: Refinement Built on the Shoulders of Giants
Teahouse: Why an action-adventure game? *Tide of Annihilation* leans toward action-adventure while also featuring ARPG progression elements, but I think the market for this genre isn’t very big, and there’s a learning curve.
Fu Kun: Our concept is relatively simple—action-adventure was the tone we set from the very beginning. As a pure action game, I’m not the best at games myself, so I found the difficulty a bit high, which is why I created the Knights system.
The Knight Order combat system was designed to help players perform more spectacularly and reduce the pressure they feel by allowing them to use strategy. Whether it’s RPG character development or action-game controls, the goal is to let players fully experience the joy of action games through the interactive fun of action-adventure gameplay.We may not have delved as deeply into the realm of pure action games, which is likely due to my own personal limitations.
Teahouse: The game’s core innovation is the knight combat system, which allows players to command multiple knights. Where did the inspiration for this system come from?
Fu Kun: Many anime and video games have provided us with inspiration. When it comes to action games, iconic titles like the original *God of War* and *Devil May Cry*—which stand as towering examples—are objects of our admiration; and as for anime,*JoJo’s Bizarre Adventure* embodies a different kind of spirit, and the image of King Arthur from *Fate* has also influenced us. I feel like we’re standing on the shoulders of giants, moving forward step by step.
Teahouse: Will it be difficult to implement this very complex combat system?
Fu Kun: In my opinion, the main challenge lies in the fact that each Knight’s design has its own distinct playstyle. Take the Scythe Knight Bedewell, for example—he’s a ground-based attacker with a wide variety of ground combos and a large attack range, so he feels very comfortable in ground combat.The Time Knight, on the other hand, likely focuses on immobilizing and incapacitating enemies to give players more room to deal damage.
Paramides has two distinct playstyles: as a secondary knight, he can throw his weapon and perform counterattacks while doing so; as a primary knight, he can charge attacks and also perform counterattacks, so counterattacks and charging are his core mechanics.We want each Knight to offer unique gameplay, giving players a distinct experience. Players can build their builds based on their preferences and playstyle, and combine them with our Emblem System to execute more visually impressive combos.
Teahouse: This combat system was designated as the core of the project from the very beginning. Was it ever scrapped during development?
Fu Kun: There aren’t any major issues, but there are certainly many small details that need to be tweaked. For example, with each new version or when test feedback isn’t very positive, we have to repeatedly refine and improve the product.
Teahouse: In what areas has the feedback been particularly negative?
Fu Kun: For example, the controls might not feel comfortable enough, the game mechanics might be unbalanced, or the transitions between skills might not flow smoothly—all sorts of small details like that. Polishing a game is a crucial step, so most of the time we’re fine-tuning it over and over again, always striving to deliver the best possible experience to players.
Teahouse: You mentioned earlier that boss battles should “emphasize rewards over punishment.” This philosophy isn’t actually very common in action games. Why did you decide to take this approach?
Fu Kun: The "emphasis on rewards over punishment" approach I mentioned earlier is primarily aimed at bosses in the main story. We believe that in the main story, we want as many players as possible to play as much as they can and complete the game, because that’s the only way to justify the time and money they’ve invested.
As for hardcore action challenges, you’ll see that we’ve made some efforts in this area: we’ve included some fairly tough bosses in the side quests to satisfy players looking for a challenge. We’ve also designed different difficulty levels, all of which will be clearly distinguishable in the actual gameplay experience.
Teahouse: Compared to the in-game demo released last year, the UI, combat, and level design in this playable demo have all undergone significant changes. Why were so many adjustments made in just one year?
Fu Kun: Actually, this has always been a work-in-progress, and our main focus has been on continuously refining the project. What we released previously was just a snapshot of a specific stage, reflecting the development progress at that time. So in this demo, you’ll see that we’ve added a lot of content that’s more polished and features better visual effects—all with the goal of delivering a higher-quality gaming experience to players.
To be honest, we actually take players’ expectations and hopes very seriously. The final products we create are delivered to the players—they are the true users. When it comes to our products, I hope they have a say in the matter. If we can’t meet their expectations, then the creators are simply indulging themselves, which isn’t good for the product.
Teahouse: Right now, the topic players are discussing the most is that the protagonist’s face looks a bit off. Is that because they used CG before, but this time they’re using real-time rendering?
Fu Kun: Actually, the previous PV also used real-time rendering.The female protagonist’s facial features are consistent between the latest PV and the current demo; however, because we’re optimizing the lighting to make it run more smoothly, there may be some differences and imperfections in the facial rendering. Of course, this version may have been rushed a bit, so we’ll further optimize the facial rendering under lighting conditions in the future.
Teahouse: Action games generally have short playtimes. How do you plan to address this issue?
Fu Kun: As for the content, we can’t say for sure just yet how much we’ll be able to include. However, we still hope to add as much content as possible within the constraints of the development process and meet players’ needs with a substantial volume of content.
Also, personally, I don’t really like just reusing the same gameplay mechanic over and over and then presenting it to players as-is. I’d much rather incorporate more varied content into the game so that players can experience as many interesting gameplay elements as possible.
03
A team of over 150 people in Chengdu where “it’s okay to speak your mind”
Teahouse: How many people are currently on the team?
Fu Kun: Our team currently consists of about 150+ people.
Teahouse: It doesn't seem to have changed much from before.
Fu Kun: Right, there haven't been any major changes. Actually, the team's structure has become fairly stable, so what we need to do is pretty straightforward: just work harder to create more content.
Teahouse: Is there any problem you find particularly difficult to solve?
Fu Kun: It probably stems more from my own tendency to “nitpick”—for example, if I don’t quite understand how a system works, or if a knight doesn’t seem to be performing as well as it should—these things can be a major source of frustration for me.
Teahouse: I understand that many of the team’s core members have experience working on major international titles such as *Yakuza* and *Assassin’s Creed*. So, what management challenges does this combination of “international experience and local creativity” present?
Fu Kun: I think for a team like ours, the most important thing is to reach a consensus and establish development processes that are broadly accepted. These processes are based on our past experience, so we can quickly align our understanding.
Then we might make some process optimizations based on the issues we encountered during this development cycle. These mainly involve relationships between people and across teams, or how to make upstream and downstream processes run more efficiently—all very detailed matters. I think every team faces these challenges; there’s no “one-size-fits-all” process—only the process that best suits the team’s members.
Teahouse: How Can We Use Overseas Experience to Address Weaknesses in Domestic Development?
Fu Kun: Overseas companies do indeed have a head start over us in terms of accumulated experience, and they’ve been at it for much longer. But we Chinese developers actually possess superior qualities—our diligence and our ability to learn from experience and mistakes have led to truly outstanding results.
Teahouse: You once said that team culture is about “equality for all, like the Knights of the Round Table,” but the gaming industry is highly specialized. How can equality be put into practice? Who makes the final decision when there are major disagreements?
Fu Kun: We all respect each other’s opinions, and we get along pretty well. If the producer is right, we just go with what’s right—everyone agrees on that.If the producer is wrong, then they’re wrong—we’re allowed to call each other out within our team (laughs), and that’s totally fine. After all, what we’re ultimately aiming for is a result we all agree on, not to establish an authority figure in the development process—the producer cannot speak for the entire team and serve as the sole standard for project development.
Teahouse: I’m a little curious—Chengdu isn’t as teeming with talent as Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou, and Shenzhen. Why did you decide to set up shop in Chengdu back then?
Fu Kun: It’s simple—I’m from Chengdu. Plus, I think every city in our country has a lot of outstanding developers. I’ve been very fortunate to find many like-minded colleagues, and there are also many classmates willing to come to Chengdu, so I feel really lucky.
Teahouse: So, are you having trouble hiring people right now?
Fu Kun: I think recruitment is going okay. Look, the headcount has remained so stable—that’s pretty good.
Teahouse: Between Tencent’s investment track record and developing AAA single-player games, which of these two factors is more attractive to talent?
Fu Kun: I haven't really compared them.
Teahouse: But generally speaking, I feel we might give more consideration to AAA single-player games, since there aren’t that many opportunities like that in China.
Fu Kun: That’s right. Since we operate largely independently, our focus—and that of our team members—remains on our own project: whether we truly share the same vision for what we’re doing.Most of our conversations with others revolve around our project itself; if we can’t fully commit to the project, it will be very difficult to move forward later on. Given the generous grace period the investors have granted us, our primary focus right now is on completing the product.
04
“Results are earned through exams”—we’ll do right by the players and by ourselves.
Teahouse: Since its announcement, *Tide of Oblivion* has been the most low-key Chinese AAA title I’ve ever seen. Why is it so low-key?
Fu Kun: I think this is just a normal R&D process. First, we focus on getting the work done. Then, at a certain point, we need to gather feedback from players, so we do our best to organize an event—whether it’s an exhibition or a playtest—that players will find worthwhile. Our guiding principle is this: if we’re going to do something, we’ll do our best to make sure players feel it’s worth their time.
Teahouse: We’ve had a lot of international guests and media representatives visit us this time. You’ve also exhibited your products at major trade shows overseas in the past. Is the overseas market one that you place a high priority on?
Fu Kun: We’re probably focusing more on overseas players. From the very beginning, we’ve approached our work with a global perspective, and we hope that all players will be able to enjoy our games. Whether as Chinese developers or simply as game developers, we want as many players as possible to experience our games.We’ve played games from various countries, and we’d very much like more overseas players to experience our Chinese titles—which is only natural.
Teahouse: As the first major domestic single-player game you’ve led the development of, do you feel any pressure?
Fu Kun: There’s definitely pressure. But I’m fortunate to have a team working alongside me on this—I’m not fighting this battle alone. Just like our Knights system, this is the result of a team effort. So even though I feel the pressure, I still believe it provides me and our team with endless motivation.Whether it’s players’ requests or expectations, they ultimately inspire us to create even more great content.
Teahouse: Where does this pressure come from? Is it from other players, or from your own high expectations?
Fu Kun: Players don’t put pressure on us; rather, they have expectations of us—they expect us to do better, without demanding that we meet specific KPIs or fulfill any onerous conditions. So we simply want to do our best to meet their expectations. Even if those expectations require us to stand on tiptoe, we’ll do our best to take that extra step.
Teahouse: With landmark titles like *Black Myth: Wukong* already out there, and *Shadow Blade Zero* set to be released soon, do you think these outstanding titles will have an impact on you?
Fu Kun: I see this as a form of encouragement. Outstanding titles like *Black Myth* and *Shadow Blade Zero* have raised players’ expectations and awareness of what games should be. For us developers, these high standards serve as an incentive—we should strive to do better and avoid creating games that we ourselves don’t approve of. So I view this as a form of encouragement, motivating us to challenge ourselves to achieve even higher quality.
Teahouse: Large-scale domestic single-player games are high-risk, high-reward ventures. During development, is there ever a moment—or even a period of time—when you suddenly wonder what would happen if the game failed? Do you go all in, or take a more gradual approach through iterative updates?
Fu Kun: When making games, we spend most of our time on development. As for what failure would look like—we haven’t really thought about that yet. If we don’t give it our all, we’re bound to fail; we just need to do our best.
Teahouse: At the very least, don’t let yourself have any regrets—give it your all.
Fu Kun: Ensuring that the entire team has no regrets—that is our development philosophy.
Teahouse: What are your internal expectations or hopes for *Tide of Oblivion* right now? What kind of game do you hope it will ultimately be?
Fu Kun: I hope it will be a high-quality action-adventure game. Actually, my expectations aren’t as defined as one might imagine; what I hope for most is to complete it and refine it as much as possible—that’s our starting point. As for what kind of results we can expect—results are determined by performance; they’re the outcome of the product and are judged by the players.We need to work hard to prepare for the “exam” ourselves, and then aim to achieve a good result—we’ll do our best to get a good result.
Teahouse: What are your thoughts on the current domestic single-player game market and development environment?
Fu Kun: I can only say I’ve been very lucky—I really happened to be in the right place at the right time. It’s so wonderful to see such a diverse and vibrant scene today, with so many players supporting it and so much attention—something I never would have dared to imagine before.
Teahouse: For you, does the completion of *Tide of Oblivion* represent the fulfillment of a dream, a milestone in your career, or a project that still needs to be driven forward?
Fu Kun: Both my work and my dreams are the most important parts of my life. I feel that they have left an indelible mark on the past few years of my life, and I want to work hard to make that mark even better. More than anything, I hope that the games I’m working on now will live up to the expectations of our players and my team—that is what I should prioritize above all else right now.

Our team has always been big fans of action-adventure games, so when the opportunity arose, why not go for it?

Fu Kun, Producer of *Tide of Oblivion*

Teahouse: When you launched the project in 2011, the concept of a “domestic AAA game” didn’t exist yet. How did you convince investors to back it? As the main investor, what role did Tencent play?

Fu Kun: Let me clarify something—we actually didn’t officially launch the project until early 2023. Before that, it was just a series of small tasks the company was handling; we gradually built up the team and evolved into a game development company, taking it one step at a time.Our investor, Tencent, has been very accommodating toward us; we have complete autonomy over the project. Tencent has provided us with a great deal of material and technical support, as we’ve discussed before.

Teahouse: You once said that the team consists of creators in their “Zhongdeng years,” and that their core goal is to do things that are worthwhile within a limited amount of time. So what exactly counts as “worthwhile”?

Fu Kun: “Worth it”—for developers, the definition is relatively simpler and more straightforward. After all, as we get older, all we want to do is make the games we love; we just want to do what we’re passionate about as much as possible. If we don’t have that passion, by the time our years are up, all that will be left is regret.Of course, even without passion, you can still support your family—but you won’t have the same passion and drive you have now to take a chance and make the games you love.

Teahouse: *Tide of Oblivion* isn’t set in China. How do you tell a story with a Chinese core in a game framed by a foreign culture?

Fu Kun: To be honest, we didn’t really think too much about using cultural elements as a gimmick at the time. The whole project started out as an action-adventure game; action was the primary focus, and combat was at its core.Our main goal was to see if we could add some flair to the combat and incorporate a bit of our own vision. So we kept exploring in that direction, and eventually developed the Knights’ Combat System.

Our idea was this: as the protagonist battles, other characters would accompany the player through the challenges, eventually forming a group of knights surrounding the protagonist as the central figure. With this concept in place, we asked ourselves what was most closely associated with knights, and ultimately traced it back to the origins of knighthood—the most elegant of which is the myth of the Knights of the Round Table.Whether it’s London or Britain as a whole, it is, after all, the birthplace of the Knights of the Round Table, so the two concepts came together quite naturally. This was our starting point; we never intended to use that culture merely as a veneer—it simply fit perfectly on its own.

Teahouse: It’s like first considering the core combat system, and then developing a suitable theme or backstory around it. As it happens, knights are quite similar to the chivalric culture of Europe, particularly Northern Europe.

Fu Kun: Right. Actually, we didn't draw on any specific cultural elements; we just felt that the myth of King Arthur was better suited to shaping and portraying the image of a knight.

Teahouse: You once quoted Feng Ji, the producer of *Black Myth*, who said, “As long as it’s told by a Chinese person, it’s a Chinese story.” How should we interpret this statement?

Fu Kun: This is how I see it: Our culture stems from our education. We are a generation that grew up under a purely Chinese cultural education system, so the content we present is inevitably influenced by that education, and our stories will certainly differ from how people in Europe and America understand them.We aim to incorporate action sequences typical of the action-adventure genre—such as challenging mighty deities and fighting alongside orders of knights. Therefore, our game is essentially a Chinese team’s interpretation of the King Arthur myth; it is not a direct representation of the original culture.

Teahouse: I’ve noticed that your character designs aren’t quite as Western-influenced as they used to be. So, in what ways do you incorporate elements that better suit Eastern aesthetics?

Fu Kun: You could say that the Eastern cultural interpretations we’ve incorporated are actually everywhere.First, take character design: our top priority was to create an aesthetic that would be appealing to both Eastern and Western audiences, so we blended the two in a comprehensive way. Beyond that, there are elements that our team finds particularly honorable in Chinese culture—such as the Martial Saint, a symbol of Eastern chivalry or a representative of traditional Chinese culture. Characters like this are naturally presented to the audience as Gwen’s mentor.

Teahouse: The topic of “Lord Guan Beating a Japanese Samurai” has been all the rage on Xiao Hei Hei these past couple of days. At first, everyone was complaining about how they gave a dragon to a Japanese character, but it turned out that the Martial Saint subdued him with a single Azure Dragon.

Fu Kun: The Chinese dragon used in *Wusheng* is an authentic Yellow Dragon. The dragon imagery in Japanese characters differs from our Eastern dragons, and we want to subtly convey this distinction.

Teahouse: I noticed that the China Pavilion appeared in the demo’s side quest. How will Chinese culture be represented in the game going forward?

Fu Kun: That’s right. The character of the Martial Saint is closely tied to the protagonist. As for the connection between the Martial Saint and the China Gallery, since the British Museum itself embodies the fusion of Eastern and Western cultures, we thought it was a perfect fit to incorporate the Martial Saint there.We hope that within the game, this character fits seamlessly into the levels and the game’s world. By approaching it in this organic way, we can ensure that future elements of Chinese culture will be integrated naturally into our levels and world—rather than forcing in various elements of traditional Chinese culture in a contrived manner.

02

From “Clumsy Hands” to the Knights’ Order System: Refinement Built on the Shoulders of Giants

Teahouse: Why an action-adventure game? *Tide of Annihilation* leans toward action-adventure while also featuring ARPG progression elements, but I think the market for this genre isn’t very big, and there’s a learning curve.

Fu Kun: Our concept is relatively simple—action-adventure was the tone we set from the very beginning. As a pure action game, I’m not the best at games myself, so I found the difficulty a bit high, which is why I created the Knights system.

The Knight Order combat system was designed to help players perform more spectacularly and reduce the pressure they feel by allowing them to use strategy. Whether it’s RPG character development or action-game controls, the goal is to let players fully experience the joy of action games through the interactive fun of action-adventure gameplay.We may not have delved as deeply into the realm of pure action games, which is likely due to my own personal limitations.

Teahouse: The game’s core innovation is the knight combat system, which allows players to command multiple knights. Where did the inspiration for this system come from?

Fu Kun: Many anime and video games have provided us with inspiration. When it comes to action games, iconic titles like the original *God of War* and *Devil May Cry*—which stand as towering examples—are objects of our admiration; and as for anime,*JoJo’s Bizarre Adventure* embodies a different kind of spirit, and the image of King Arthur from *Fate* has also influenced us. I feel like we’re standing on the shoulders of giants, moving forward step by step.

Teahouse: Will it be difficult to implement this very complex combat system?

Fu Kun: In my opinion, the main challenge lies in the fact that each Knight’s design has its own distinct playstyle. Take the Scythe Knight Bedewell, for example—he’s a ground-based attacker with a wide variety of ground combos and a large attack range, so he feels very comfortable in ground combat.The Time Knight, on the other hand, likely focuses on immobilizing and incapacitating enemies to give players more room to deal damage.

Paramides has two distinct playstyles: as a secondary knight, he can throw his weapon and perform counterattacks while doing so; as a primary knight, he can charge attacks and also perform counterattacks, so counterattacks and charging are his core mechanics.We want each Knight to offer unique gameplay, giving players a distinct experience. Players can build their builds based on their preferences and playstyle, and combine them with our Emblem System to execute more visually impressive combos.

Teahouse: This combat system was designated as the core of the project from the very beginning. Was it ever scrapped during development?

Fu Kun: There aren’t any major issues, but there are certainly many small details that need to be tweaked. For example, with each new version or when test feedback isn’t very positive, we have to repeatedly refine and improve the product.

Teahouse: In what areas has the feedback been particularly negative?

Fu Kun: For example, the controls might not feel comfortable enough, the game mechanics might be unbalanced, or the transitions between skills might not flow smoothly—all sorts of small details like that. Polishing a game is a crucial step, so most of the time we’re fine-tuning it over and over again, always striving to deliver the best possible experience to players.

Teahouse: You mentioned earlier that boss battles should “emphasize rewards over punishment.” This philosophy isn’t actually very common in action games. Why did you decide to take this approach?

Fu Kun: The "emphasis on rewards over punishment" approach I mentioned earlier is primarily aimed at bosses in the main story. We believe that in the main story, we want as many players as possible to play as much as they can and complete the game, because that’s the only way to justify the time and money they’ve invested.

As for hardcore action challenges, you’ll see that we’ve made some efforts in this area: we’ve included some fairly tough bosses in the side quests to satisfy players looking for a challenge. We’ve also designed different difficulty levels, all of which will be clearly distinguishable in the actual gameplay experience.

Teahouse: Compared to the in-game demo released last year, the UI, combat, and level design in this playable demo have all undergone significant changes. Why were so many adjustments made in just one year?

Fu Kun: Actually, this has always been a work-in-progress, and our main focus has been on continuously refining the project. What we released previously was just a snapshot of a specific stage, reflecting the development progress at that time. So in this demo, you’ll see that we’ve added a lot of content that’s more polished and features better visual effects—all with the goal of delivering a higher-quality gaming experience to players.

To be honest, we actually take players’ expectations and hopes very seriously. The final products we create are delivered to the players—they are the true users. When it comes to our products, I hope they have a say in the matter. If we can’t meet their expectations, then the creators are simply indulging themselves, which isn’t good for the product.

Teahouse: Right now, the topic players are discussing the most is that the protagonist’s face looks a bit off. Is that because they used CG before, but this time they’re using real-time rendering?

Fu Kun: Actually, the previous PV also used real-time rendering.The female protagonist’s facial features are consistent between the latest PV and the current demo; however, because we’re optimizing the lighting to make it run more smoothly, there may be some differences and imperfections in the facial rendering. Of course, this version may have been rushed a bit, so we’ll further optimize the facial rendering under lighting conditions in the future.

Teahouse: Action games generally have short playtimes. How do you plan to address this issue?

Fu Kun: As for the content, we can’t say for sure just yet how much we’ll be able to include. However, we still hope to add as much content as possible within the constraints of the development process and meet players’ needs with a substantial volume of content.

Also, personally, I don’t really like just reusing the same gameplay mechanic over and over and then presenting it to players as-is. I’d much rather incorporate more varied content into the game so that players can experience as many interesting gameplay elements as possible.

03

A team of over 150 people in Chengdu where “it’s okay to speak your mind”

Teahouse: How many people are currently on the team?

Fu Kun: Our team currently consists of about 150+ people.

Teahouse: It doesn't seem to have changed much from before.

Fu Kun: Right, there haven't been any major changes. Actually, the team's structure has become fairly stable, so what we need to do is pretty straightforward: just work harder to create more content.

Teahouse: Is there any problem you find particularly difficult to solve?

Fu Kun: It probably stems more from my own tendency to “nitpick”—for example, if I don’t quite understand how a system works, or if a knight doesn’t seem to be performing as well as it should—these things can be a major source of frustration for me.

Teahouse: I understand that many of the team’s core members have experience working on major international titles such as *Yakuza* and *Assassin’s Creed*. So, what management challenges does this combination of “international experience and local creativity” present?

Fu Kun: I think for a team like ours, the most important thing is to reach a consensus and establish development processes that are broadly accepted. These processes are based on our past experience, so we can quickly align our understanding.

Then we might make some process optimizations based on the issues we encountered during this development cycle. These mainly involve relationships between people and across teams, or how to make upstream and downstream processes run more efficiently—all very detailed matters. I think every team faces these challenges; there’s no “one-size-fits-all” process—only the process that best suits the team’s members.

Teahouse: How Can We Use Overseas Experience to Address Weaknesses in Domestic Development?

Fu Kun: Overseas companies do indeed have a head start over us in terms of accumulated experience, and they’ve been at it for much longer. But we Chinese developers actually possess superior qualities—our diligence and our ability to learn from experience and mistakes have led to truly outstanding results.

Teahouse: You once said that team culture is about “equality for all, like the Knights of the Round Table,” but the gaming industry is highly specialized. How can equality be put into practice? Who makes the final decision when there are major disagreements?

Fu Kun: We all respect each other’s opinions, and we get along pretty well. If the producer is right, we just go with what’s right—everyone agrees on that.If the producer is wrong, then they’re wrong—we’re allowed to call each other out within our team (laughs), and that’s totally fine. After all, what we’re ultimately aiming for is a result we all agree on, not to establish an authority figure in the development process—the producer cannot speak for the entire team and serve as the sole standard for project development.

Teahouse: I’m a little curious—Chengdu isn’t as teeming with talent as Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou, and Shenzhen. Why did you decide to set up shop in Chengdu back then?

Fu Kun: It’s simple—I’m from Chengdu. Plus, I think every city in our country has a lot of outstanding developers. I’ve been very fortunate to find many like-minded colleagues, and there are also many classmates willing to come to Chengdu, so I feel really lucky.

Teahouse: So, are you having trouble hiring people right now?

Fu Kun: I think recruitment is going okay. Look, the headcount has remained so stable—that’s pretty good.

Teahouse: Between Tencent’s investment track record and developing AAA single-player games, which of these two factors is more attractive to talent?

Fu Kun: I haven't really compared them.

Teahouse: But generally speaking, I feel we might give more consideration to AAA single-player games, since there aren’t that many opportunities like that in China.

Fu Kun: That’s right. Since we operate largely independently, our focus—and that of our team members—remains on our own project: whether we truly share the same vision for what we’re doing.Most of our conversations with others revolve around our project itself; if we can’t fully commit to the project, it will be very difficult to move forward later on. Given the generous grace period the investors have granted us, our primary focus right now is on completing the product.

04

“Results are earned through exams”—we’ll do right by the players and by ourselves.

Teahouse: Since its announcement, *Tide of Oblivion* has been the most low-key Chinese AAA title I’ve ever seen. Why is it so low-key?

Fu Kun: I think this is just a normal R&D process. First, we focus on getting the work done. Then, at a certain point, we need to gather feedback from players, so we do our best to organize an event—whether it’s an exhibition or a playtest—that players will find worthwhile. Our guiding principle is this: if we’re going to do something, we’ll do our best to make sure players feel it’s worth their time.

Teahouse: We’ve had a lot of international guests and media representatives visit us this time. You’ve also exhibited your products at major trade shows overseas in the past. Is the overseas market one that you place a high priority on?

Fu Kun: We’re probably focusing more on overseas players. From the very beginning, we’ve approached our work with a global perspective, and we hope that all players will be able to enjoy our games. Whether as Chinese developers or simply as game developers, we want as many players as possible to experience our games.We’ve played games from various countries, and we’d very much like more overseas players to experience our Chinese titles—which is only natural.

Teahouse: As the first major domestic single-player game you’ve led the development of, do you feel any pressure?

Fu Kun: There’s definitely pressure. But I’m fortunate to have a team working alongside me on this—I’m not fighting this battle alone. Just like our Knights system, this is the result of a team effort. So even though I feel the pressure, I still believe it provides me and our team with endless motivation.Whether it’s players’ requests or expectations, they ultimately inspire us to create even more great content.

Teahouse: Where does this pressure come from? Is it from other players, or from your own high expectations?

Fu Kun: Players don’t put pressure on us; rather, they have expectations of us—they expect us to do better, without demanding that we meet specific KPIs or fulfill any onerous conditions. So we simply want to do our best to meet their expectations. Even if those expectations require us to stand on tiptoe, we’ll do our best to take that extra step.

Teahouse: With landmark titles like *Black Myth: Wukong* already out there, and *Shadow Blade Zero* set to be released soon, do you think these outstanding titles will have an impact on you?

Fu Kun: I see this as a form of encouragement. Outstanding titles like *Black Myth* and *Shadow Blade Zero* have raised players’ expectations and awareness of what games should be. For us developers, these high standards serve as an incentive—we should strive to do better and avoid creating games that we ourselves don’t approve of. So I view this as a form of encouragement, motivating us to challenge ourselves to achieve even higher quality.

Teahouse: Large-scale domestic single-player games are high-risk, high-reward ventures. During development, is there ever a moment—or even a period of time—when you suddenly wonder what would happen if the game failed? Do you go all in, or take a more gradual approach through iterative updates?

Fu Kun: When making games, we spend most of our time on development. As for what failure would look like—we haven’t really thought about that yet. If we don’t give it our all, we’re bound to fail; we just need to do our best.

Teahouse: At the very least, don’t let yourself have any regrets—give it your all.

Fu Kun: Ensuring that the entire team has no regrets—that is our development philosophy.

Teahouse: What are your internal expectations or hopes for *Tide of Oblivion* right now? What kind of game do you hope it will ultimately be?

Fu Kun: I hope it will be a high-quality action-adventure game. Actually, my expectations aren’t as defined as one might imagine; what I hope for most is to complete it and refine it as much as possible—that’s our starting point. As for what kind of results we can expect—results are determined by performance; they’re the outcome of the product and are judged by the players.We need to work hard to prepare for the “exam” ourselves, and then aim to achieve a good result—we’ll do our best to get a good result.

Teahouse: What are your thoughts on the current domestic single-player game market and development environment?

Fu Kun: I can only say I’ve been very lucky—I really happened to be in the right place at the right time. It’s so wonderful to see such a diverse and vibrant scene today, with so many players supporting it and so much attention—something I never would have dared to imagine before.

Teahouse: For you, does the completion of *Tide of Oblivion* represent the fulfillment of a dream, a milestone in your career, or a project that still needs to be driven forward?

Fu Kun: Both my work and my dreams are the most important parts of my life. I feel that they have left an indelible mark on the past few years of my life, and I want to work hard to make that mark even better. More than anything, I hope that the games I’m working on now will live up to the expectations of our players and my team—that is what I should prioritize above all else right now.

title: Die Standardversion von „Shadow Blade Zero“ ist ab 268 Yuan erhältlich – Moment mal, was soll das heißen, Meister Ye wärmt sich gerade auf?
text:
Heute wurde endlich der Verkaufspreis für das in China entwickelte Martial-Arts-Punk-Singleplayer-Meisterwerk „Shadow Blade Zero“ bekannt gegeben: Die Standardversion kostet 268 Yuan, die Deluxe-Version 328 Yuan – genau wie beim früheren Aushängeschild der chinesischen Spielebranche, „Black Myth: Wukong“.
Schon zuvor hatten viele Spieler spekuliert, dass der Preis vielleicht bei 298 Yuan oder 328 Yuan liegen könnte. Nun, zwei Jahre nach der Veröffentlichung durch Black Monkey, hat „Shadow Blade Zero“ diesen fairen Preis beibehalten, was viele Spieler dazu veranlasst, „Liang Sheng ist großartig!“ auszurufen.
Neben dem überraschenden Preis hat natürlich vor allem das gleichzeitig veröffentlichte 11-minütige Vorverkaufs-PV die größte Aufmerksamkeit auf sich gezogen.Zuvor hatten das „Teahouse“ und verschiedene Medienpartner diesen Vorverkaufs-PV bereits einen halben Tag früher gesehen. Wir waren gerade noch ganz in den ultimativen Nervenkitzel der Wuxia-Kämpfe versunken, als – kaum dass das Logo erschien – Meister Yes plötzlicher Auftritt die Stimmung im Saal fast augenblicklich zum Kochen brachte.
Das ist doch ein Wuxia-Spiel, oder? Moment mal, was meinst du damit, dass Meister Ye sich aufwärmt?
Der PV beginnt mit einer Verfolgungsjagd mit einer Kutsche, woraufhin der Protagonist Hun auf der Kutsche steht und sich einem „Kampf auf beiden Flanken“ gegen die Verfolger zu Pferd stellt.
Wie man sieht, handelt es sich bei diesem Kampf trotz einiger QTE-Elemente um ein echtes „Manual“-Spielerlebnis. Der Spieler muss in einem extrem beengten Raum alle bekannten Standardaktionen wie Angriffe, Ausweichen, Parieren und Spezialfähigkeiten einsetzen, was stark an traditionelle Wuxia-Filme erinnert.
Anschließend betrat ein BOSS-Verfolger mit zwei Sicheln die Bühne, und die beiden lieferten sich auf dem Wagen einen atemberaubenden Kampf. Bemerkenswert ist, dass zwar bewusst auf filmische Kameraführungen verzichtet wurde, jedoch fast jede Szene des Kampfes sorgfältig gestaltet wurde, um sicherzustellen, dass jede Kampfperspektive ein filmähnliches Erlebnis bietet.
Nach dem Kampf traten alle Charaktere nacheinander in Erscheinung. Zu meiner großen Überraschung übertraf die Detailgenauigkeit der Charaktermodelle in „Shadow Blade Zero“ das Niveau aller bisher von mir gesehenen Einzelspieler-Spiele und erreichte sogar ein geradezu atemberaubendes Niveau.
Ich habe selten erlebt, dass das Erscheinungsbild einer Figur so stark von der östlichen Ästhetik geprägt wurde. Damit wurde nicht nur das zuvor von vielen Spielern kritisierte Problem der „Influencer-Gesichter“ gelöst, sondern es gelang im wahrsten Sinne des Wortes ein bisher beispielloser Durchbruch bei der Gestaltung von Gesichtsmodellen im Stil der östlichen Ästhetik.
Auch in „Shadow Blade Zero“ nimmt die Handlung einen großen Stellenwert ein. Der größte Unterschied dieses PVs besteht daher darin, dass neben den für das Spiel charakteristischen Martial-Arts-Kämpfen auch die verschiedenen Figuren, denen „Hun“ in dieser Welt der Kampfkünste begegnet, sowie die Verbindungen zwischen ihnen ausführlich gezeigt werden. Wie es so schön heißt: „Nur wo Menschen sind, gibt es auch die Welt der Kampfkünste.“
Darauf folgt eine Reihe bisher unveröffentlichter Bosskämpfe, von denen eine schlangenähnliche Frau, die mit Fäden gesteuert wird, besonders interessant ist – das wird sicherlich wieder ein fantasievolles Kampferlebnis.
Es tauchen auch immer wieder Szenen im Stil einer Mischung aus Wuxia und Cyberpunk auf, wie zum Beispiel die riesige Kettensäge, die aus dem Nichts aus dem Kopf herausragt – das ist wirklich typisch für „Yuxue“.
Darin gibt es auch einen Monolog des Bösewichts, der ebenfalls den klassischen Wuxia-Charakter hat. Nicht jeder Bösewicht ist von Natur aus böse; vielleicht haben sie einst das Volk und die Welt gerettet, sind aber aufgrund widersprüchlicher Ideale schließlich auf die schiefe Bahn geraten, was den Zuschauer neugierig macht, was genau passiert ist.
Natürlich waren die vorherigen Action-Szenen zwar spannend, aber „Meister Ye“, der am Ende als Höhepunkt auftrat, war wohl wirklich die Figur, die das Publikum in Begeisterung versetzte.
Nach einer Reihe fließender Schwertkämpfe sorgte der charakteristische Wing-Chun-Schlag sofort für Begeisterungsstürme im gesamten Saal, und der Applaus wollte fast gar nicht mehr abreißen. Am Ende wurde schließlich auch die Identität des mysteriösen maskierten Mannes enthüllt, und Meister Yes Auftritt versetzte das Publikum erneut in Staunen.
Nach dem Ende des PVs erschien der Produzent Liang Qiwei (S) und unterhielt sich kurz mit uns.Aus S’ Sicht geht es in „Shadow Blade Zero“ vor allem um drei Arten von Beziehungen: die Konfrontation zwischen dem Protagonisten Hun und dem Bösewicht, die freundschaftlichen Beziehungen zwischen den Gefährten sowie die universelle Beziehung zur Rettung aller Lebewesen auf der Welt – genau das ist in seinen Augen die wahre Bedeutung von Ritterlichkeit.
„Shadow Blade Zero“ präsentiert sich äußerlich im Stil eines Punk-Wuxia-Spiels, weshalb man hier äußerst frei interpretierte Wuxia-Kämpfe erleben kann.mit einer künstlerischen Gestaltung im Cyberpunk- und Fantasy-Stil, doch der eigentliche Kern bleibt ein klassisches und zugleich etwas innovatives Wuxia-Konzept – ein Leitgedanke, der sich von den Anfängen mit „Rain Blood“ bis hin zu „Shadow Blade Zero“ zieht.
Was ist wahre Ritterlichkeit?

Darauf folgt eine Reihe bisher unveröffentlichter Bosskämpfe, von denen eine schlangenähnliche Frau, die mit Fäden gesteuert wird, besonders interessant ist – das wird sicherlich wieder ein fantasievolles Kampferlebnis.

Es tauchen auch immer wieder Szenen im Stil einer Mischung aus Wuxia und Cyberpunk auf, wie zum Beispiel die riesige Kettensäge, die aus dem Nichts aus dem Kopf herausragt – das ist wirklich typisch für „Yuxue“.

Darin gibt es auch einen Monolog des Bösewichts, der ebenfalls den klassischen Wuxia-Charakter hat. Nicht jeder Bösewicht ist von Natur aus böse; vielleicht haben sie einst das Volk und die Welt gerettet, sind aber aufgrund widersprüchlicher Ideale schließlich auf die schiefe Bahn geraten, was den Zuschauer neugierig macht, was genau passiert ist.

Natürlich waren die vorherigen Action-Szenen zwar spannend, aber „Meister Ye“, der am Ende als Höhepunkt auftrat, war wohl wirklich die Figur, die das Publikum in Begeisterung versetzte.

Nach einer Reihe fließender Schwertkämpfe sorgte der charakteristische Wing-Chun-Schlag sofort für Begeisterungsstürme im gesamten Saal, und der Applaus wollte fast gar nicht mehr abreißen. Am Ende wurde schließlich auch die Identität des mysteriösen maskierten Mannes enthüllt, und Meister Yes Auftritt versetzte das Publikum erneut in Staunen.

Nach dem Ende des PVs erschien der Produzent Liang Qiwei (S) und unterhielt sich kurz mit uns.Aus S’ Sicht geht es in „Shadow Blade Zero“ vor allem um drei Arten von Beziehungen: die Konfrontation zwischen dem Protagonisten Hun und dem Bösewicht, die freundschaftlichen Beziehungen zwischen den Gefährten sowie die universelle Beziehung zur Rettung aller Lebewesen auf der Welt – genau das ist in seinen Augen die wahre Bedeutung von Ritterlichkeit.

„Shadow Blade Zero“ präsentiert sich äußerlich im Stil eines Punk-Wuxia-Spiels, weshalb man hier äußerst frei interpretierte Wuxia-Kämpfe erleben kann.mit einer künstlerischen Gestaltung im Cyberpunk- und Fantasy-Stil, doch der eigentliche Kern bleibt ein klassisches und zugleich etwas innovatives Wuxia-Konzept – ein Leitgedanke, der sich von den Anfängen mit „Rain Blood“ bis hin zu „Shadow Blade Zero“ zieht.

Was ist wahre Ritterlichkeit?

title: "Shadow Blade Zero" Standard Edition starts at 268 yuan. Wait a minute—what do you mean Master Ye is just warming up?
text:
Today, the Chinese-developed wuxia-punk single-player blockbuster *Shadow Blade Zero* finally announced its retail prices: 268 yuan for the Standard Edition and 328 yuan for the Deluxe Edition—the same pricing as the previous "pride of Chinese gaming," *Black Myth: Wukong*.
Even before this, many players had speculated that the price might be 298 yuan or 328 yuan. Now, two years after its release on Black Monkey, *Shadow Blade Zero* has managed to maintain such a reasonable price, leading many players to exclaim, “Liang Sheng is great!”
Of course, aside from the surprise price, the biggest draw was undoubtedly the 11-minute pre-sale PV released at the same time.Prior to this, our team at the Teahouse and our media partners had already viewed this pre-release PV half a day earlier. We had been completely immersed in the sheer thrill of the wuxia combat, and just as the logo was about to appear, Master Ye’s sudden appearance practically set the room ablaze in an instant.
This is a wuxia game, right? Wait, what do you mean by "Master Ye is warming up"?
The PV opens with a carriage chase, after which the protagonist, Hun, stands atop the carriage and engages in a “fight on both sides” against the pursuers on horseback on either side.
As you can see, despite the inclusion of some QTE sequences, this battle is truly a “manual” experience. Players must fight within an extremely confined space, utilizing all the standard mechanics—such as attacks, dodges, parries, and skills—which evokes the feel of a traditional wuxia movie.
Shortly thereafter, a boss enemy wielding twin scythes appeared, and the two engaged in a spectacular showdown on the wagon. It’s worth noting that, although the camerawork wasn’t intentionally cinematic, nearly every scene in the battle was meticulously designed to ensure that every combat angle delivered a cinematic viewing experience.
After the battle ended, all the characters made their appearance. To my great surprise, the level of detail in the character models in *Shadow Blade Zero* surpassed that of any single-player game I’ve ever seen—it was truly breathtaking.
I’ve rarely seen character designs polished to such a high standard of Eastern aesthetics. This not only addresses the issue—previously criticized by many players—of characters having “influencer-style” faces, but also represents a truly unprecedented breakthrough in facial models based on Eastern aesthetics.
The storyline also plays a major role in *Shadow Blade Zero*, so the biggest difference in this PV is that, in addition to the iconic martial arts combat at the heart of the game, it showcases the various characters Hun encounters in this martial arts world and the connections he forms with them. As the saying goes, “Where there are people, there is the martial arts world.”
This is immediately followed by a series of previously unrevealed boss battles, one of which—a snake-like woman controlled by strings—is particularly intriguing; it’s sure to be another wildly imaginative combat experience.
There were also several scenes with a cyberpunk-meets-wuxia vibe, such as a giant chainsaw materializing out of thin air from inside someone’s head—that’s so typical of *Rain Blood*.
There’s also a line of dialogue from the villain that really captures the classic wuxia spirit. Not every villain is inherently evil; they may once have saved the people and the world, but due to conflicting ideals, they ultimately chose to fall from grace—which can’t help but make one wonder what exactly happened.
Of course, while the action sequences earlier in the film were certainly spectacular, “Master Ye,” who made his grand entrance at the very end, was perhaps the character who truly set the crowd on fire.
After a series of fluid and graceful sword-fighting moves, the iconic Wing Chun techniques were unleashed, instantly setting the entire audience ablaze with excitement, and the applause was almost nonstop. Finally, the identity of the mysterious masked man was revealed, leaving the audience once again in awe of Master Ye’s entrance.
After the PV ended, producer Liang Qiwei (S) appeared and had a brief conversation with us.In S’s view, *Shadow Blade Zero* aims to convey three types of relationships: the conflict between the protagonist, Hun, and the antagonist; the bonds of friendship among companions; and the universal mission to save all living beings. In his eyes, this is the true essence of chivalry.
"Shadow Blade Zero" is wrapped in a cyberpunk wuxia aesthetic, so you'll see extremely stylized wuxia combat,featuring cyberpunk and fantasy-inspired art styles, but at its core lies a classic yet slightly innovative wuxia philosophy—a core concept that has run through the series from the very first *Rain Blood* all the way to *Shadow Blade Zero*.
What is true chivalry?

title: 『影之刃ゼロ』スタンダード版が268元から発売開始……ちょっと待って、「葉師匠がウォームアップ中」ってどういうこと？
text:
本日、中国製の武侠パンク系シングルプレイ大作『影之刃ゼロ』の発売価格がようやく発表された。通常版は268元、デラックス版は328元で、これは以前「中国ゲーム界の誇り」と称された『黒神話：悟空』と同価格となっている。
これ以前にも、多くのプレイヤーが「298元か328元ではないか」と推測していましたが、黒猴による発売から2年が経過した今、『影之刃ゼロ』がこれほど良心的な価格を維持できていることに、多くのプレイヤーが「梁聖は偉大だ」と感嘆せずにはいられません。
もちろん、驚きの価格に加え、最も注目を集めたのは、同時に公開された11分間の先行PVに他なりません。これに先立ち、当メディアと各メディア関係者は、この先行PVを半日早く視聴していました。当初は武侠バトルがもたらす極上の快感に浸っていたのですが、ロゴが表示された直後、葉師匠の突然の登場が瞬く間に会場を沸かせました。
これは武侠ゲームだよね？　ちょっと待って、葉師匠が「ウォームアップ中」ってどういう意味？
PVは冒頭から馬車による追跡戦から幕を開け、続いて主人公の「魂」が馬車の上に立ち、両側から馬に乗って追ってくる追っ手たちと「左右から同時に戦う」展開となる。
ご覧の通り、いくつかのQTE操作は登場するものの、この戦闘は紛れもなく「手動操作」によるプレイとなっています。プレイヤーは極めて狭い空間の中で、攻撃、回避、パリィ、スキルなど、既存のあらゆる基本操作を駆使して戦わなければならず、まるで伝統的な武侠映画のような趣があります。
その後、二本の鎌を手にした追手であるボスが登場し、二人は馬車の上で息をのむような対決を繰り広げた。特筆すべきは、映画のようなカメラワークを意図的に用いたわけではないにもかかわらず、戦闘シーンのほぼすべてが綿密に設計されており、どの戦闘アングルも映画さながらの視覚体験を実現している点だ。
戦闘が終わると、さまざまなキャラクターが次々と登場した。驚いたことに、『シャドウブレード ゼロ』のキャラクターモデルの精細さは、私がこれまでプレイしたどのシングルプレイゲームよりもはるかに優れており、まさに息をのむほどだった。
キャラクターのビジュアルをこれほどまでに東洋的な美意識に磨き上げた例はめったに見かけない。これは、これまで多くのプレイヤーから「ネット有名人のような顔」だと批判されていた問題を解決しただけでなく、真の意味で、東洋的な美意識に基づいた顔モデルにおいて、これまでにない画期的な進歩を遂げたと言える。
『影之刃ゼロ』においてもストーリーは大きな比重を占めており、今回のPVの最大の特徴は、象徴的な中核体験である武侠バトルに加え、この江湖で「魂」が出会う様々な人物や、彼らとのつながりがたっぷりと描かれている点にある。まさに「人がいてこそ江湖がある」という通りだ。
続いて、これまで一度も公開されたことのないボス戦が次々と繰り広げられます。中でも、糸で操られる蛇のような女性は特に興味深く、またしても型破りな戦闘体験になることでしょう。
武侠とサイバーパンクを融合させたようなシーンも度々登場し、例えば頭の中から突如として現れる巨大なチェーンソーなどは、『雨血』ならではの特色が存分に表れている。
その中には、悪役のセリフも一節あり、これもまた古典的な武侠小説の趣を漂わせている。すべての悪役が生まれつき悪人というわけではない。彼らもかつては民を救い、世を救ったことがあるかもしれないが、理想が衝突したために、ついには自ら堕落の道を歩むことになってしまったのだ。一体何が起きたのか、思わず気になってしまう。
もちろん、前半のアクションシーンも確かに見応えがあったが、最後に大トリとして登場した「葉師匠」こそ、まさに会場を沸かせたキャラクターだったと言えるだろう。
流れるような剣術の演武が終わると、象徴的な詠春拳が披露され、会場はたちまち沸き立ち、拍手はほぼ途切れることなく続いた。そして最後に、謎の仮面男の正体がついに明かされ、葉師範の登場に再び観客は震撼させられた。
PVの終了後、プロデューサーの梁其偉（S）氏が登場し、私たちと短い交流の時間を持ちました。S氏によれば、『影之刃ゼロ』が最も表現したいのは、3つの関係性である。主人公「魂」と敵対者との対立関係、仲間同士の友好関係、そして天下の衆生を救うという普遍的な関係。これこそが、彼の目から見た真の意味での「侠義」である。
『影之刃ゼロ』は、一見するとパンク・武侠という装いをしているため、極めて自由奔放な武侠バトルを楽しむことができます。サイバーパンクやファンタジー風の美術表現も取り入れられていますが、その真髄は依然として、古典的でありながらも斬新な武侠の理念にあり、これは最初の『雨血』から『影之刃ゼロ』に至るまで一貫して貫かれている核心的な理念です。
真の侠義とは何だろうか？

title: La edición estándar de «Shadow Blade Zero» sale a la venta a partir de 268 yuanes. Un momento, ¿qué significa que el maestro Ye está calentando?
text:
Hoy, el gran título chino de acción y punk «Shadow Blade Zero» ha revelado por fin su precio de venta: 268 yuanes para la edición estándar y 328 yuanes para la edición de lujo, en línea con el anterior éxito nacional «Black Myth: Wukong».
Antes de esto, muchos jugadores ya habían especulado con que el precio podría ser de 298 o 328 yuanes; ahora, dos años después del lanzamiento de «Black Monkey», «Shadow Blade Zero» sigue manteniendo un precio tan razonable que muchos jugadores no pueden evitar exclamar: «¡Liang Sheng es genial!».
Por supuesto, además del precio sorpresa, lo que más ha llamado la atención ha sido el vídeo promocional de 11 minutos que se ha publicado al mismo tiempo.Antes de eso, el equipo de la «Casa de Té» y los medios amigos ya habíamos visto este vídeo promocional con medio día de antelación. Estábamos inmersos en la emoción extrema que provocan las escenas de combate de las películas de artes marciales, y cuando ya había aparecido el logotipo, la aparición repentina del maestro Ye hizo estallar el ambiente casi al instante.
Esto es un juego de artes marciales, ¿no? Un momento, ¿qué quieres decir con que el maestro Ye está calentando?
El PV comienza con una persecución en carruaje, tras lo cual el protagonista, Hun, se sitúa sobre el carruaje y se enfrenta a los perseguidores a caballo que vienen por ambos lados.
Como se puede observar, aunque hay algunas secuencias QTE, este combate es, sin lugar a dudas, una experiencia de juego «manual». El jugador debe luchar en un espacio extremadamente reducido, utilizando todas las acciones habituales, como ataques, esquivas, contraataques y habilidades, lo que le da un aire muy parecido al de las películas tradicionales de artes marciales.
A continuación, apareció un jefe enemigo armado con dos hoces, y ambos protagonizaron un duelo espectacular en el carruaje. Cabe destacar que, aunque no se utilizaron movimientos de cámara deliberadamente cinematográficos, casi todas las escenas de la batalla se diseñaron minuciosamente para garantizar que cada ángulo de combate ofreciera una experiencia visual comparable a la de una película.
Una vez finalizada la batalla, aparecieron todos los personajes. Lo que más me sorprendió fue que el nivel de detalle de los modelos de los personajes de «Shadow Blade Zero» superaba con creces el de cualquier otro videojuego para una sola jugadora que hubiera visto hasta entonces, llegando incluso a un nivel realmente asombroso.
Pocas veces he visto que se haya pulido la imagen de un personaje hasta alcanzar un nivel tan elevado de estética oriental; esto no solo ha resuelto el problema, criticado anteriormente por muchos jugadores, de que los personajes tuvieran una «cara de influencer», sino que, en el sentido más auténtico, ha supuesto un avance sin precedentes en los modelos faciales basados en la estética oriental.
La trama también ocupa un lugar muy importante en «Shadow Blade Zero», por lo que la principal novedad de este tráiler es que, además de los combates de artes marciales —que constituyen la experiencia central y emblemática del juego—, se muestran en profundidad los diversos personajes con los que «Hun» entra en contacto en este mundo de las artes marciales, así como las relaciones que se establecen con ellos. Como dice el refrán: «Donde hay gente, hay mundo de las artes marciales».
A continuación viene una serie de combates contra jefes finales nunca antes revelados, entre los que destaca especialmente una mujer con aspecto de serpiente controlada por hilos; sin duda, será otra experiencia de combate llena de fantasía.
También aparecen en varias ocasiones algunas escenas con un estilo que combina el género de las novelas de artes marciales con el ciberpunk, como esa enorme sierra eléctrica que surge de la nada de dentro de la cabeza, algo que refleja a la perfección el estilo característico de «Lluvia de Sangre».
Además, hay un diálogo del villano que también tiene ese aire clásico de las novelas de artes marciales. No todos los villanos nacen malos; es posible que en algún momento también hayan salvado al pueblo y al mundo, pero, debido a un conflicto de ideales, acabaron cayendo en la maldad, lo que nos lleva a preguntarnos qué fue lo que ocurrió exactamente.
Por supuesto, aunque las escenas de acción anteriores fueron sin duda espectaculares, el «maestro Ye», que apareció al final como colofón, puede que haya sido realmente el personaje que hizo enloquecer al público.
Tras una serie de combates con espada de una fluidez impresionante, la aparición del emblemático Wing Chun hizo enloquecer al público al instante, y los aplausos fueron prácticamente incesantes. Al final, se desveló por fin la identidad del misterioso hombre enmascarado, lo que volvió a dejar a todos boquiabiertos con la aparición del maestro Ye.
Una vez finalizado el PV, el productor Liang Qiwei (S) hizo acto de presencia y mantuvo una breve conversación con nosotros.En opinión de S, lo que «Shadow Blade Zero» quiere expresar sobre todo son tres tipos de relaciones: la oposición entre el protagonista, Hun, y el villano; la relación de amistad entre compañeros; y la relación universal de salvar a todos los seres del mundo. Esto es, a su juicio, el verdadero significado de la caballerosidad.
«Shadow Blade Zero» se presenta con una estética de wuxia punk, por lo que podrás disfrutar de combates de wuxia de un estilo extremadamente libre,con una estética que combina el cyberpunk y la fantasía, pero cuyo verdadero núcleo sigue siendo una filosofía de las artes marciales clásica y, a la vez, ligeramente innovadora; esta es la idea central que ha estado presente desde el primer título, «Rain Blood», hasta «Shadow Blade Zero».
¿Qué es realmente la caballerosidad?

title: 『섀도우 블레이드 제로』 스탠다드 에디션이 268위안부터 판매된다. 잠깐, ‘예 사부’가 워밍업 중이라니?
text:
오늘, 중국산 무협 펑크 장르의 싱글플레이어 대작 《섀도우 블레이드 제로》의 판매 가격이 드디어 공개되었는데, 일반판은 268위안, 디럭스판은 328위안으로, 앞서 ‘중국 게임계의 자랑’이라 불렸던 《블랙 미스틱: 우공》과 동일한 가격대를 유지했다.
그 전에도 많은 플레이어들이 가격이 298위안이나 328위안이 아닐까 추측했었는데, ‘흑원숭이’ 출시 2년이 지난 지금도 《섀도우 블레이드 제로》가 이토록 합리적인 가격을 유지하고 있어, 많은 플레이어들이 “량셩은 위대하다”고 감탄하고 있다.
물론, 놀라운 가격 외에도 가장 주목을 끈 것은 함께 공개된 11분 분량의 사전 판매 PV였다.이에 앞서, ‘차관’과 여러 언론사 관계자들은 이 예고편을 반나절 먼저 시청했는데, 원래는 무협 전투가 주는 극한의 쾌감에 푹 빠져 있다가 로고가 등장했을 무렵, 예 사부의 갑작스러운 등장이 현장을 순식간에 뜨겁게 달궜습니다.
이거 무협 게임인가? 잠깐, 예 사범님이 준비 운동을 하고 있다고 한 게 무슨 뜻이야?
PV는 마차 추격전으로 막을 올렸고, 이어 주인공 혼이 마차 위에 서서 양쪽에서 말을 타고 쫓아오는 추격자들과 “좌우를 오가며 싸운다”.
보시다시피, 몇 가지 QTE 조작이 등장하긴 하지만 이 전투는 그야말로 ‘수동 조작’ 방식의 플레이입니다. 플레이어는 극히 좁은 공간에서 공격, 회피, 반격, 스킬 등 기존의 모든 기본 조작을 활용해 싸워야 하는데, 이는 마치 전통적인 무협 영화의 분위기를 자아냅니다.
이어 쌍낫을 든 추격자 보스가 등장했고, 두 사람은 마차 위에서 눈부시게 화려한 대결을 펼쳤다. 특히 주목할 점은, 의도적으로 영화 같은 카메라 워크를 사용하지는 않았지만, 전투 장면 하나하나가 세심하게 설계되어 모든 전투 앵글이 마치 영화 같은 시각적 경험을 선사하도록 했다는 것이다.
전투가 끝난 후, 다양한 캐릭터들이 차례로 등장했다. 놀라웠던 점은 『섀도우 블레이드 제로』의 캐릭터 모델링 정교함이 내가 지금까지 본 그 어떤 싱글 플레이어 게임보다도 뛰어났을 뿐만 아니라, 심지어 경이로울 정도였다는 것이다.
캐릭터의 외형을 이토록 동양적인 미적 감각으로 다듬어낸 사례는 드물다. 이는 단순히 그동안 많은 플레이어들이 지적해 온 ‘인플루언서 같은 얼굴’이라는 문제를 해결한 것뿐만 아니라, 진정한 의미에서 동양적 미학을 바탕으로 한 얼굴 모델링에 있어 전례 없는 돌파구를 마련해 냈다.
『섀도우 블레이드 제로』에서도 스토리는 여전히 큰 비중을 차지하기 때문에, 이번 PV의 가장 큰 차이점은 상징적인 핵심 경험인 무협 전투 외에도, ‘혼’이 이 무협 세계에서 마주치는 다양한 인물들과 그들과 맺는 관계들이 대거 소개되었다는 점이다. 말 그대로 “사람이 있는 곳에야 비로소 무협 세계가 존재한다”는 것이다.
그 직후에는 지금까지 한 번도 공개된 적 없는 일련의 보스전이 이어지는데, 그중 실에 조종당하는 뱀 같은 여성이 특히 흥미롭습니다. 분명 또 한 번의 기상천외한 전투 경험이 될 것입니다.
무협과 사이버펑크 스타일이 혼합된 듯한 장면들도 여러 번 등장했는데, 예를 들어 머리 속에서 갑자기 튀어나온 거대한 전기 톱은 정말 『우혈』 특유의 분위기를 물씬 풍깁니다.
그중에는 악당의 대사 한 구절도 있는데, 이 역시 고전 무협물의 정취가 물씬 풍긴다. 모든 악당이 태생적으로 나쁜 사람은 아니다. 그들도 한때는 백성을 구하고 세상을 구하려 했을지 모르지만, 이상 간의 충돌로 인해 결국 타락의 길을 택하게 되었기에, 도대체 무슨 일이 있었는지 궁금해지지 않을 수 없다.
물론, 앞부분의 액션 장면들도 훌륭했지만, 마지막을 장식한 ‘예 사부’야말로 정말로 관객들의 열광을 이끌어낸 캐릭터라고 할 수 있겠다.
흐르는 물처럼 매끄러운 검술 대결이 이어진 후, 상징적인 윙춘권 동작이 등장하자마자 현장은 순식간에 열광의 도가니로 변했고, 박수갈채는 거의 끊이지 않고 이어졌다. 그리고 마지막에는 신비로운 가면을 쓴 남자의 정체가 마침내 밝혀지며, 예 사범의 등장에 다시 한번 관객들은 큰 감동을 받았다.
PV가 끝난 후, 프로듀서 양기위(S)가 모습을 드러내어 우리와 짧은 대화를 나누었습니다.S의 관점에서 볼 때, 《영의검 제로》가 가장 표현하고자 하는 것은 세 가지 관계, 즉 주인공 ‘혼’과 악당 사이의 대립 관계, 동료들 간의 우호적인 관계, 그리고 천하의 중생을 구원하는 보편적인 관계이며, 이것이야말로 그가 보는 진정한 의미의 의리라고 한다.
『섀도우 블레이드 제로』는 겉으로는 펑크 무협이라는 외피를 씌우고 있어, 극도로 자유분방한 무협 전투를 볼 수 있으며,사이버펑크와 판타지 스타일의 미술적 표현이 돋보이지만, 진정한 핵심은 여전히 고전적이면서도 약간의 참신함을 더한 무협 철학입니다. 이는 초기작인 『우혈』부터 『섀도우 블레이드 제로』에 이르기까지 줄곧 이어져 온 핵심 철학이기도 합니다.
진정한 의로움이란 무엇일까?

이어 쌍낫을 든 추격자 보스가 등장했고, 두 사람은 마차 위에서 눈부시게 화려한 대결을 펼쳤다. 특히 주목할 점은, 의도적으로 영화 같은 카메라 워크를 사용하지는 않았지만, 전투 장면 하나하나가 세심하게 설계되어 모든 전투 앵글이 마치 영화 같은 시각적 경험을 선사하도록 했다는 것이다.

전투가 끝난 후, 다양한 캐릭터들이 차례로 등장했다. 놀라웠던 점은 『섀도우 블레이드 제로』의 캐릭터 모델링 정교함이 내가 지금까지 본 그 어떤 싱글 플레이어 게임보다도 뛰어났을 뿐만 아니라, 심지어 경이로울 정도였다는 것이다.

캐릭터의 외형을 이토록 동양적인 미적 감각으로 다듬어낸 사례는 드물다. 이는 단순히 그동안 많은 플레이어들이 지적해 온 ‘인플루언서 같은 얼굴’이라는 문제를 해결한 것뿐만 아니라, 진정한 의미에서 동양적 미학을 바탕으로 한 얼굴 모델링에 있어 전례 없는 돌파구를 마련해 냈다.

『섀도우 블레이드 제로』에서도 스토리는 여전히 큰 비중을 차지하기 때문에, 이번 PV의 가장 큰 차이점은 상징적인 핵심 경험인 무협 전투 외에도, ‘혼’이 이 무협 세계에서 마주치는 다양한 인물들과 그들과 맺는 관계들이 대거 소개되었다는 점이다. 말 그대로 “사람이 있는 곳에야 비로소 무협 세계가 존재한다”는 것이다.

그 직후에는 지금까지 한 번도 공개된 적 없는 일련의 보스전이 이어지는데, 그중 실에 조종당하는 뱀 같은 여성이 특히 흥미롭습니다. 분명 또 한 번의 기상천외한 전투 경험이 될 것입니다.

무협과 사이버펑크 스타일이 혼합된 듯한 장면들도 여러 번 등장했는데, 예를 들어 머리 속에서 갑자기 튀어나온 거대한 전기 톱은 정말 『우혈』 특유의 분위기를 물씬 풍깁니다.

그중에는 악당의 대사 한 구절도 있는데, 이 역시 고전 무협물의 정취가 물씬 풍긴다. 모든 악당이 태생적으로 나쁜 사람은 아니다. 그들도 한때는 백성을 구하고 세상을 구하려 했을지 모르지만, 이상 간의 충돌로 인해 결국 타락의 길을 택하게 되었기에, 도대체 무슨 일이 있었는지 궁금해지지 않을 수 없다.

물론, 앞부분의 액션 장면들도 훌륭했지만, 마지막을 장식한 ‘예 사부’야말로 정말로 관객들의 열광을 이끌어낸 캐릭터라고 할 수 있겠다.

흐르는 물처럼 매끄러운 검술 대결이 이어진 후, 상징적인 윙춘권 동작이 등장하자마자 현장은 순식간에 열광의 도가니로 변했고, 박수갈채는 거의 끊이지 않고 이어졌다. 그리고 마지막에는 신비로운 가면을 쓴 남자의 정체가 마침내 밝혀지며, 예 사범의 등장에 다시 한번 관객들은 큰 감동을 받았다.

PV가 끝난 후, 프로듀서 양기위(S)가 모습을 드러내어 우리와 짧은 대화를 나누었습니다.S의 관점에서 볼 때, 《영의검 제로》가 가장 표현하고자 하는 것은 세 가지 관계, 즉 주인공 ‘혼’과 악당 사이의 대립 관계, 동료들 간의 우호적인 관계, 그리고 천하의 중생을 구원하는 보편적인 관계이며, 이것이야말로 그가 보는 진정한 의미의 의리라고 한다.

『섀도우 블레이드 제로』는 겉으로는 펑크 무협이라는 외피를 씌우고 있어, 극도로 자유분방한 무협 전투를 볼 수 있으며,사이버펑크와 판타지 스타일의 미술적 표현이 돋보이지만, 진정한 핵심은 여전히 고전적이면서도 약간의 참신함을 더한 무협 철학입니다. 이는 초기작인 『우혈』부터 『섀도우 블레이드 제로』에 이르기까지 줄곧 이어져 온 핵심 철학이기도 합니다.

진정한 의로움이란 무엇일까?

title: A edição padrão de «Shadow Blade Zero» está à venda a partir de 268 yuan. Espera lá… o que quer dizer que o Mestre Ye está a aquecer?
text:
Hoje, o grande jogo single-player de ação e aventura de estilo «wuxia punk» de produção nacional, «Shadow Blade Zero», revelou finalmente o seu preço de venda: 268 yuan para a edição normal e 328 yuan para a edição de luxo, em linha com o anterior «orgulho da indústria nacional», «Black Myth: Wukong».
Antes disso, muitos jogadores já tinham especulado que o preço poderia ser de 298 ou 328 yuan. Agora, dois anos após o lançamento da Black Monkey, o facto de o «Shadow Blade Zero» continuar a manter um preço tão acessível leva muitos jogadores a exclamar: «Liang Sheng é fantástico.»
Claro que, para além do preço surpresa, o que mais chamou a atenção foi, sem dúvida, o vídeo promocional de pré-venda de 11 minutos divulgado em simultâneo.Antes disso, a Chaguan e os nossos amigos da imprensa já tinham assistido a este vídeo promocional com meia hora de antecedência. Estávamos todos imersos na emoção extrema proporcionada pelas lutas de artes marciais, mas quando o logótipo já tinha aparecido, a entrada repentina do Mestre Ye fez com que a sala explodisse de entusiasmo quase num instante.
Isto é um jogo de artes marciais, não é? Espera lá, o que queres dizer com «o Mestre Ye está a aquecer»?
O PV começa com uma perseguição de carruagens e, em seguida, o protagonista, Hun, fica em cima da carruagem e luta «ao mesmo tempo contra os dois lados» contra os perseguidores a cavalo que vêm de ambos os lados.
Como se pode ver, apesar de haver algumas ações QTE, esta batalha é, na verdade, uma experiência de jogo totalmente «manual». O jogador tem de lutar num espaço extremamente estreito, utilizando todas as ações convencionais existentes — ataques, esquivas, contra-ataques e habilidades —, o que confere ao jogo um certo ambiente de filmes tradicionais de artes marciais.
Em seguida, surgiu um chefe inimigo, um perseguidor armado com duas foices, e os dois travaram um duelo espetacular na carroça. Vale a pena referir que, apesar de não terem sido utilizadas intencionalmente técnicas de filmagem cinematográficas, praticamente todas as cenas da batalha foram cuidadosamente concebidas para garantir que cada ângulo de combate proporcionasse uma experiência visual comparável à de um filme.
No final da batalha, todos os personagens entraram em cena. O que mais me surpreendeu foi que o nível de detalhe da modelação dos personagens de «Shadow Blade Zero» ultrapassou o de qualquer outro jogo para uma única plataforma que eu já tivesse visto, chegando mesmo a um nível impressionante.
Raramente vi alguém conseguir aperfeiçoar a imagem de uma personagem de forma a transmitir tão bem a estética oriental. Isto não só resolveu o problema, anteriormente criticado por muitos jogadores, de as personagens terem um rosto típico de «influenciador», como também representou, no verdadeiro sentido da palavra, um avanço sem precedentes no que diz respeito aos modelos faciais baseados na estética oriental.
O enredo também ocupa um lugar de destaque em «Shadow Blade Zero»; por isso, a principal diferença deste PV reside no facto de, para além dos combates de artes marciais — que constituem a experiência central e emblemática do jogo —, terem sido amplamente apresentadas as várias personagens com quem «Hun» interage neste mundo das artes marciais, bem como as ligações que o unem a elas. Como se costuma dizer: «Só onde há pessoas é que existe o mundo das artes marciais».
Segue-se então uma série de combates contra chefes nunca antes revelados, sendo que uma mulher com aspecto de cobra, controlada por fios, é particularmente interessante; será certamente mais uma experiência de combate cheia de imaginação.
Também surgiram várias vezes algumas cenas com um estilo misto de wuxia e cyberpunk, como, por exemplo, a enorme serra elétrica que surgiu do nada da cabeça — algo que é mesmo característico de «Rain Blood».
Há também um monólogo do vilão que tem um toque clássico de ficção marcial. Nem todos os vilões são maus por natureza; podem até ter salvado o povo e o mundo no passado, mas, devido a conflitos de ideais, acabaram por se deixar levar pela depravação, o que nos leva a questionar o que é que realmente aconteceu.
É claro que as cenas de ação anteriores foram, sem dúvida, espetaculares, mas o «Mestre Ye», que entrou em cena no final como grande atração, pode realmente ser considerado a personagem que fez o público explodir de entusiasmo.
Após uma sequência de combates com espadas fluidos e graciosos, a icónica técnica de Wing Chun, assim que foi executada, incendiou imediatamente toda a plateia, com aplausos que se mantiveram praticamente ininterruptos. No final, a identidade do misterioso homem enmascarado foi finalmente revelada, deixando o público mais uma vez impressionado com a entrada em cena do Mestre Ye.
Após o término do PV, o produtor Liang Qiwei (S) apareceu e teve uma breve conversa connosco.Na opinião de S, o que «Shadow Blade Zero» mais pretende expressar são três tipos de relações: a relação de oposição entre o protagonista, Hun, e o vilão; a relação de amizade entre companheiros; e a relação universal de salvar todos os seres vivos do mundo. É isto que, aos seus olhos, constitui o verdadeiro significado do cavalheirismo.
«Shadow Blade Zero» apresenta-se sob uma roupagem de wuxia punk, pelo que é possível assistir a combates de wuxia extremamente artísticos,com uma expressão artística que combina cyberpunk e fantasia, mas o seu verdadeiro cerne continua a ser um conceito de artes marciais clássico e, ao mesmo tempo, inovador — este é o princípio central que se mantém desde o início, com «Rain Blood», até ao «Shadow Blade Zero».
O que é, afinal, o verdadeiro espírito de cavalheirismo?

title: KI in den Spielabläufen, native Spiele und langfristiges Denken: Die Spiel-KI tritt in eine neue Ära des Konsenses ein
text:
Der Moment, in dem mir zum ersten Mal bewusst wurde, wie „cyber“ diese Ausgabe der ChinaJoy ist, ereignete sich, als ich in der Schlange stand, um „Resisters“ auszuprobieren.
Der Besucher vor mir hatte einen etwas seltsamen Gang. Bei genauerem Hinsehen stellte ich fest, dass er am Unterkörper ein motorisiertes Exoskelett trug. Er erzählte mir, dass es sich dabei nicht um ein Cosplay-Requisit handele, sondern um eine echte Ausrüstung, die man zu einem sehr erschwinglichen Preis am Eingang des Messegeländes mieten könne und die speziell dazu diene, das „Marschieren“ durch die Messe etwas zu erleichtern.Weiter vorne kämpften am Stand von Yushu Technology Roboter gegeneinander, und im Gang huschten immer wieder als Roboter verkleidete Cosplayer vorbei. Die unterschiedlichsten KI-Stände und Elemente futuristischer Technologie zogen sich durch die einzelnen Hallen des Shanghai New International Expo Centre.
Das offizielle Motto der diesjährigen ChinaJoy lautet „Gemeinsam mit KI auf Entdeckungsreise“ – es ist das erste Mal, dass eine konkrete Technologie zum Thema der Messe erklärt wurde. Spieler, die auf der Suche nach purem Spielspaß sind, werden vielleicht das Gefühl haben, dass es dieser CJ im traditionellen Sinne ein wenig an „Gamer-Flair“ mangelt; für Fachleute aus der Spielebranche hingegen dürfte die Ausrichtung der CJ auf breite Resonanz stoßen.
Gerade jetzt braucht die Branche einen Raum, in dem alle gemeinsam über die Zukunft der KI diskutieren können, und die Anziehungskraft dieser Leitmesse ist genau das Richtige, um die Pioniere, die ursprünglich auf verschiedene Unternehmen und Bereiche verteilt waren, an einem Ort zusammenzubringen.
Insbesondere nachdem ich die gesamte CJ-Messe besucht hatte, hatte ich zwei ganz deutliche Eindrücke.
Erstens: „Alle ziehen an einem Strang“ – im Vergleich zu vor etwas mehr als einem halben Jahr, als bei Veranstaltungen wie der GDC die meisten Branchenvertreter noch mehr oder weniger Angst vor KI hatten und berufliche Unsicherheit verspürten, ist die Stimmung mittlerweile deutlich gelassener.Bei den gemeinsamen Abendessen drehen sich die Gespräche mittlerweile um Themen wie „Welches Modell ist kostengünstiger?“ oder „Welcher Harness lässt sich besser nutzen?“. Schließlich entwickelt sich die KI weiter, und konkrete Produktivitätssteigerungen überzeugen die Menschen ganz von selbst.
Bei Geschäftstreffen befragten Investoren die Produzenten dazu, wie ihr Team KI einsetzt – die Frage, ob das Team über „KI-Denken“ verfügt, ist für viele Geldgeber mittlerweile zu einem wichtigen Kriterium bei der Beurteilung des Werts eines Spielprojekts geworden.In diesem Jahr waren deutlich mehr ausländische Besucher in den CJ-Hallen als in den Vorjahren. Obwohl allgemein angenommen wird, dass ausländische Hersteller gegenüber KI eine eher zurückhaltende Haltung einnehmen, haben mich viele im Gespräch von sich aus gefragt: „Wie setzen chinesische Unternehmen KI ein?“
Laut dem „Bericht zur Entwicklung der KI in der chinesischen Spieleindustrie 2026“ haben 80 % der 50 umsatzstärksten Unternehmen der chinesischen Spieleindustrie Maßnahmen im Bereich der KI ergriffen, und fast 60 % haben öffentlich bekannt gegeben, dass sie KI-Labore oder spezielle Teams eingerichtet haben.
Zweitens: „Es gibt mehr Richtungen“ – Was die Frage betrifft, in welcher Form KI das Gaming verändern wird, hat die Branche in den letzten zwei Jahren vor allem aus dem Nichts heraus nach Wegen gesucht; mittlerweile hat sich hier jedoch schon einiges geklärt.
Viele vage Ziele wurden in klare Aussagen zerlegt und in konkrete Schritte unterteilt; in einigen Bereichen hat sich sogar eine gemeinsame Ausrichtung herauskristallisiert, um die mehrere Unternehmen miteinander konkurrieren.Die sechs Branchen-Gipfel von CJ in diesem Jahr drehten sich alle um das übergeordnete Thema „KI-getriebene Erstellung digitaler Inhalte“.
