title: 高阶性能赋予高能战力 7X新作高帧稳定畅玩
text:
双十一开门红火热开启，恰逢《影之刃零》等多款重磅新游集中上线，一台高战力台式机可助玩家高帧高画质沉浸式畅玩全新大作。华硕天选7X搭载移动版英特尔®酷睿™Ultra 9处理器275HX，显卡配备华硕Dual GeForce RTX 5060Ti，还有四风扇散热系统与240mm一体式水冷散热器加持，直面3A新作与高强度任务都能稳定应对。购机可享主要部件3年上门服务与7×9小时热线支持，双十一开门红期间下单直降700元，部分地区还可叠加15%国家补贴，晒单再返50元京东E卡。
高阶性能赋予高能战力 新作高帧稳定运行
想要在新作的开放世界与激烈对战中稳住高帧率，核心硬件的性能表现是关键。酷睿Ultra 200HX，六边形战士来袭！华硕天选7X搭载移动版英特尔®酷睿™Ultra 9处理器275HX，24核心24线程，性能核睿频至高可达5.4GHz，辅以76MB L2+L3大容量缓存，多任务调度能力强劲；处理器内置APO游戏加速器，可对游戏负载进行底层优化，可在热门网游中获得更平稳的帧率表现。
显卡配备华硕Dual GeForce RTX 5060Ti，Blackwell架构打造，支持全景光线追踪与DLSS 4.5动态多帧生成技术。《影之刃零》华丽的武侠打斗特效、《使命召唤 23》真实的枪战光影细节都能细腻还原，即使开启2K高画质，帧率表现同样保持在流畅区间，带来沉浸式的游戏观感。
四风扇+240mm一体式水冷 鏖战新作冷静低噪
长时间鏖战新游大作，持续稳定的散热是性能全程在线的重要保障。华硕天选7X采用四风扇散热系统与240mm一体式水冷散热器，四枚120mm风扇布置于机箱前侧与后侧，持续引入冷空气，在机箱内形成立体循环风道，能够快速带走处理器与显卡产生的核心热量。240mm一体式水冷散热器覆盖处理器核心区域，高效带走热量，长时间高负载运行时也不会发生降频，画面帧率持续稳定。风扇采用环路动态轴承搭配自润滑设计，最长使用寿命可达160000小时，运行噪音维持在较低水平，沉浸游戏时不会被多余风噪干扰，酣战体验更专注。
47L次元海景房颜值在线 全能配置适配多场景
作为长期摆放在桌面上的设备，华硕天选7X的颜值同样可圈可点。整机延续天选家族次元美学风格，47L次元海景房机箱以6.5H硬度的强化钢化玻璃作为侧板，机箱内部的硬件排布与RGB灯光清晰可见；机箱正面配备炫彩灯带，借助AURA SYNC神光同步，键盘、鼠标、耳机等外设的灯光可实现统一联动，营造出更具个性的电竞桌面氛围。
存储上，出厂配备32GB DDR5内存与1TB SSD，游戏加载与文件读写响应迅速，同时预留充足扩展空间，至高支持64GB DDR5内存及2TB SSD+2TB HDD存储组合，新作陆续入库、素材持续累积也无需再为容量顾虑；玩家自行加装内存、硬盘不影响整机保修，为后续升级留足余地。接口涵盖6×USB 3.2 Gen1 Type-A、2×USB 2.0 Type-A、1×USB 3.2 Gen1 Type-C、2×HDMI 2.1b、DP 1.4等，显示器、手柄、耳机、移动硬盘等外设均可直连，可进一步增强游戏体验。
眼下双十一开门红，正是入手华硕天选7X的好时机。购机可享700元立减优惠，部分地区还能叠加15%国家补贴，完成晒单好评再返 50E卡；售后更提供主要部件3年上门服务与7×9小时热线支持，计划近期畅玩热门新作的玩家，不妨重点考虑华硕天选7X高性能游戏台式机。

title: 硬核音游《韵律源点Arcaea》国服现已上线，专属成长助力，百万预约送开服大礼！
text:
如果你喜欢音乐，也许早先就听过《韵律源点Arcaea》这个名字。这款由lowiro工作室开发，于2017年上线的下落式音游，凭借绚丽的二次元画面和优美动听的音乐曲目吸引了大量玩家。同时，其独创的双层立体式下落方式，也让原本下落式音游的复杂性和操作难度更上一层楼，被不少玩家奉为玩法最硬核的音游之一。
所谓双层立体式下落，是在传统下落式音游的基础上再多加一层，让整个谱面分为天空和地面两个维度，玩家在弹奏时需要通过画面的3D透视关系来判断Note的落点是在哪个层面，这大大增加了精准操作难度，而且不同层线条还可能会跨越层级，再次挑战玩家的双手协调性与反应极限。

title: Revenue Tops 300 Million in Three Weeks: An Interview with the Producer—How Was an "Unsafe" Sequel Made?
text:
Remedy recently announced that *Control: Resonance* has surpassed one million copies sold worldwide, setting the fastest sales record in the Finnish studio’s 31-year history. Previously, the record was held by *Alan Wake 2*, which took about two months to reach that milestone.
Based on estimates using the Standard Edition price of $59.99, the Deluxe Edition price of $69.99, and actual pricing in different regions,revenue from 1 million copies of *Control: Resonance* would be approximately $45 million to $52 million, equivalent to over 300 million yuan.
The game has received Metacritic scores ranging from 81 to 84 across various platforms, and since its release, its global “Positive” rating on Steam has remained between 87% and 91%. Players in different regions have different perspectives on this sequel, but most of the discussion centers on how it builds upon the series’ legacy:
How did Remedy take *Control* in a new direction while preserving the series’ original essence?
At this point in time, this issue deserves extra attention. Over the past few years, the gaming industry in Europe and the United States has experienced massive layoffs, project cancellations, and extended development cycles.As the investment required for AAA games continues to rise, any shift in a project’s direction can rapidly increase both the time and costs involved. Under heightened commercial pressure, sticking with proven franchises, gameplay mechanics, and market segments has become the more straightforward choice. In contrast, *Control: Resonance* has opted for a more pronounced change in direction.
These changes are most evident in the game itself: the protagonist has shifted from Jesse Faden to Dylan Faden, combat has shifted from shooting to melee, and the main setting has moved from Taiguya to Manhattan.A studio known for its first-person shooters is now re-exploring how to execute close-quarters combat effectively; at the same time, Remedy has also taken on the responsibility of self-publishing *Resonance*, a buy-to-play single-player game.
So what makes *Control: Resonance* worth discussing isn’t just its sales figures, but also how it was made.
Previously, during a talk in Cologne, Juha Vainio, executive producer of *Control: Resonance*, described the production process of the original *Control* as “crazy.” During the final year, the team was constantly in a state of panic and had to constantly put out fires; some of the features they had originally planned to include were ultimately cut due to budget constraints.
When discussing *Control: Resonance*, Juha presented a set of results that were almost the opposite. According to him, each stage gate was passed quite smoothly, the quality certification process didn’t involve any back-and-forth, and the release date came earlier than the internal timeline set during pre-production.In employee surveys, the team scored higher than both the company average and the industry average on every metric.
This is not a sequel with fewer changes and a safer approach.
“We wanted to do something different, rather than a ‘safe’ sequel,” Vainio said. For Remedy, the challenge was how to maintain creative freedom while ensuring these new experiments had a more solid production foundation.
His explanation focused first on pre-production. Remedy used a small team—about 20 percent of its full staff—to spend more time validating the core gameplay and fine-tuning the production pipeline before scaling up to begin full-scale production. This is how melee combat was repeatedly refined and confirmed to be viable. For a studio with no prior experience developing melee-based games, this risk was identified and validated as early as possible.
However, not all issues can be resolved during pre-production.
The “gravity anomaly” that allows Dylan to walk on walls and ceilings was still being tested right up until the official production phase. The initial version caused severe motion sickness, but the team felt this feature couldn’t be cut: as Juha put it, if they abandoned it, the entire game would fall apart.They tried at least four or five different solutions and spent several years before finally arriving at the current version, which causes almost no dizziness.
As a result, “risk management” is no longer just a procedural issue. Which questions must be answered early on, and which can be carried over to the next phase? When a feature isn’t fully developed yet, how does the team determine whether to continue investing in it? Phase gates, checklists, and production pipelines can provide guidance, but ultimately, someone still needs to participate in the discussion and make the decision.
At the TapTap Game Festival, we had the opportunity to chat with Juha about the development process of *Control: Resonance*.This interview took place prior to the game’s release. Building on the production changes Vainio discussed in his presentation, we asked further questions about how prototype validation, stage sign-offs, team collaboration, and user testing worked in practice.
This discussion focuses on how Remedy established a more reliable production framework for creative changes in a bold sequel.
The following is the edited transcript of the interview.
01
Don’t Make a Safe Sequel
Q: This installment features a new protagonist, a revamped core combat system, and new main settings. For a sequel to a highly acclaimed title, these are quite radical choices. How did you weigh these decisions at the time?
Juha: We wanted to do something different, rather than a “safe” sequel.One of the core pillars of the *Control* series is called “The World of Control,” and it has guided us from the very beginning—starting with the fact that the first game was titled *Control* rather than being named after the protagonist, “Jesse Faden,” like *Max Payne* or *Alan Wake*.
In all “Control” games, the world is the key element, and most changes are driven by it: the protagonist was changed so that “Control” wouldn’t be solely about Jesse Faden; the characters left the ancient house to more vividly showcase the world of “Control”; and the shift from shooting to melee combat was made to distinguish Dylan’s gameplay from Jesse’s.
Q: Now that the game has shifted to melee combat, what new experiences does it offer that the previous games didn’t?
Juha: Melee and ranged combat are completely different experiences. With ranged combat, you keep your distance from enemies and don’t get as deeply embroiled in the thick of battle; melee combat, on the other hand, is true “hand-to-hand combat.”One feature we added specifically for melee combat is the visually striking “execution”—something you won’t find in shooter combat: when an enemy’s health is very low, pressing the left stick on the controller allows you to execute them in a spectacular fashion.
Another important point is that we use supernatural abilities to complement melee combat: you can still create distance using abilities like “Throw,” and then close in for melee combat. This takes the strategic depth of combat to a whole new level.
Q: Some players believe that a closed indoor environment is better suited for creating a sense of tension. Why did you still choose to leave the old house?
Juha: First, we approach the issue as “two sides of the same coin”: the original and the sequel—one set indoors, the other outdoors;one is the older sister, the other the younger brother; one is a shooter, the other a melee game… Almost everything is built on this contrast, so stepping out of Taiguya and into Manhattan felt very natural to us.
Second, this actually gives us more tools to create a sense of tension. In Manhattan, you can still enter the building; it’s not entirely open-air. By starting with some slower-paced outdoor sections before entering an extremely tense underground space, the atmosphere can build up layer by layer.
Q: For many players, what they love most about *Control* is actually its setting, world-building, and storyline. Internally, how do you prioritize gameplay and content?
Juha: We still place a great deal of emphasis on storytelling—it’s the foundation of Remedy. We make narrative-driven, story-driven games; it’s in our DNA. When it comes to storytelling and world-building, I’d say *Resonance* is at least on par with the original—if not better.
What we particularly wanted to achieve with *Resonance*—and what is the goal of the entire series—is to elevate gameplay to the same level as the narrative. To that end, we assembled the largest gameplay team in Remedy’s history, included a wider variety of enemies than in the original game, and overall, the gameplay has indeed taken on greater significance.
As for the order of things, in traditional Remedy projects, the gameplay was generally shaped by the writing and narrative. Now it’s the other way around: gameplay priorities drive the narrative and determine what goes into the script.
02
Use a smaller team to address all issues early on
Q: How long did the early validation phase of *Resonance* last? How large was the team at that time?
Juha: Our pre-production phase was quite long—almost as long as the entire development period for the first game. The idea was to use a small team and take more time to address all the issues that arose during pre-production before expanding the team and moving into full-scale production. That’s exactly where we fell short with the first game.
The pre-production team is currently about 20% of full capacity, with slight fluctuations depending on the phase.The advantage of a small team is the ability to iterate quickly and find answers to questions such as “Can we implement melee combat?” or “How exactly do gravity anomalies work?”… In addition, there are a number of relatively simple supernatural abilities that we also hope to prototype as early as possible. That way, once we actually begin production and the team expands to full capacity, everyone will no longer need to ask questions—they’ll just need to execute.
Q: Before scaling up and moving into full-scale production, what is the key question this small team must answer?
Juha: It all comes down to the basics: What are the biggest unknowns and risks we’ll face? How can we minimize the probability of these risks occurring? We also need to figure out the appropriate production pipeline and pace so we know exactly how much content we can handle within the given budget and timeline.
Q: Melee combat is one of the biggest risks in the early stages of the project. How did you validate it?
Juha: For a studio known for its shooting games, developing a melee-focused game is risky, so we put a lot of effort into it right from the start of pre-production, using prototypes to test the feel of the melee combat, and we really spent several years polishing it. From the outside, it might seem simple—”Hey, let’s make a melee game”—but in reality, it’s not that easy.
We only move on to the production phase once we’re satisfied with the melee combat and are confident we know what to do. If we leave the iterative development of melee combat until the production phase, the costs will be much higher, and it will lead to a lot of last-minute firefighting.
Q: Many of the creative ideas in the *Control* series are difficult to explain using existing works. The vision that designers, artists, and programmers have for the same line of dialogue can be completely different. Have you ever encountered this kind of misalignment in understanding?
Juha: That’s true. Most of our concepts are quite abstract, so it’s hard to find existing examples to compare them to. A typical example is gravitational anomalies: Dylan can walk on walls and ceilings. It’s easy to write on paper, “We have gravitational anomalies,” but everyone understands it differently.
So during the pre-production phase, we created a large number of prototypes to gradually clarify exactly what this concept meant for different disciplines, such as programming, game design, visual effects, and sound design. Take “gravity anomalies” as an example: What sound should play when gravity switches to the wall? Which areas are walkable, and how should they be visualized?What would it look like to walk along a wall under abnormal gravity? We iterated on the design repeatedly and finally made a decision: any surface that looks walkable is actually walkable, so we no longer use any special effects to indicate this—if it looks like you can step on it, you really can.
Simply put, the answer is plenty of prototyping and repeated iterations.
Q: Were there any particularly memorable difficulties or challenges during this process?
Juha: When I first started working on gravity anomalies, I was very prone to motion sickness—it was really bad at first.
We also conducted extensive prototyping and user testing; it took several years of development to arrive at this version, which causes virtually no motion sickness. We conducted multiple rounds of motion sickness testing specifically targeting gravitational anomalies and tried at least four or five different methods to improve the experience.
Gravity anomalies are one of the most important features of this game, so this issue was a major concern for us. If we couldn’t resolve the motion sickness problem, we wouldn’t be able to release the game—because we couldn’t possibly cut this feature; doing so would ruin the entire game. We had no choice but to solve it, so we invested a great deal of effort and resources into it.
Q: Were “Gravity Anomaly” and “Close Combat” designed from the start as a pair of complementary gameplay mechanics? Which one supports the other?
Juha: These were separate ideas. The first thing we decided on for this game was “we’re going to make a melee game”—that was the foundation for everything. Of course, as I’ve said, we can’t cut either the gravity anomalies or the melee combat; we have to get both right.
The difference is this: Although melee combat was a risk for Remedy, we always knew—especially after pre-production—that we could pull it off. It already felt solid during pre-production, and there was never any risk that we wouldn’t be able to make it work;Gravity Anomaly, on the other hand, was still undergoing extensive testing and refinement during active development, and even once we entered the production phase, the question of “whether we could pull it off” remained a constant source of anxiety.
03
Use a door to determine whether you can go down
Q: From early exploration to pre-release polishing, how are release schedules and milestones planned?
Juha: We use what’s known as the “stage-gate” model. We had a very simplified version of it when we were working on the first generation, but since we made a full transition to managing multiple projects in parallel, we’ve placed much greater emphasis on it. Because a delay at any one stage can have a ripple effect on other projects, we must set very clear criteria for each stage.
Taking pre-production as an example, it is divided into several stages: concept development, proof of concept, and production readiness, each with its own set of standards. A project must pass the “production readiness” stage before it can move on to production.
During the concept development phase, the game’s overall concept must first be finalized; during the proof-of-concept phase, a large number of prototypes are created, such as gravity anomalies and various supernatural abilities; once satisfied with the prototypes, the project moves into the pre-production phase, whose main goal is to ensure that all production pipelines are fully operational so that production doesn’t hit any snags during the official development phase. By that point, the team is quite large, and if production stalls, the costs will be far higher than during the early stages of development.
Q: If a release has all the planned features but the user experience falls short of expectations, how should the team decide whether to release it, continue refining it, or adjust the scope?
Juha: There are checklists for each phase, and sometimes it’s simply not possible to complete them all. In those cases, the most important thing is to identify where we fell short and make it a priority for the next phase.For example, suppose a phase lasts five months. If a prototype isn’t completed during the proof-of-concept phase, we’ll make it the top priority for the first month of the production-ready phase and work on it in parallel with other important tasks in that phase to ensure it’s resolved, thereby avoiding delays.
In theory, if a phase fails badly, we could extend the deadline, but we usually don’t, because that would mean delaying the entire project and affecting other projects. So we prefer a “conditional pass”: first, we identify the most critical issues that must be resolved as soon as possible; only if even those aren’t resolved will we reconsider the schedule.However, *Resonance* passed every stage gate quite smoothly.
Q: In the original *Control*, the variety of enemies was reduced due to budget cuts, but the new game features more factions and more variants. What has the team improved upon to move from “a one-time effort” to “consistent mass production”?
Juha: The prototypes and iterations for all enemy factions and types were completed during the early production phase, with the highest-risk ones tackled first and the simpler ones left for later. By the time we reached the production-ready stage, we had reliable data on production rates, knew how many variants we could create, and had a general idea of what they would look like.
At that point, we were already very confident in the scope we could deliver, and we had a clear understanding of the size of the world as well as the overall requirements for different enemy types and variants. For us, scope management is an ongoing process; we dynamically take everything into account and adjust it to fit the project parameters, striving to reduce the scope as early as possible to avoid waste.
Q: This project was completed ahead of the internal schedule. Looking back, what do you attribute this to?
Juha: There are many factors that contributed to this. Compared to the first game, one of the key factors was that we made sure all open questions from pre-production were answered during that phase, rather than waiting until the production phase—when the team is larger and everything is more expensive—to find the answers. This, in turn, led to faster decision-making during production; the planning was more solid, and naturally, there was less last-minute firefighting down the line.
04
Provide support rather than lead the project
Q: *Resonance* is Remedy’s first major title since the company shifted to a multi-project approach and began self-publishing. What has been the biggest change within the company as it transitioned from a single-project model to a multi-project one?
Juha: Moving from a single project to multiple projects has undoubtedly been a journey filled with learning. A key change at Remedy following *Control* has been the development of a better holistic view of all projects—such as personnel dependencies across projects. Today, the studio is better equipped to meet the needs of each project and make better prioritization decisions across them.
Q: I’ve heard that you have a Project Management Office (PMO) that took two or three years to shift from “leading projects” to “supporting projects.” What did it stop doing, and what did it start doing?
Juha: When we transition from a single-project (or dual-project) company to a multi-project company, we need an organization to manage the entire project portfolio—which is why I discussed the establishment of a PMO in my presentation. For Remedy, this has been a learning curve: how to transform from a highly project-centric organization into one with a dedicated department that specifically handles the relationships between projects.
Initially, the PMO’s role was to lead projects. However, when all responsibilities—such as delivering results and ensuring a return on investment—fell on the project teams, this structure didn’t work very well, so it had to evolve into a support organization. Now, projects operate independently, but they turn to the PMO to resolve conflicts.
The most common issue is personnel conflicts—for example, when we need a visual effects artist, and another project needs one as well. The PMO is the party we turn to; it facilitates discussions to determine which project needs the artist more—or whether we should hire another one. That’s how it’s set up now: the PMO doesn’t lead projects; it supports them.
Q: Can we choose a cross-discipline feature to see how it progresses over the course of an iteration? Who is responsible for the final gameplay experience?
Juha: Most of our features span multiple disciplines; let’s take a “weapon variant” as an example. This work spans the entire process, from the early stages of pre-production to the end of production, and depending on the situation, some phases may overlap.
First, the gameplay design team decides what to create, develops an initial design and prototype, and refines it to a point where it’s roughly ready for implementation; they then ask the gameplay programmers to implement the various supporting features required for implementation.Concept artists are responsible for the weapon’s visual design, which is then brought to life by hard-surface artists and character artists. Animators create the animations showing Dylan using the weapon. Once the weapon is roughly finalized, the audio team designs the various sound effects associated with it; the visual effects team then finalizes the weapon’s visual appearance in all its states, including all abilities that might affect its appearance.
Iterations take place within each team’s individual development cycles, as well as at a higher level, to ensure that all components fit together seamlessly. The gameplay experience is the responsibility of the gameplay designers, while the Creative Director is ultimately responsible for it as part of the overall creative experience.
Q: So how are decisions communicated from leadership to the team? Is there a bottom-up mechanism?
Juha: Most of the time, it depends on the specific situation. However, the project has a core leadership team that typically makes high-level strategic decisions. In the creative realm, the Game Director communicates with the leads of each creative discipline—such as the Lead Level Designer, Lead Game Designer, and Lead Environment Artist—who then communicate with their respective team members.On the production management side, the Development Director communicates with the various producers, who then oversee the implementation of production tasks.
There is certainly a bottom-up mechanism in place: as long as it’s not a particularly high-level strategic decision, we typically involve the team in any decisions that pertain to them directly, and their input can be escalated to the leadership team and then fed back to the team. Moreover, each team tends to operate quite independently.For example, the team responsible for creating enemies develops the enemies themselves; we review the final results, and all decisions are made by them—we simply provide feedback as reviewers.
05
Use Testing to Disprove Unreasonable Designs
Q: The number of users in this round of testing was significantly higher than in previous iterations. Were there any test results that were particularly unexpected—or even overturned a design we were originally very confident in?
Juha: We conducted a lot of user testing and learned a great deal, but most of it just confirmed what we already knew.
A good example is the “melee-supernatural ability resource mechanism,” which forms the foundation of the entire combat system. We didn’t want players to rely solely on supernatural abilities and turn the game into a ranged experience, so we designed a resource system where successful melee hits recharge supernatural abilities.
Originally, this system was bidirectional: players had to use supernatural abilities to engage in melee combat, and they had to use melee combat to use supernatural abilities. But for some reason, players felt that this didn’t feel right and wasn’t as fun. Later, we conducted an A/B test: in the other version, melee combat could be used freely, and only supernatural abilities required resources.After extensive player testing, we found that this one-way resource mechanism was more fun and felt more like a typical ARPG. This is an example of how we revised our original design based on user research findings.
Q: Team well-being has been identified as a key metric. Aside from confidence in the work itself, what specific changes have actually taken place in our day-to-day work practices?
Juha: The internal communication structure within the team has matured significantly. Team members now have a clearer understanding of the decisions made by leadership and the reasoning behind them, which has led to greater overall satisfaction.On the other hand, there’s the production model: we now have much better control over the production schedule and no longer have to constantly “put out fires.” This also means that the project’s direction and what the next phase will look like are more predictable—unlike the chaos we experienced with the first game. Compared to the first game, everyone is much more satisfied with this project.
Q: Since we started self-publishing, the marketing and development teams have been working more closely together. Has this had any practical impact on product decisions?
Juha: We work very closely together—especially the leadership team and the marketing team—on aspects such as positioning and how to communicate the game. This hasn’t affected the game itself on a creative level; the game team still makes all decisions with a high degree of independence. However, it has certainly influenced “how we talk about” the game.
Take the first game as an example: many people who played it later didn’t pick it up at first precisely because the marketing message at the time was “this game is weird,” but after playing it, they all said they loved it. This is undoubtedly one of the lessons we’ve learned from the marketing team.The game is still weird, and *Resonance* is still weird—that’s in Remedy’s DNA. But the way we talk about it now is that it’s so much more than just “weird.”
html:
Remedy recently announced that *Control: Resonance* has surpassed one million copies sold worldwide, setting the fastest sales record in the Finnish studio’s 31-year history. Previously, the record was held by *Alan Wake 2*, which took about two months to reach that milestone.

Based on estimates using the Standard Edition price of $59.99, the Deluxe Edition price of $69.99, and actual pricing in different regions,revenue from 1 million copies of *Control: Resonance* would be approximately $45 million to $52 million, equivalent to over 300 million yuan.

The game has received Metacritic scores ranging from 81 to 84 across various platforms, and since its release, its global “Positive” rating on Steam has remained between 87% and 91%. Players in different regions have different perspectives on this sequel, but most of the discussion centers on how it builds upon the series’ legacy:

How did Remedy take *Control* in a new direction while preserving the series’ original essence?

At this point in time, this issue deserves extra attention. Over the past few years, the gaming industry in Europe and the United States has experienced massive layoffs, project cancellations, and extended development cycles.As the investment required for AAA games continues to rise, any shift in a project’s direction can rapidly increase both the time and costs involved. Under heightened commercial pressure, sticking with proven franchises, gameplay mechanics, and market segments has become the more straightforward choice. In contrast, *Control: Resonance* has opted for a more pronounced change in direction.

These changes are most evident in the game itself: the protagonist has shifted from Jesse Faden to Dylan Faden, combat has shifted from shooting to melee, and the main setting has moved from Taiguya to Manhattan.A studio known for its first-person shooters is now re-exploring how to execute close-quarters combat effectively; at the same time, Remedy has also taken on the responsibility of self-publishing *Resonance*, a buy-to-play single-player game.

So what makes *Control: Resonance* worth discussing isn’t just its sales figures, but also how it was made.

Previously, during a talk in Cologne, Juha Vainio, executive producer of *Control: Resonance*, described the production process of the original *Control* as “crazy.” During the final year, the team was constantly in a state of panic and had to constantly put out fires; some of the features they had originally planned to include were ultimately cut due to budget constraints.

When discussing *Control: Resonance*, Juha presented a set of results that were almost the opposite. According to him, each stage gate was passed quite smoothly, the quality certification process didn’t involve any back-and-forth, and the release date came earlier than the internal timeline set during pre-production.In employee surveys, the team scored higher than both the company average and the industry average on every metric.

This is not a sequel with fewer changes and a safer approach.

“We wanted to do something different, rather than a ‘safe’ sequel,” Vainio said. For Remedy, the challenge was how to maintain creative freedom while ensuring these new experiments had a more solid production foundation.

His explanation focused first on pre-production. Remedy used a small team—about 20 percent of its full staff—to spend more time validating the core gameplay and fine-tuning the production pipeline before scaling up to begin full-scale production. This is how melee combat was repeatedly refined and confirmed to be viable. For a studio with no prior experience developing melee-based games, this risk was identified and validated as early as possible.

However, not all issues can be resolved during pre-production.

The “gravity anomaly” that allows Dylan to walk on walls and ceilings was still being tested right up until the official production phase. The initial version caused severe motion sickness, but the team felt this feature couldn’t be cut: as Juha put it, if they abandoned it, the entire game would fall apart.They tried at least four or five different solutions and spent several years before finally arriving at the current version, which causes almost no dizziness.

As a result, “risk management” is no longer just a procedural issue. Which questions must be answered early on, and which can be carried over to the next phase? When a feature isn’t fully developed yet, how does the team determine whether to continue investing in it? Phase gates, checklists, and production pipelines can provide guidance, but ultimately, someone still needs to participate in the discussion and make the decision.

At the TapTap Game Festival, we had the opportunity to chat with Juha about the development process of *Control: Resonance*.This interview took place prior to the game’s release. Building on the production changes Vainio discussed in his presentation, we asked further questions about how prototype validation, stage sign-offs, team collaboration, and user testing worked in practice.

This discussion focuses on how Remedy established a more reliable production framework for creative changes in a bold sequel.

The following is the edited transcript of the interview.

01

Don’t Make a Safe Sequel

Q: This installment features a new protagonist, a revamped core combat system, and new main settings. For a sequel to a highly acclaimed title, these are quite radical choices. How did you weigh these decisions at the time?

Juha: We wanted to do something different, rather than a “safe” sequel.One of the core pillars of the *Control* series is called “The World of Control,” and it has guided us from the very beginning—starting with the fact that the first game was titled *Control* rather than being named after the protagonist, “Jesse Faden,” like *Max Payne* or *Alan Wake*.

In all “Control” games, the world is the key element, and most changes are driven by it: the protagonist was changed so that “Control” wouldn’t be solely about Jesse Faden; the characters left the ancient house to more vividly showcase the world of “Control”; and the shift from shooting to melee combat was made to distinguish Dylan’s gameplay from Jesse’s.

Q: Now that the game has shifted to melee combat, what new experiences does it offer that the previous games didn’t?

Juha: Melee and ranged combat are completely different experiences. With ranged combat, you keep your distance from enemies and don’t get as deeply embroiled in the thick of battle; melee combat, on the other hand, is true “hand-to-hand combat.”One feature we added specifically for melee combat is the visually striking “execution”—something you won’t find in shooter combat: when an enemy’s health is very low, pressing the left stick on the controller allows you to execute them in a spectacular fashion.

Another important point is that we use supernatural abilities to complement melee combat: you can still create distance using abilities like “Throw,” and then close in for melee combat. This takes the strategic depth of combat to a whole new level.

Q: Some players believe that a closed indoor environment is better suited for creating a sense of tension. Why did you still choose to leave the old house?

Juha: First, we approach the issue as “two sides of the same coin”: the original and the sequel—one set indoors, the other outdoors;one is the older sister, the other the younger brother; one is a shooter, the other a melee game… Almost everything is built on this contrast, so stepping out of Taiguya and into Manhattan felt very natural to us.

Second, this actually gives us more tools to create a sense of tension. In Manhattan, you can still enter the building; it’s not entirely open-air. By starting with some slower-paced outdoor sections before entering an extremely tense underground space, the atmosphere can build up layer by layer.

Q: For many players, what they love most about *Control* is actually its setting, world-building, and storyline. Internally, how do you prioritize gameplay and content?

Juha: We still place a great deal of emphasis on storytelling—it’s the foundation of Remedy. We make narrative-driven, story-driven games; it’s in our DNA. When it comes to storytelling and world-building, I’d say *Resonance* is at least on par with the original—if not better.

What we particularly wanted to achieve with *Resonance*—and what is the goal of the entire series—is to elevate gameplay to the same level as the narrative. To that end, we assembled the largest gameplay team in Remedy’s history, included a wider variety of enemies than in the original game, and overall, the gameplay has indeed taken on greater significance.

As for the order of things, in traditional Remedy projects, the gameplay was generally shaped by the writing and narrative. Now it’s the other way around: gameplay priorities drive the narrative and determine what goes into the script.

02

Use a smaller team to address all issues early on

Q: How long did the early validation phase of *Resonance* last? How large was the team at that time?

Juha: Our pre-production phase was quite long—almost as long as the entire development period for the first game. The idea was to use a small team and take more time to address all the issues that arose during pre-production before expanding the team and moving into full-scale production. That’s exactly where we fell short with the first game.

The pre-production team is currently about 20% of full capacity, with slight fluctuations depending on the phase.The advantage of a small team is the ability to iterate quickly and find answers to questions such as “Can we implement melee combat?” or “How exactly do gravity anomalies work?”… In addition, there are a number of relatively simple supernatural abilities that we also hope to prototype as early as possible. That way, once we actually begin production and the team expands to full capacity, everyone will no longer need to ask questions—they’ll just need to execute.

Q: Before scaling up and moving into full-scale production, what is the key question this small team must answer?

Juha: It all comes down to the basics: What are the biggest unknowns and risks we’ll face? How can we minimize the probability of these risks occurring? We also need to figure out the appropriate production pipeline and pace so we know exactly how much content we can handle within the given budget and timeline.

Q: Melee combat is one of the biggest risks in the early stages of the project. How did you validate it?

Juha: For a studio known for its shooting games, developing a melee-focused game is risky, so we put a lot of effort into it right from the start of pre-production, using prototypes to test the feel of the melee combat, and we really spent several years polishing it. From the outside, it might seem simple—”Hey, let’s make a melee game”—but in reality, it’s not that easy.

We only move on to the production phase once we’re satisfied with the melee combat and are confident we know what to do. If we leave the iterative development of melee combat until the production phase, the costs will be much higher, and it will lead to a lot of last-minute firefighting.

Q: Many of the creative ideas in the *Control* series are difficult to explain using existing works. The vision that designers, artists, and programmers have for the same line of dialogue can be completely different. Have you ever encountered this kind of misalignment in understanding?

Juha: That’s true. Most of our concepts are quite abstract, so it’s hard to find existing examples to compare them to. A typical example is gravitational anomalies: Dylan can walk on walls and ceilings. It’s easy to write on paper, “We have gravitational anomalies,” but everyone understands it differently.

So during the pre-production phase, we created a large number of prototypes to gradually clarify exactly what this concept meant for different disciplines, such as programming, game design, visual effects, and sound design. Take “gravity anomalies” as an example: What sound should play when gravity switches to the wall? Which areas are walkable, and how should they be visualized?What would it look like to walk along a wall under abnormal gravity? We iterated on the design repeatedly and finally made a decision: any surface that looks walkable is actually walkable, so we no longer use any special effects to indicate this—if it looks like you can step on it, you really can.

Simply put, the answer is plenty of prototyping and repeated iterations.

Q: Were there any particularly memorable difficulties or challenges during this process?

Juha: When I first started working on gravity anomalies, I was very prone to motion sickness—it was really bad at first.

We also conducted extensive prototyping and user testing; it took several years of development to arrive at this version, which causes virtually no motion sickness. We conducted multiple rounds of motion sickness testing specifically targeting gravitational anomalies and tried at least four or five different methods to improve the experience.

Gravity anomalies are one of the most important features of this game, so this issue was a major concern for us. If we couldn’t resolve the motion sickness problem, we wouldn’t be able to release the game—because we couldn’t possibly cut this feature; doing so would ruin the entire game. We had no choice but to solve it, so we invested a great deal of effort and resources into it.

Q: Were “Gravity Anomaly” and “Close Combat” designed from the start as a pair of complementary gameplay mechanics? Which one supports the other?

Juha: These were separate ideas. The first thing we decided on for this game was “we’re going to make a melee game”—that was the foundation for everything. Of course, as I’ve said, we can’t cut either the gravity anomalies or the melee combat; we have to get both right.

The difference is this: Although melee combat was a risk for Remedy, we always knew—especially after pre-production—that we could pull it off. It already felt solid during pre-production, and there was never any risk that we wouldn’t be able to make it work;Gravity Anomaly, on the other hand, was still undergoing extensive testing and refinement during active development, and even once we entered the production phase, the question of “whether we could pull it off” remained a constant source of anxiety.

03

Use a door to determine whether you can go down

Q: From early exploration to pre-release polishing, how are release schedules and milestones planned?

Juha: We use what’s known as the “stage-gate” model. We had a very simplified version of it when we were working on the first generation, but since we made a full transition to managing multiple projects in parallel, we’ve placed much greater emphasis on it. Because a delay at any one stage can have a ripple effect on other projects, we must set very clear criteria for each stage.

Taking pre-production as an example, it is divided into several stages: concept development, proof of concept, and production readiness, each with its own set of standards. A project must pass the “production readiness” stage before it can move on to production.

During the concept development phase, the game’s overall concept must first be finalized; during the proof-of-concept phase, a large number of prototypes are created, such as gravity anomalies and various supernatural abilities; once satisfied with the prototypes, the project moves into the pre-production phase, whose main goal is to ensure that all production pipelines are fully operational so that production doesn’t hit any snags during the official development phase. By that point, the team is quite large, and if production stalls, the costs will be far higher than during the early stages of development.

Q: If a release has all the planned features but the user experience falls short of expectations, how should the team decide whether to release it, continue refining it, or adjust the scope?

Juha: There are checklists for each phase, and sometimes it’s simply not possible to complete them all. In those cases, the most important thing is to identify where we fell short and make it a priority for the next phase.For example, suppose a phase lasts five months. If a prototype isn’t completed during the proof-of-concept phase, we’ll make it the top priority for the first month of the production-ready phase and work on it in parallel with other important tasks in that phase to ensure it’s resolved, thereby avoiding delays.

In theory, if a phase fails badly, we could extend the deadline, but we usually don’t, because that would mean delaying the entire project and affecting other projects. So we prefer a “conditional pass”: first, we identify the most critical issues that must be resolved as soon as possible; only if even those aren’t resolved will we reconsider the schedule.However, *Resonance* passed every stage gate quite smoothly.

Q: In the original *Control*, the variety of enemies was reduced due to budget cuts, but the new game features more factions and more variants. What has the team improved upon to move from “a one-time effort” to “consistent mass production”?

Juha: The prototypes and iterations for all enemy factions and types were completed during the early production phase, with the highest-risk ones tackled first and the simpler ones left for later. By the time we reached the production-ready stage, we had reliable data on production rates, knew how many variants we could create, and had a general idea of what they would look like.

At that point, we were already very confident in the scope we could deliver, and we had a clear understanding of the size of the world as well as the overall requirements for different enemy types and variants. For us, scope management is an ongoing process; we dynamically take everything into account and adjust it to fit the project parameters, striving to reduce the scope as early as possible to avoid waste.

Q: This project was completed ahead of the internal schedule. Looking back, what do you attribute this to?

Juha: There are many factors that contributed to this. Compared to the first game, one of the key factors was that we made sure all open questions from pre-production were answered during that phase, rather than waiting until the production phase—when the team is larger and everything is more expensive—to find the answers. This, in turn, led to faster decision-making during production; the planning was more solid, and naturally, there was less last-minute firefighting down the line.

04

Provide support rather than lead the project

Q: *Resonance* is Remedy’s first major title since the company shifted to a multi-project approach and began self-publishing. What has been the biggest change within the company as it transitioned from a single-project model to a multi-project one?

Juha: Moving from a single project to multiple projects has undoubtedly been a journey filled with learning. A key change at Remedy following *Control* has been the development of a better holistic view of all projects—such as personnel dependencies across projects. Today, the studio is better equipped to meet the needs of each project and make better prioritization decisions across them.

Q: I’ve heard that you have a Project Management Office (PMO) that took two or three years to shift from “leading projects” to “supporting projects.” What did it stop doing, and what did it start doing?

Juha: When we transition from a single-project (or dual-project) company to a multi-project company, we need an organization to manage the entire project portfolio—which is why I discussed the establishment of a PMO in my presentation. For Remedy, this has been a learning curve: how to transform from a highly project-centric organization into one with a dedicated department that specifically handles the relationships between projects.

Initially, the PMO’s role was to lead projects. However, when all responsibilities—such as delivering results and ensuring a return on investment—fell on the project teams, this structure didn’t work very well, so it had to evolve into a support organization. Now, projects operate independently, but they turn to the PMO to resolve conflicts.

The most common issue is personnel conflicts—for example, when we need a visual effects artist, and another project needs one as well. The PMO is the party we turn to; it facilitates discussions to determine which project needs the artist more—or whether we should hire another one. That’s how it’s set up now: the PMO doesn’t lead projects; it supports them.

Q: Can we choose a cross-discipline feature to see how it progresses over the course of an iteration? Who is responsible for the final gameplay experience?

Juha: Most of our features span multiple disciplines; let’s take a “weapon variant” as an example. This work spans the entire process, from the early stages of pre-production to the end of production, and depending on the situation, some phases may overlap.

First, the gameplay design team decides what to create, develops an initial design and prototype, and refines it to a point where it’s roughly ready for implementation; they then ask the gameplay programmers to implement the various supporting features required for implementation.Concept artists are responsible for the weapon’s visual design, which is then brought to life by hard-surface artists and character artists. Animators create the animations showing Dylan using the weapon. Once the weapon is roughly finalized, the audio team designs the various sound effects associated with it; the visual effects team then finalizes the weapon’s visual appearance in all its states, including all abilities that might affect its appearance.

Iterations take place within each team’s individual development cycles, as well as at a higher level, to ensure that all components fit together seamlessly. The gameplay experience is the responsibility of the gameplay designers, while the Creative Director is ultimately responsible for it as part of the overall creative experience.

Q: So how are decisions communicated from leadership to the team? Is there a bottom-up mechanism?

Juha: Most of the time, it depends on the specific situation. However, the project has a core leadership team that typically makes high-level strategic decisions. In the creative realm, the Game Director communicates with the leads of each creative discipline—such as the Lead Level Designer, Lead Game Designer, and Lead Environment Artist—who then communicate with their respective team members.On the production management side, the Development Director communicates with the various producers, who then oversee the implementation of production tasks.

There is certainly a bottom-up mechanism in place: as long as it’s not a particularly high-level strategic decision, we typically involve the team in any decisions that pertain to them directly, and their input can be escalated to the leadership team and then fed back to the team. Moreover, each team tends to operate quite independently.For example, the team responsible for creating enemies develops the enemies themselves; we review the final results, and all decisions are made by them—we simply provide feedback as reviewers.

05

Use Testing to Disprove Unreasonable Designs

Q: The number of users in this round of testing was significantly higher than in previous iterations. Were there any test results that were particularly unexpected—or even overturned a design we were originally very confident in?

Juha: We conducted a lot of user testing and learned a great deal, but most of it just confirmed what we already knew.

A good example is the “melee-supernatural ability resource mechanism,” which forms the foundation of the entire combat system. We didn’t want players to rely solely on supernatural abilities and turn the game into a ranged experience, so we designed a resource system where successful melee hits recharge supernatural abilities.

Originally, this system was bidirectional: players had to use supernatural abilities to engage in melee combat, and they had to use melee combat to use supernatural abilities. But for some reason, players felt that this didn’t feel right and wasn’t as fun. Later, we conducted an A/B test: in the other version, melee combat could be used freely, and only supernatural abilities required resources.After extensive player testing, we found that this one-way resource mechanism was more fun and felt more like a typical ARPG. This is an example of how we revised our original design based on user research findings.

Q: Team well-being has been identified as a key metric. Aside from confidence in the work itself, what specific changes have actually taken place in our day-to-day work practices?

Juha: The internal communication structure within the team has matured significantly. Team members now have a clearer understanding of the decisions made by leadership and the reasoning behind them, which has led to greater overall satisfaction.On the other hand, there’s the production model: we now have much better control over the production schedule and no longer have to constantly “put out fires.” This also means that the project’s direction and what the next phase will look like are more predictable—unlike the chaos we experienced with the first game. Compared to the first game, everyone is much more satisfied with this project.

Q: Since we started self-publishing, the marketing and development teams have been working more closely together. Has this had any practical impact on product decisions?

Juha: We work very closely together—especially the leadership team and the marketing team—on aspects such as positioning and how to communicate the game. This hasn’t affected the game itself on a creative level; the game team still makes all decisions with a high degree of independence. However, it has certainly influenced “how we talk about” the game.

Take the first game as an example: many people who played it later didn’t pick it up at first precisely because the marketing message at the time was “this game is weird,” but after playing it, they all said they loved it. This is undoubtedly one of the lessons we’ve learned from the marketing team.The game is still weird, and *Resonance* is still weird—that’s in Remedy’s DNA. But the way we talk about it now is that it’s so much more than just “weird.”

title: The anguish of *Souls-like* games and the thrill of *Devil May Cry*—all crammed into a single battle in *Shadow Blade Zero*
text:
In late July of last year, at the Beijing Shougang Park, I participated in an in-person hands-on demo of *Shadow Blade Zero*.
Due to a rushed itinerary and the exhaustion from traveling, I didn’t arrive at the hotel until 3 a.m. After sleeping for only a few hours, I got up and rushed to the venue. Although my condition and the weather that day weren’t ideal, I still clearly remember the shouts of the foreign players at the venue, as well as one of the most memorable gaming experiences I’ve had in recent years.
After that, I became an unofficial advocate for the game, mentioning and recommending it from time to time during my daily gaming sessions and when hanging out with friends. The reason I like this game is simple: aside from that stunning hands-on experience, it gave me a new option in the ARPG genre—one other than *Souls-like* games.
As most people in the industry say: Combat is the one area where *Shadow Blade Zero* has the least to prove.
As Liang Qiwei wrote in his lengthy post titled “Rationality and Madness” on his personal Weibo account yesterday (October 28): You’ve probably seen plenty of reviews of *Shadow Blade Zero*, but in reality, you may not need to read too many of them.When you log into the game tomorrow (October 29), you’ll find that all the gameplay mechanics feel natural, simple, and familiar—but we’ve reimagined these familiar elements and woven them together into a brand-new whole.
This statement actually sums up my impressions of the combat experience in *Shadow Blade Zero* perfectly: natural, simple, familiar—yet unique . So this time, I’d like to approach the topic from a different angle—simply as a player—and discuss the combat experience in *Shadow Blade Zero* based on my own experiences and understanding.
01
The player himself is a martial arts prodigy.
In some action games, players are often challenged to hone their skills. As they engage in battles with enemies, they gradually become familiar with their opponents’ moves, eventually learning to counter each attack and defeat one powerful foe after another. This process is also a time for players to adapt to their characters.
For this reason, in some action games (such as the *Souls-like* genre), characters’ initial stats are set very low—even approaching those of ordinary humans in the real world.The progression process places greater emphasis on exploring the map, familiarizing oneself with the behavior patterns of different enemies, and devising countermeasures (such as using items, making character progression choices, and responding to enemy behavior patterns), ultimately allowing a mortal to defeat gods and achieve seemingly impossible feats within the game.
For example, the final boss battle in *Elden Ring* conveys a very strong sense of “mortals slaying gods.”
For players, the advantage of this mode is the immense sense of accomplishment that comes from defeating powerful enemies; however, the downside is that it requires a higher cost to play (in terms of time, effort, etc.) and relies more heavily on the player’s own experience with the game.If a player gives up partway through, the cost of returning to continue the challenge isn’t limited to the “new material” in subsequent levels—they’ll also need to “brush up” on the skills and experience they’ve already acquired.
Another action game genre—high-speed action (such as the *Devil May Cry* series)—follows a different model. The characters themselves possess powerful abilities and versatility, and as players cut through enemies like they’re slicing through watermelons and defeat powerful foes along the way, they’re actually gradually adapting to the characters, exploring, and unleashing their full potential.
Even complete beginners can pull off some flashy combos in a short time, but this also creates a sense of being out of control—the controls for combos are highly precise, so even with the same input pattern, one combo might trigger one sequence, while the next might trigger a completely different one.Controlling a character you can’t fully master while taking on powerful foes leaves you with a somewhat clumsy feeling, even when you manage to defeat them.
There are two types: one in which the player character adapts to the enemy’s behavior patterns (which I refer to as “learning” mode), and the other in which the enemy’s behavior patterns adapt to the player character (which I refer to as “rehabilitation” mode). Although many action games attempt to address their respective shortcomings by combining these approaches, very few are able to truly strike a balance between the two.
In my opinion, what makes *Shadow Blade Zero* such a stunning experience is that it strikes a balance between these two aspects.
First of all, the protagonist, “Hun,” is a top-tier martial arts master in his own right. Not only is he proficient in the use of various weapons, but he also possesses formidable combat abilities, allowing him to take on multiple opponents at once. We can see this demonstrated both in offline hands-on demos and in various online gameplay videos.
This setup may sound similar to fast-paced combat games like *Devil May Cry*, where the protagonist also possesses formidable abilities and players must explore ways to unlock their full potential during battles against numerous powerful foes. However, *Shadow Blade Zero* has significantly simplified and streamlined its combat mechanics.
In many action games, a single button corresponds to a single simple action, and to pull off a series of fluid moves, the game practically expects you to press every button on the controller.In *Shadow Blade Zero*, however, a single button press often corresponds to an entire martial arts sequence—even the game’s most spectacular combos can be executed with just two or three buttons.
To give a simple example, the incredibly cool “Killer Combo” requires nothing more than a “light attack” followed by a “heavy attack,” while the finishing move “Execution” is simply a QTE, and so on.
This is also something many people have pointed out: the combat in *Shadow Blade Zero* has a somewhat “showy” quality to it, since players don’t need to perform particularly complex controls to pull off a series of flashy combos.
With just a few simple key combinations, you can perform a highly spectacular martial arts routine.
Especially in fast-paced combat games like *Shadow Blade Zero*, simplifying the controls does more than just reduce the player’s workload; its primary purpose is to lower the learning curve—allowing players to clearly understand the function of every button and every key combination.
This approach naturally has its pros and cons. Compared to other games, the action in *Shadow Blade Zero* may seem a bit flashy, but its execution is incredibly clever, as its action mechanics are firmly rooted in Chinese martial arts—with the “Zhen Family Troupe” serving as action consultants.In the game, we can see the ruthless intensity of “Kung Fu is a killing art” from *A Man’s Martial Arts World*, the sweeping, wide-ranging mixed martial arts moves from *Kill Zone*, and the martial arts philosophy from *Ip Man*.
What’s even more impressive is that even these flashy combos, executed with simple controls, adapt differently depending on the combat situation. For example, when facing multiple grunts, the same combo might hit two enemies at once, whereas when facing multiple powerful foes, the combo will feature a different animation sequence.
This also means that even though the game’s controls are simple, these unique action sequences ensure that the combat never feels monotonous; on the contrary, the excitement builds as the battle scenarios change.
The combination of “simplified input controls” and “realistic and varied action sequences” allows players to perform a wide variety of spectacular moves with a limited set of controls. By understanding the purpose of each button press, players naturally feel as though they are the “martial arts prodigy” sought after by countless martial artists in the game.
02
You’re strong, but the enemies you’re facing are even more sinister.
This is just the first step that *Shadow Blade Zero* has achieved: making it easier for players to master the high-performance protagonist and quickly “get back into the swing of things.” What amazed me most about *Shadow Blade Zero* is that, building on this foundation, the game features a wide variety of challenging enemies that naturally guide players into a gradual “learning” process.
In the world of *Shadow Blade*, “killer intent” is the source of power that drives all martial arts techniques within the “Shadow Realm.”According to the lore, “Killer Qi” is primarily used in three ways: first, to enhance physical prowess and sword techniques; second, to power various mystical arts, including “sword energy,” “magic,” “witchcraft,” and so on; and third, to operate mechanical devices.
As the martial arts world evolved, the applications of “killing intent” became increasingly diverse. In addition to even more ruthless killing intent techniques, there were also killing intent spells capable of controlling corpses and transforming them into “ghostly enforcers,” as well as enhancement technologies that provided a constant supply of killing intent, and so on.
In this worldview driven by a “killing intent,” the battles players encounter are naturally not limited to swords and blades. Mystical arts, traps, and even cyborgs—monsters that appear inhuman—will become the norm.
Although this worldview may seem quite “dark”—and even somewhat unsettling—it also influences the combat in *Shadow Blade Zero*, making it more than just a clash of swords and introducing many “cruel and devious moves” that most players have never seen before.
For example, in the early gameplay footage of *Shadow Blade Zero*, a powerful enemy wielding a “blood drop” decapitated the protagonist with a single strike, clearly demonstrating the ruthlessness of this type of foe.
Another example is during the early stages of the game, when players encounter one of the regional bosses, the “Captain of the Ghostly Enforcers,” in Pang Town. After defeating the first phase of the battle, the Captain of the Ghostly Enforcers uses his “Killing Qi” spell to instantly transform into a headless specter.This transformation isn’t just meant to intimidate the player; the severed neck also spews out “Kill Qi” magic, launching surprise attacks against the player during combat.
Therefore, in Phase Two, players will face a style of attack that is even more frenzied and defies biological instincts; even martial arts prodigies are likely to suffer a setback when first encountering such a bizarre enemy.
And this is how *Shadow Blade Zero* uses its brutal world to tell players: you’re strong, but many of the enemies you face will also fight “dirty.” Players will find it difficult to rely on their experience from other games to sweep through all enemies; instead, they’ll need to closely observe enemy behavior patterns and figure out how to counter them.
At this point, a hidden theme in the combat of *Shadow Blade Zero* comes to light: “Overcoming the Enemy.” These seemingly mysterious foes often have specific vulnerabilities.Here’s a very clear example: in the “Seven-Star Sword Formation” featured in the game’s Year of the Snake celebratory gameplay footage, players must defeat seven enemies one by one. If you use the “Soft Sword” at this point and take advantage of its agile area-of-effect attacks, you can achieve remarkable results.Another example: when players defeat a boss wielding a “Giant Shield,” the “Giant Shield” they obtain will most likely prove useful in the subsequent stages of the game…
The game offers 30 primary weapons and 25 secondary weapons. While not every weapon may be the perfect choice for defeating every enemy, players will at least have a variety of strategies to choose from when facing different powerful foes.
In fact, this combat progression system relies heavily on the “fairness” of the game’s mechanics—specifically, a design that ensures parity between the player and the enemy. In boss battles, the player’s core combat resource is “Kill Energy,” a system that balances offense and defense. Kill Energy can be used not only to execute Kill Energy combos and quickly deal higher damage but also to sustain blocks and seek opportunities to counterattack.Enemies operate in the same way, using “Kill Energy” to block the protagonist’s attacks or unleash powerful Kill Energy skills.
Therefore, depending on how well players know their enemies and their own skill level, they can adopt two completely different combat styles. The first style leverages the “Kill Energy” system’s ability to combine offense and defense, using sustained blocks to read the enemy’s moves. When the enemy emits a “blue glow” or“red light” skills and an opening appears, you can execute precise blocks and dodges to rapidly deplete the enemy’s “Kill Energy,” then capitalize on your Kill Energy advantage to unleash a burst of damage, repeating this cycle. This combat style is particularly suitable for the first few battles when you’re still unfamiliar with the enemy’s tactics.
Once players become familiar with their enemies’ tactics, they can fully leverage their weapon advantages to launch sustained attacks, thereby suppressing the enemies’ kill meter and gaining a decisive upper hand.Of course, for players seeking an even greater challenge, the game also offers the “Defier” and “66 Days” difficulty modes—enemies will behave even more unpredictably, actively exploiting weaknesses in the player’s strategies, and the one-trick approach of continuously suppressing the enemy’s “Kill Meter” will no longer work.Players must not only find ways to counter them but also engage in intense positional battles and precise counterattacks, resulting in an experience akin to hardcore fighting games.
03
Getting Started, Learning, and the Path to Becoming a Martial Arts Master
Let’s go back to the original question—what exactly impressed me so much about *Shadow Blade Zero*? The reason is actually quite simple: it integrates “rehab” and “learning” into the same battle, and the transition between the two feels almost seamless.
The first impression players get is definitely “I’m really strong.” With a large number of grunts and relatively conservative enemy design in the early game, it makes you feel like a seasoned fighter within just a few minutes.Plus, the thirty primary weapons each have their own unique characteristics: light swords are fast, heavy swords are powerful, and flexible swords can wrap around opponents and sweep them aside. Switching weapons completely changes the feel of combat, yet the controls themselves remain simple. Even better, switching weapons replenishes your Rage meter, so by alternating between two primary weapons, combos flow naturally—no need to memorize a long list of command sequences.
But the enemies won’t let you have it easy forever. Later on, many of the game’s bosses and elite monsters have playstyles that you can’t overcome just by relying on “my character is overpowered.”The developers have designed the game to prioritize aggressive play; you’ll need to maintain the offensive to chip away at about 70 percent of a boss’s health—relying purely on defense and waiting for openings is actually quite inefficient. This forces you to step out of your “rehab” comfort zone and pay close attention to what your opponent is actually doing.
What’s more, many enemies don’t just rely on swords and blades—they also use traps, magic, and hybrid human-weapon combinations. Trying to hack at a heavy shield with a light sword is just asking for trouble; switch to a heavy weapon or pull out the appropriate secondary weapon, and the situation changes immediately.The arsenal itself becomes your “learning” toolkit—if you can’t win, change your approach instead of stubbornly sticking to a single combo.
Once you reach the “Defier” difficulty level, enemy AI changes, and bosses will adjust their next moves based on the outcome of your previous encounter. No matter how well you’ve memorized the patterns, they might not follow the script.At this point, the muscle memory and weapon understanding you’ve built up through “rehab” are still there, but you must truly shift into “learning” mode—reading your opponent, making judgments, and fighting for position.Fortunately, the game keeps the cost of trial and error very low: the respawn point is right at the boss’s entrance, and if you lose a multi-stage battle, you simply restart from the current stage—no need to traverse the map or grind for levels.
At this point, I’m even more convinced of one thing: *Shadow Blade Zero* offers action gamers not just another “Souls-like” or “Devil May Cry-like” alternative, but a truly new option.It doesn’t force you to choose between “suffering” and “mowing down enemies”; instead, it first lets you execute martial arts combos with just a few buttons, making you feel like a martial arts prodigy—only to have ferocious enemies teach you the harsh realities of the martial arts world, forcing you to read their moves, switch weapons, and fight for position.
Natural, simple, familiar—yet unique. When applied to the combat in *Shadow Blade Zero*, this isn’t just a platitude. The game doesn’t force players to choose between “simplicity” and “depth”; instead, it lets them step through the door naturally and discover the depth within.
For an action game player, this is probably why I’m willing to be an “unpaid advocate,” and it’s also the most genuine meaning behind the phrase “new choice.”
