Repetitive tasks—another hunt for a rare material, another trek across the map—can become exasperating even in the best survival crafting games. There's a thin line between tedium and satisfaction, and Enshrouded walks it better than most. Much of that is thanks to the game's philosophy around punishment and reward, but its RPG elements add a layer of complexity that more than makes up for anything missing from Enshrouded's "survival-lite" approach.

Take my group, for example. I play with seven other friends, while that feels like a lot for most survival crafting games, Enshrouded's combat roles give us distinctly useful jobs. Rather than dumping points into three or four barebones stats, your Flameborn can specialize across 12 different skill trees. I mostly opt for tank, athlete, and assassin perks, but my allies fill other needs with mix-and-match builds for glass-cannon wizards, battlemage healers, or stealthy assassins. We also have our preferred responsibilities, like mining, woodcutting, gardening, cooking, and all those other usual genre chores.

Enshrouded's boss fights are a blast and more dynamic than similar games. Fights aren't as mechanically heavy as a Conan Exiles dungeon boss, but the traditional tank-and-spank approach won't cut it.

Hollow Halls—Enshrouded's massive dungeons that practically demand group play—are where combat roles shine the most. I beat one playing solo, but also wiped several times in a group of four.

A word of caution: multiplayer groups of more than two or three people should consider a dedicated server. Version 1.0 significantly improves performance, but not enough to spare bigger parties from the occasional murderous lag spike.

Multiplayer is also where some of my biggest gripes with Enshrouded remain, and despite heavy reworks to its questing systems, my group still struggled to make sense of the journal when our objectives fell out of sync. Our confusion mostly stemmed from completing world progression quests without the full party, so when absent friends logged back in, their to-do list didn't look the same and they had a list of missed quests. There are separate, personal quests to do at your own leisure, but we constantly compared our journals to make sure no one had gone off course.

I'm still not sure if any of that even mattered. No one was ever locked out of crafting recipes or new biomes because of the discrepancies, so the punishment boiled down to a smidge of missed XP and simply missing out on the moment. It didn't end up being a big deal, and I'm starting to think the journal's 'missed quest' label made the whole thing feel more consequential than it actually was. I clenched my jaw in frustration a few times, but if that's my biggest nitpick, then Enshrouded is survival crafting gold.

There's got to be a high fantasy Ikea hidden somewhere in Embervale, because the amount of furniture and decor in Enshrouded is absurd.

As much as I love the genre, I can't pretend it isn't filled with seemingly eternal early access pits. I've played in plenty of messy sandboxes, a handful of good ones, and just a few great ones. Then there's Enshrouded, operating in a league of its own. But even then, Enshrouded isn't just a good survival crafting game: it's a damn good game by any measure. Its building tools reward even my most impractical ambitions, and I'll never grow tired of exploring Embervale's hidden nooks and crannies.

Few games in the genre match its distinct identity or degree of polish, and after 500+ hours of adventuring, there's little left to wish for. My biggest dilemma post-Enshrouded will be moving on from a survival crafting RPG so lovingly handcrafted. I fear Keen Games has cooked up something that has forever changed my palate.

title: Queen's Domain might be the best game like Metroid Prime since Metroid Prime
author: Ted Litchfield
text:
I tried the demo for Queen's Domain last year and liked it a lot⁠—though it definitely had some friction I wasn't sure about. The full game launched on October 30 , and I eagerly rushed through the parts I'd already played in the demo.
Turns out, that demo cut out right when things were about to go nuts.
Five hours in out of an estimated 30+, and Queen's Domain is easily one of my top games of the year. I am only begrudgingly writing this, because I'd rather be playing right now.
Queen's Domain starts out resembling other entries in a growing subgenre of indie King's Field-likes , paying homage to the first-person dark fantasy RPG series FromSoftware put out before its soulsward turn. In its first half hour or so, Queen's Domain distinguishes itself similarly to fellow genre standout Lunacid: Fantastic art, maybe even better music , and a mastery of nostalgic intangibles (menu, UI, sound cues, etc.) After beating the first boss, Queen's Domain rewards you with a magic airdash sword, and it's at that point that the game truly begins.
Queen of the skies
Queen's Domain is a very deliberately paced game and, like a lot of first-person RPGs, it starts out feeling like your boots will always be on the ground. Think the difference between Doom and Quake: You can mostly tell when a game will let you get some air or not.
Freshly Baked Games Freshly Baked Games Freshly Baked Games Freshly Baked Games But once I was rocking the Holy Sword, Endu? Holy shit . Queen's Domain's first area opens up like some wonderful clockwork contraption. A lot of the verticality reminds me of Destiny raids, the way hidden paths blend into the environment, and reaching them feels like you're sequence breaking.
Endu can be upgraded with special gems throughout the game, with each giving you an extra dash while airborne. I'm up to three at the time of writing, and each upgrade has felt like it radically opened up my traversal options: There are parts of the first few maps I'm pretty sure I'll only be able to reach once I'm up to four or five dashes, zooming from one end of the map to the other without touching the ground.
Endu's a standout, but it's not the only tool available: Queen's Domain seems to have an expansive arsenal, and weapons can transform as they're upgraded. You upgrade weapons just by using them, and the game has no stat allocation on level up, encouraging experimentation with the arsenal⁠—PC Gamer hardware writer James Bentley managed to max upgrade 20 weapons across his full playthrough. You can effectively create a "build" via your choice of which weapons to hotkey (limit of three) and upgrade, a system that more resembles BioShock or the System Shock Remake rather than something like Dark Souls or Lunacid.
My favorite alongside Endu so far has been the Caestus, a type of medieval knuckle duster that's been a standby of the Souls games. Here, it's a fast-attacking blunt weapon useful against slashing-resistant skeletons. Instead of a horizontal dash like Endu, its special attack is an uppercut that launches my character into the air. Plenty of fun to use on enemies, but I've loved deploying it as an effective double jump to reach otherwise-inaccessible areas⁠—and there's always been a surprise or meaningful reward waiting for me when I do.
Don't give up, skeleton
Freshly Baked Games Freshly Baked Games Freshly Baked Games Freshly Baked Games Freshly Baked Games My coworker, PCG staff writer Morgan Park, initially bounced off the pre-Endu, demo-equivalent portion of Queen's Domain. I'm here to say stay strong, prayer warriors. It is worth getting through that first half hour. While there's something to be said about it potentially putting new players off, I think the contrast between pre-and post-Endu gameplay is so strong, it makes the air dash feel all the more powerful. You know what it's like to be stuck on the ground, and you won't take it for granted.
It's the sort of contrast metroidvanias thrive on⁠—I always think of how dinky you feel before you get the wall jump in Hollow Knight⁠—and Queen's Domain's brilliant level design might leave it the best first-person metroidvania anyone's made since the first Metroid Prime.
And I think Prime's a strong comparison point overall here: The cryptic atmosphere, breathtaking vistas, and genuinely unique approach to first-person movement and level design speak to that. I'm already seeing hints toward game-spanning backtracking in my future, but I've got reason to suspect Queen's Domain's backtracking will be less frustrating and obtuse than Metroid Prime's.
I already love this game, and I am about to mainline it over the next 30 hours or so of my free time⁠—stay tuned for our full Queen's Domain review to come. Meanwhile, Queen's Domain is available on Steam for a launch price of $17, down from an MSRP of $20.

title: Users pull $3.6 bn from Binance as it reopens following $6.3 billion mega-hack - FBI says North Korean hacking group 'TraderTraitor' to blame, North Korea says nuh-uh
author: Jacob Ridley
text:
Binance saw a huge outpouring of withdrawals when it re-opened to customers on Sunday following a hack for the history books. The cryptocurrency exchange lost $6.3 billion, roughly $3 billion of which was frozen in transit and the rest covered by the company, but it lost a bunch more once it let customers take their money out on November 1.
Customers withdrew $4.649 billion from the exchange in just under 10 hours since it reopened. That's a whole lot of value to lose in a day, and not wholly surprising given the context, but what is more surprising is how many deposits were made in that same timeframe: roughly $1 billion worth.
"Withdrawals were temporarily suspended as a precaution while our teams worked to contain the incident loss, assess its impact, restore affected services, and complete security checks," Binance said of the move.
Users may face slowdowns as systems get back up and running, the company has said.
In later updates, Binance says that deposits into the exchange have begun to creep back up in excess of withdrawals; the total cashflow of the crypto exchange is still a net negative, at -$5 billion by November 3, but the withdrawals are no longer outpacing the deposits by any significant amount. It's still early days and a long way to go to make up for the initial loss in customer funds, but the exchange may still live to fight another day.
Withdrawal data updateBy 03:00 UTC, we are seeing hourly deposits exceed withdrawals, reflecting improving user activity and stabilizing flows. https://t.co/UiXmYC2lm3 November 3, 2026
Meanwhile, the exact details of the attack are still being deliberated. The FBI holds North Korea responsible , agreeing with experts that a group going by the name of TraderTraitor is behind it. The FBI says that it, along with USSS and IRS-CI, has observed the group converting the stolen crypto into Ether, with a view to launder it away into obscurity later.
North Korea, unsurprisingly, denies the FBI's claim . Kim Yo Jong, an official in the NK government, and Kim Jong Un's sister, said it was nothing more than a "sinister attempt" by the US to damage the country's reputation.
"The US has made a trite provocation of linking it with the Democratic People's Republic of Korea again," Kim Yo Jong said.

title: Upcoming Final Fantasy 14 update should massively cut down on dungeon queue times
author: Harvey Randall
text:
Final Fantasy 14's queues can get long—not for roulettes, mind, those are usually pretty nippy—but if you're trying to complete a specific alliance raid as a newer player, you can be stuck twiddling your thumbs for ages.
Square Enix is planning to make a change that'll fix that soon, though. In a recent blog post to the game's website , it's been announced that same-region player matchmaking'll be available starting November 10 after a successful trial period on its Japanese servers.
What does that mean? Basically, FF14's server architecture is into physical data centers (Japan, Europe, Oceania, and North America), then logical data centers, which are sort of like realms in other MMOs. For instance, the NA servers have Crystal, Aether, Dynamis, and Primal (then within those centers are "worlds", which can be travelled and matchmade between pretty easily).
You've been able to hop between these logical data centers manually for some time—it's pretty common, for instance, for Crystal players to hop on over to Aether to group up with folks for high-end content. But you need to log out to do so, with said parties constructed through the in-game party finder.
After November 10, however, matchmaking for things like roulettes will also be possible within the same physical data center, as will the party finder writ large, cross-world linkshells, fellowships, and friend list and /tell functionality. Travelling between data centers will also be made easier, too.
This is a huge quality-of-life boost that should massively cut down on queueing times—but it'll also make organising or creating groups for the aforementioned high-end content way easier, too, allowing folks to see and join listings for different logical data centers without having to hop between them.
My secret hope, as an EU player who's currently stuck on North American ping for community reasons (it's where all my mates are), is that this sort of functionality might one day lead to cross region travel so I can hop on over to the EU whenever I actually want to do content. A guy can dream.

title: The Overwatch devs hear your complaints about skin distribution but concede that some cosmetics need to 'support the actual bottom-line business'
author: Elie Gould
text:
Overwatch's skin distribution is, in one word, lopsided. With a roster of 54 heroes and counting it can be hard to ensure that every character gets their fair share of cosmetics as is, but when you add popularity into the mix it gets even harder.
As a free-to-play game, Overwatch makes the bulk of its money through cosmetics like bundles or standalone skins. Skins also take a good amount of time to prototype and create, so to ensure its efforts aren't wasted the team needs to pick heroes based on how many players will actually buy the end product.
(Image credit: Blizzard) "Every new piece of content that we introduce to the game, whether it's a hero or even a map, you know, means that the pool of everything that we've got, it is spread out a little bit," game director Aaron Keller says in a group interview (via Kotaku ). This leaves room for two kinds of heroes to get regular skins. There's popular heroes like Ana, Genji, and Soldier 76 which are played by a large proportion of players and then there's the fan favourites who aren't just popular but have a dedicated playerbase who will consistently buy skins like Mercy, Kiriko, Juno, and Widowmaker.
However, Team 4 has, in recent years, made a clear effort to bulk up cosmetics for new heroes. "Constantly expanding our capacity" to create skins for characters like Anran, Freyja, and Vendetta who have all been included in recent skin collabs. And while the devs have been able to create more skins than those that just "support the actual bottom-line business", money still needs to be made.
(Image credit: Blizzard Entertainment) It's kind of like a pay-it-forward system. By making cosmetics that will sell well, Team 4 are able to dedicate time and energy to heroes that won't yield as much of a monetary gain. "The place that you can see that most transparently is the Mythic skins that we release," Keller adds. "Each season we release two Mythic skins, and typically one of those is going to be for a hero that we think is actually going to really drive a lot of that support for the business. And then another one is going to be for a hero that typically hasn't gotten either a Mythic or a lot of other skins in the recent past."
I recognise that I'm probably in a fortunate position where my main, Ana, has always had a healthy amount of new and very cool cosmetics. But the point still stands that this is a business, so Team 4 needs to make responsible financial decisions for reasons that are at times out of their control.
"We recognize it's important to players," Keller says. "We want to be doing as much of it as we can, but we still always want to be doing it in a way that's also responsible, and [lets us] know that we can continue supporting this game going forward."

title: Modders bring Steam Frame build of SteamOS and all of its translation layer goodness to Mac
author: Jess Kinghorn
text:
Gaming on Mac has come a long way. Gone are the days of limited releases, though not absolutely everything is playable on the platform. Thankfully, community developers are only too keen to plug the gaps.
FX Steam Launcher on GitHub brings SteamOS to Apple Silicon Macs. Specifically, this independent, open-source project is based on the ARM64 Steam Frame version of the operating system. Therefore, you're getting Windows game compatibility on Mac thanks to Proton 11 and FEX , alongside the very swish SteamOS interface (via Videocardz ).
Obviously, there are a few things to bear in mind if you want to go all in as a Mac gamer. For one thing, this is not a native installation, and is instead running SteamOS by way of a virtual machine on your Mac. For another, this is a GitHub download to begin with, but once you've got it installed, the launcher directly downloads the official SteamOS image from Valve and then even handles OS updates too. Neat!
As this is an unofficial effort, there are a few more caveats still. The FX Steam Launcher itself currently only supports Apple Silicon Macs running either macOS 15 (from September, 2024) or newer. However, to actually get the latest and greatest running, you may need something much more recent than that.
Bear with me here, but Proton and FEX are essentially only the first hurdle. DXVK is required to run DirectX 9, 10, and 11 games, while DirectX 12 releases rely on VKD3D-Proton. Then either MoltenVK or KosmicKrisp is the next hurdle graphics instructions will need to pass before finally handing off the baton to Apple’s Metal API (though there's some experimental support for DXMT, which allows DirectX 10 and 11 games to run without VKD3D-Proton).
(Image credit: ETA Prime , YouTube) Anyway, all of that is to say KosmicKrisp, a pretty pivotal translation layer in this whole process, requires at least macOS 26 or later to run. That's a fair amount of hoops to jump through, though; if you can get it running, the launcher does allow you to run SteamOS either windowed or fullscreen, while letting you still access macOS either way.
On account of not being a Mac power user, I've not had a chance to test it out myself, but YouTube creator ETA Prime tested the launcher with The Witcher 3, Stellar Blade, and Left 4 Dead 2 on their Apple M4 Max. At high settings, the creator saw performance to the tune of over 70 FPS for each of these games, with Left 4 Dead 2 breezing past 200.
That said, Stellar Blade was running at a mere 800p resolution, while the rest of their tests ran at a maximum of 1080p. Furthermore, not all the games they tested even ran as well as these cherry-picked examples (to say nothing of The Witcher 3's funky-looking trees).
Still, what's possible with this launcher remains impressive, though gaming on Mac even without it is far more viable than it once was. For Apple's big 50th birthday earlier this year, our Jacob explored the things Mac does better than PC . Our Ian was also mighty impressed with the Apple Mac Studio M4 Max —though he does also note, "Christ, what are you doing? Buy something else for gaming".
On that front, any would-be Mac gamer could do much worse than the MacBook Neo , which is now going for $699/£699. Not even Apple is safe from the memory supply crisis , but as the situation continues to drive up the cost of traditional gaming PC parts , who could blame a gamer on a budget still picking up the MacBook Neo instead? Especially with unofficial projects like FX Steam Launcher at their fingertips.

Then either MoltenVK or KosmicKrisp is the next hurdle graphics instructions will need to pass before finally handing off the baton to Apple’s Metal API (though there's some experimental support for DXMT, which allows DirectX 10 and 11 games to run without VKD3D-Proton).

Anyway, all of that is to say KosmicKrisp, a pretty pivotal translation layer in this whole process, requires at least macOS 26 or later to run. That's a fair amount of hoops to jump through, though; if you can get it running, the launcher does allow you to run SteamOS either windowed or fullscreen, while letting you still access macOS either way.

On account of not being a Mac power user, I've not had a chance to test it out myself, but YouTube creator ETA Prime tested the launcher with The Witcher 3, Stellar Blade, and Left 4 Dead 2 on their Apple M4 Max. At high settings, the creator saw performance to the tune of over 70 FPS for each of these games, with Left 4 Dead 2 breezing past 200.

That said, Stellar Blade was running at a mere 800p resolution, while the rest of their tests ran at a maximum of 1080p. Furthermore, not all the games they tested even ran as well as these cherry-picked examples (to say nothing of The Witcher 3's funky-looking trees).

Still, what's possible with this launcher remains impressive, though gaming on Mac even without it is far more viable than it once was. For Apple's big 50th birthday earlier this year, our Jacob explored the things Mac does better than PC. Our Ian was also mighty impressed with the Apple Mac Studio M4 Max—though he does also note, "Christ, what are you doing? Buy something else for gaming".

On that front, any would-be Mac gamer could do much worse than the MacBook Neo, which is now going for $699/£699. Not even Apple is safe from the memory supply crisis, but as the situation continues to drive up the cost of traditional gaming PC parts, who could blame a gamer on a budget still picking up the MacBook Neo instead? Especially with unofficial projects like FX Steam Launcher at their fingertips.

title: Mike Flanagan thinks 'Warhammer is a fascinating world' but can't tell us anything else about the upcoming Warhammer 40,000 project because 'Henry Cavill would be furious'
author: Elie Gould
text:
(Image credit: Prime Video) Game Workshop and Henry Cavill's Warhammer 40,000 project has been in the works for two years now , with the most recent news being that renowned horror director, writer, and showrunner Mike Flanagan—known for projects such as the Carrie miniseries or The Haunting of Hill House—has joined the crew and will be writing the script.
Otherwise mum's the word concerning this project, with very little being shared about it. In fact, the most we've got so far has been Flanagan recently chatting about a few bits and pieces during his Carrie press tour.
Flanagan describes the process of discovering all that Warhammer 40,000 has to offer as "a very cool and unexpected on-ramp into it, which I think is very exciting. I’m sworn to secrecy on all of it, but I'm having the time of my life working on it."
It's good to hear that, at the very least, he's having fun. There's certainly a lot of material to work with here and a lot to get stuck into for a horror director. I haven't been completely convinced by some of Flanagan's projects. Midnight Mass took too long to get going, The Fall of the House of Usher felt confused, and The Haunting of Bly Manor was too much of a Hill House clone. Though, I am still intrigued to see how this Warhammer 40,000 will turn out, especially with Cavill working on it.
I actually quite enjoyed Amazon's Secret Level Warhammer 40,000 short. You can hardly go wrong when focusing on the Deathwatch, but the gore and the violence still went down really well in my book. So I'd like more of that please.

title: 2 of my favorite studios are teaming up for their first-ever showcase this week, and have a Steam sale going right now
author: Andy Chalk
text:
Two of my favorite game studios getting together for a tag-team showcase in a classic PC gaming genre that doesn't get the love it deserves? You better believe I'm going to have a word or two to say about that—so allow me to draw your attention to the upcoming Point-and-Click Showcase being co-hosted by Amanita Design and Rusty Lake.
The Point-and-Click Showcase will feature world premieres, release date announcements, and new demos for more than 35 adventure games of all types, including ghost stories, murder mysteries, cozy puzzle games, and whatever's going on here:
(Image credit: Amanita Design/Rusty Lake) The Point-and-Click Showcase takes place on November 4, but ahead of that—as in, right now —you can take advantage of the Point-and-Click Showcase Steam Sale . Running until November 9, the sale features discounts on dozens of adventure games across a range of styles, from the classic Excavation of Hob's Barrow to the award-winning Heaven's Vault , the bizarre Dropsy , the horror of Stories Untold , and the time-wasting of The Longing .
Primordia is a steal for $3, and yes, I am once again going to foist The Night of the Rabbit upon you, because it's brilliant and you can get it right now for just $2.49. You can pick up Rusty Lake's latest, Servant of the Lake , for $5.35—33% off—and while Amanita's most recent release, Phonopolis, is not on sale, Chuchel is, and I will never not recommend that.
So, long story short, it's a good time to be an adventure gamer and if you haven't sampled the delights already, this is the perfect opportunity to change that. The Point-and-Click Showcase begins at 9 am PT/12 pm ET/6 pm CET on November 4, and will be streamed on YouTube and Steam.

title: Morrowind's gravity is no longer '0.01% off' in the new release of its fan-made engine, finally making it playable
author: Joshua Wolens
text:
If you are playing Morrowind in 2026, my recommendation is that you do so using OpenMW , its 18-year-old fan-made and open-source engine reimplementation that makes it run smooth as butter on any modern machine you point it at, whether you're running Windows, Linux, macOS or, hell, FreeBSD if you wanna get really sicko with it. It's simply the most convenient way to get a cromulent version of Bethesda's best game running on modern systems.
And now it has a new version. Or rather, a new release candidate that will prove the basis of its upcoming 0.52 version. Released a couple of days ago, OpenMW 0.52 RC1 contains a bunch of fixes, some new features, and one minor alteration to the fundamental forces of the universe. It's not the doozy of, say, OpenMW 0.50—which added gamepad support and thereby made Morrowind on Steam Deck dizzyingly easy—but it's still pretty meaty.
For instance, consider: "Water-walking actors now drown when knocked out" and "Implemented terminal velocity". Say what you like, but the second of those seems pretty meaningful for a game that contains Scrolls of Icarian Flight and the first is quite a funny sentence. The terminal velocity fix contains, within itself, a sub-fix for the basic laws of reality: "fixed gravity being 0.01% off"). We are free of our shared hell.
The biggest new feature in OpenMW 0.52 is probably the lighting stuff. It's called clustered lighting and it removes "the normal per-object light limit". I don't really know what that means either, but the short and tall of it, per an explanatory August blog post , is that "it has a dramatically lower performance impact than raising the limit to Aetherius. In fact, the performance can in some cases be better than with the regular light limit."
Morrowind, one of the best videogames ever made, continues to get better.

title: The top 100 PC games
author: Phil Savage
text:
Welcome to the PC Gamer Top 100—our annual list of the best games you can play right now. Every year, we look at the hundreds of thousands of PC games that are available to buy, and think, "yes, we can whittle this down into a numbered list". Hubris? Yes. A months-long crucible of heated arguments and impassioned pleas? Also yes.
More than anything, the Top 100 is designed to capture a moment in time. It's a place where the 'canon' classics of the past rub shoulders against the fresh new hotness. Where being a game that a significant portion of the team currently loves is as important as being a game that is recognised worldwide for its contributions to the medium.
It is a deeply subjective process—a way for PC Gamer's editorial team to advocate for the games they're passionate about. One member of our team has spent years attempting to get Overwatch back on the list, taking every opportunity to persuade their fellow editors to give it a chance. Not every entry required that level of dedication to earn its spot, but every pick is a game that at least a handful of our staff cares deeply about.
How we make the list
Ahead of the vote, the PC Gamer team is free to nominate any PC game for voting, giving us a longlist of over 300 games. Each member of the team is then asked to rate those games subjectively across three weighted categories:
Quality: Is it good? A rating of the game's calibre. (60% of the Top 100 Score)
Importance: Is it noteworthy? A rating of the game's influence. (20% of the Top 100 Score)
Freshness: Is it unique? A rating of the game's originality. (20% of the Top 100 Score)
The weightings are designed around the Top 100's function as an annual, ever-changing list. Too much weight to Importance, and the list stagnates. Too much to Freshness, and there's no consistency year-to-year. Quality is the most important category because, ultimately, if we don't think a game is actually very good, it doesn't make the list.
The sum of each game's ratings is divided by its number of voters, and then run through a few special formulae—including a penalty for games that receive too few votes—to produce the final Top 100 Score for each game.
We then make some manual adjustments. In the interest of variety we mostly restrict the list to one game per series—only including multiple if we think the games are different enough from each other to be worth mentioning, as with Baldur's Gate 2 and Baldur's Gate 3. Otherwise, the lower scoring game in a series is removed. We also let editors pitch for a change to the list—each of which is voted on by the wider team, and only ratified if it gets majority approval.
What's left is the 100 games you find below. Some might claim it folly—attempting to wrestle the varied tastes of our editorial team into a list of games we wholeheartedly recommend. Nevertheless, we're sure that within these entries, you'll find something new to love.
#100-91
100. Deadlock
Released: TBA | Top 100 Score: 213.58
(Image credit: Future) Elie Gould: I'm in no way a MOBA-lover but I sure do love Deadlock. I love its fantastically written characters, exciting and experimental game design, and its mode for dummies: Street Brawl.
Jacob Ridley: Welp, Elie has called me out. I play Deadlock for dummies, otherwise known as Street Brawl, and it's something special. A large cast of otherworldly characters keeps every round fresh. It's surprisingly accessible through excellent character, UI, and game design—a high skill ceiling, but fun all the way down. Great game, and I'm yet to even try the MOBA mode.
Elie Gould: That wasn't a call out, Jacob. I also love and play Deadlock for dummies, it rocks!
Andrea Shearon: It's me, the MOBA-lover logging in to say I've only put a handful of hours into Deadlock and already love it. I'm the reverse of Elie and not into hero shooters, but Deadlock (and Calico) have won me over.
Harvey Randall: It's also me, the person on the PC Gamer team with 360+ hours in this thing—and while I do (unfortunately, it's a character flaw) know how to play MOBAs, Deadlock is shaping up to be the best-in-class of the entire genre. Which means, as my fellows have stated, it also has an absolute ton going for it outside of just being a very good example of itself.
Valve has cooked up one of its coolest settings—a supernatural 1950s New York where barrel mimics lurk on street corners and Lovecraftian gods play at their own versions of the Grand Budapest. And while it's not yet finished, the fact it's getting record-high concurrents should tell you just how much Valve has cooked here.
Jake Tucker: I've tried and failed to get into Deadlock a few times now, and the main draw is the incredible world. MOBAs could be accused, usually, of being a little bit of a fantasy hodgepodge, but Deadlock's setting is consistent and fascinating, a tiny city for you to explore each game.
99. Death Stranding 2
Released: March 19, 2026 | Top 100 Score: 215.31
(Image credit: Future) Morgan Park: I consider Death Stranding 2 the perfect kind of sequel. It builds on all of the fantastic hiking, delivery, and construction stuff that ruled about the original while rethinking what kinda sucked (combat). The addition of proper bandit camps and expanded combat options really rounds out its sandbox into something special—a contemplative walking simulator, a complex logistics game, and a memorable immersive sim. The first Death Stranding is one of my favorites, but On The Beach upstages it on all fronts. Personally, it should rate higher.
Sean Martin: Death Stranding 2 has a similar magic to Control, but where that game juxtaposes the mundanity of office life with paranormal occurrences, Death Stranding 2 actually makes logistics work ridiculously fun . I built a little truck, slapped as many batteries to the outside as I could, and drove it across Australia, even through Timefall events, which is more than any delivery man should have to deal with.
Jody Macgregor: I'm the guy who thinks the first one was better. The deliveries were more challenging, and the setting more mysterious. I loved not knowing what was going on and then slowly getting to grips with this bizarro whale-themed apocalypse. By comparison Death Stranding 2 has a bad case of the exposition dumps, with Dollman in particular basically existing just to parp out explanations in case you didn't understand the thing that literally just happened.
Fraser Brown: I loved the first one, but I refuse to spend £70 on a PC game. I have a dog to feed.
98. Total War: Warhammer 3
Released: February 17, 2022 | Top 100 Score: 216.90
(Image credit: Future) Sean Martin: What we talk about when we talk about Total War: Warhammer 3 is really Immortal Empires , the colossal campaign culmination of a decade-long trilogy of games and expansions. I've played Total War almost my entire life, but Immortal Empires stands at the pinnacle of campaign gameplay—a fantastical brewing pot of fun factions and units, enough to enthral any would-be Warhammer-lover.
And it keeps growing and mutating like some endlessly ravenous troll. The Lords of the End Times expansion arrived recently and introduced the iconic period alongside a fresh endgame rework.
Jody Macgregor: One of those Lords of the End Times, the Great Necromancer Nagash, has a nailbiting campaign where basically everyone hates you and your economy is mid, but fortunately you are a gigantic bony badass (seriously, even his bootlaces look skeletal) who cannot be stopped. Your minions are constantly failing and you have to go bail them out personally, arriving like Darth Vader on the day an officer screwed up big time, then absolutely demolishing whatever opposition was causing the trouble. It's glorious.
Fraser Brown: I used to be a diehard historical Total War boy, but the work Creative Assembly has done on Warhammer has been too damn impressive. There were some bumps in the road, but the most recent string of DLCs have been incredible, culminating in one of my favourite expansions. God, Nagash is good. OK, he's actually incredibly evil. But I love this lich.
Jake Tucker: Hard same, why would I ever want to play as medieval knights smashing each other when I could play as Skaven fighting against monstrous ogres?
97. Cities: Skylines
Released: March 10, 2015 | Top 100 Score: 218.90
(Image credit: Future) Fraser Brown: Still the best urban city builder around, even after all these years. The sequel is better than it was at launch, but the OG is still comfy on its city planner throne. City planners do get thrones, right? They should.
Phil Savage: There's no shortage of options if you want a focused city builder that hones in on a particular vibe or scenario. But if you want pure, maximalist city-building—the full uncut hit of zone distribution, traffic management and tourism expansion—Cities: Skylines is still the only true game in town.
96. Doom Eternal
Released: March 20, 2020 | Top 100 Score: 219.27
(Image credit: Future) Morgan Park: The list of big-budget singleplayer shooters is depressingly small these days, but even if they were the hotness, I don't think Doom Eternal would have trouble keeping its FPS throne. Eternal is the ultimate marriage of acrobatics and heft, casting the Slayer as a helldiving fighter jet with dashes, jumps, but no wallrun. Though sometimes dinged for some brave difficulty spikes, this is still peak modern Doom, and a true PC shooter—as in, you really should play it with a mouse and keyboard.
Shaun Prescott: I've struggled to care much about new FPS games since Doom Eternal. It's so unrelenting, so exhausting, that I think it filled my cup forever.
95. Dwarf Fortress
Released: August 8, 2006 (Alpha) | Top 100 Score: 219.30
(Image credit: Future) Lincoln Carpenter: Dwarf Fortress is one of the most distilled forms of PC gaming. Acclimating to its demands and expectations is almost a lifestyle in itself, but you're rewarded for the effort with a sprawling fantasy management sim and a deeply simulated roguelike, with systems for modeling nerve damage and geographic water drainage and civilizational ruin. It's a synthesis of conscious craft and procedural generation, an engine for a long tradition of oral storytelling, and the product of the years-long and ongoing effort of obsessive software wizards. It's an absurd achievement of fantasy simulation, and its creators only intend on doubling down.
Oh, and it regularly produces patch notes like "Made the corpses of small animals that die out of water stop teleporting"—the surest sign of quality one could ask for.
Joshua Wolens: I'm genuinely convinced Dwarf Fortress might be the best game ever made. At the very least, if I were given some sort of ambassadorial role where I had to explain the power of videogames to an alien race, DF would be the first thing I showed them.
94. Inside
Released: July 7, 2016 | Top 100 Score: 220.67
(Image credit: Future) Lauren Morton: Inside is one of those bucket list puzzle games you play once and remember fondly forever. I wish I could bottle those "Oh do they want me to… Oh wow, of course," moments that you can only ever experience once in a game and only one game in a decade truly gives you. This is that game, a surreal and creepy descent into sci-fi horror that so many sidescroll puzzlers with children in imminent danger have tried to capture since. It's nigh on perfect level design: beauty and blood pressure-spiking combined.
Andy Chalk: Inside is so good. I had no idea what was going on at any given moment or what the hell it was all about when it was over, but the vibe was pure and immaculate: Horrifying yet starkly beautiful, showing just enough of its world to satisfy without surrendering the mystery, and having the balls to end inconclusively—and, frankly, incomprehensibly. Importantly, too, Inside doesn't overstay its welcome. It's a short, sharp, surreal shock that'll leave you too wondering what the hell it was all about when it's all over.
Sean Martin : If we're talking space occupied in my brain relative to hour count, Inside is one of the most memorable, atmospheric, and smart side-scrollers I've ever played.
93. BattleTech
Released: April 24, 2018 | Top 100 Score: 221.14
(Image credit: Future) Evan Lahti: Mechs are metal piñatas. Their modular durability make them the most fun-to-shoot targets in video games, more than Nazi zombies, helicopters, or terrorists. Mechs die gradually: first layers of armor, then internal structure (a mech's bones, basically), then a weapon or other component. Worst-case, an ammo compartment explodes, annihilating the equipment around it. That combat pacing is a perfect template for a video game, and it works even better in the context of an XCOM-style campaign where you're a mercenary company that's scavenging parts over time and making risk-reward judgments on which contracts to accept.
Lincoln Carpenter: The real magic trick of BattleTech is Harebrained Schemes' ability to make speed and motion so crucial in a turn-based tactics game about massive, hulking war machines. A slow mech is just an easy target.
Fraser Brown: One of the worst things Paradox ever did was not let Harebrained Schemes work on another BattleTech game. The good news is that this one has so many great mods that you can make your own sequel.
Jake Tucker: One of the best turn-based strategy games ever made, the fact this didn't spawn a multi-part series or even get the level of support of several of Paradox's other titles makes me sad. There's something about the fantasy of running an intergalactic band of mechanised mercenaries that nothing else quite hits and has got me installing this game again on my second screen while writing this entry.
92. Hollow Knight: Silksong
Released: September 4, 2025 | Top 100 Score: 221.14
(Image credit: Future) Sean Martin: Year after year, I've advocated for Hollow Knight's position on this list, but I'm more than happy to see Silksong succeed. Scaling the kingdom of Pharloom, from its abyss-shrouded depths to its towering silken spires, is a frustrating endeavour, but I'll be damned if it's not the richest action-platforming experience you'll ever have. Hollow Knight punches above its weight constantly and Silksong is no different, weaving together masterful combat, exploration, and platforming, with an infamous ability to make you delight and despair in equal measure.
Harvey Randall: Despair really is the name of the game, here—while I like Silksong for all the normal reasons (its gorgeous setting, its excellent combat, its beautiful music), part of what enraptured me about it was its animosity towards the player. Silksong is a jerk to you. Hidden benches, traps, unreasonable runbacks, poison maggot swamps and infuriating side-quests. But that acts as a counterbalance to its beauty, and gives it enough personality that I just kept coming back to it.
91. Marathon
Released: March 5, 2026 | Top 100 Score: 221.33
(Image credit: Future) Rory Norris: Time and time again, Bungie has proven it's the best in the business when it comes to the simple joy of shooting virtual guns. Marathon combines impeccable weapon feel and a deep toybox with the innate tension of an extraction shooter for truly nail-biting action. Add to that its knack for environmental and mechanics design honed with Destiny's endgame, and you've got the most intricate, cerebral, unchained extraction shooter for those sickos willing to learn its ways.
Phil Savage: Arc Raiders is definitely the better game, but damn does Marathon's PvP feel good.
Issy van der Velde: Improving is an incredibly rewarding feeling. At launch I was a scared little runner, now I'm an Arachne angel of death
Jacob Ridley: My obsessive interest in this game during its first two weeks then sudden, complete drop-off to not playing it again since—not even once—should be studied by scientists.
#90-81

12. Outer Wilds
Released: May 30, 2019 | Top 100 Score: 245.71
(Image credit: Future) Sean Martin: Poignant yet playful, this cub scout sci-fi mystery sees you explore an endlessly looping solar system, uncovering the secrets of its quaint yet terrifying planetary dioramas as they fall to entropy around you. Imagine Majora's Mask as a puzzle sandbox and you'll come close to getting a picture, but it's almost impossible to describe Outer Wilds' tonal complexity, juxtaposing, as it does, cozy campfires with the end of all things. It's a game you really need to play to understand, and you should play it.
Issy van der Velde: It sickens me that Outer Wilds is so good, because it's a game I've only been able to fully enjoy on my first playthrough. Go in knowing as little as possible as that's how you'll get the most out of it.
Phil Savage: One of the rare few perfect videogames.
11. Divinity: Original Sin 2
Released: September 14, 2017 | Top 100 Score: 247.03
(Image credit: Future) Jody Macgregor: The Kickstarter-backed CRPG revival gave us a bunch of enjoyably retro trips back to Top-Down Town like Pillars of Eternity, but Divinity: Original Sin 2 combined that nostalgia with actual forward momentum.
It mattered which of your companions you controlled while talking to NPCs, not just because of their score in the Persuasion skill but because of who they were and how they fit into the world. Plus, while almost everyone else was trying to revive realtime-with-pause combat, Larian found new space to evolve turn-based tactics and elemental damage types.
I can't think of another game that says, sure, blood is wet, of course you can use it to put out fires and conduct electricity, and that's going to matter once you figure out how to produce the stuff in truly industrial quantities.
Harvey Randall: I love DoS2, but boy am I glad that Larian decided to tone down the surfaces for Baldur's Gate 3. And I am slightly worried we'll be returning to the same screen-flooded environmental spam with the upcoming Divinity. But hey, setting an entire field of flammable ground into a scorching hellscape is a good time, and I've no qualms about DoS2 being here on this list.
Wes Fenlon: While Baldur's Gate 3 feels like a straight improvement in so many ways, the origin stories in DoS2 are still incredibly strong. Even playing through it over the course of six months in a chaotic co-op group, my character Lohse's story ended up one of my favorites in any RPG.
#10-1
10. Half-Life 2
Released: November 16, 2004 | Top 100 Score: 249.24
(Image credit: Future) Phil Savage: Half-Life 2 is by no means the best shooter you can play on PC—although the Gravity Gun remains an ingenious tool for physics shenanigans. Half-Life 2 is still the best shooter campaign you can play on PC. There's little else that even comes close to Valve's masterful pacing; the ebb and flow of encounter design, and the playful variety that each chapter brings. A fool might tell you that this game is old fashioned, out of date, maybe even surpassed. I wish that was true, because here 22 years after its release, there's still nothing else like it.
Sean Martin: You're not really a PC gamer until you've killed a headcrab with a crowbar. I don't make the rules!
9. Doom (1993)
Released: December 10, 1993 | Top 100 Score: 250.21
(Image credit: Future) Andy Chalk: Doom is more than 30 years old, and in my heart of hearts I believe it still deserves a place on this list. Its importance and impact simply cannot be overstated, and beyond being a foundational FPS from the old times, it remains relevant to this day through ports, mods, and expansions. Doom matters in ways that even games like Half-Life 2 don't, and the fact that you can still fire it up and see that significance for yourself is proof of its fundamental greatness.
Jody Macgregor: My favorite part of Doom is the early techbase levels, where the most complicated thing that is likely to happen is that you'll see a tease of an outdoor area, only to arrive at it later on. Eventually the teleporters show up and it becomes a game of navigating labyrinths while flipping switches and juggling keys, but Doom at its best is pure and primal, a cave-painting of a videogame where the cavemen have only just discovered the color red.
Wes Fenlon: You guys heard of the new hotness, Doom 2? Why settle for a single shotgun when you can have both barrels?
Shaun Prescott: The super shotgun is overrated: it's basically as powerful as the rocket launcher but uses two units of shotgun ammo, spreads too far, and doesn't gib as spectacularly.
8. Crusader Kings 3
Released: September 1, 2020 | Top 100 Score: 250.29
(Image credit: Future) Fraser Brown: Murder your cousin! Eat your uncle! Declare all the wars! I don't know why I'm shouting! I can't help but become irritatingly enthusiastic about Crusader Kings 3—the pinnacle of Paradox Development Studio's experiments in combining grand strategy with roleplaying.
Lincoln Carpenter: CK3 is like participating in a multigenerational murder mystery dinner, but there's at least as many additional murders in progress as there are participants, there's a religious war for Bohemia going on upstairs, and the building's going to catch on fire when the Holy Roman Empire collapses. But in a fun way.
Joshua Wolens: With repeated kidnappings, murder plots against family members, and myriad invasions, I once made a rival's life such a living hell in CK3 that I began feeling genuinely bad about it in reality.
7. XCOM 2
Released: February 4, 2016 | Top 100 Score: 251.90
(Image credit: Future) Lincoln Carpenter: There's an incomparable magic to taking a raw, untested recruit, giving him the name of one of your old high school friends, subjecting him to dozens of high-stakes anti-alien guerilla deployments with all the associated battlefield tragedies, devastating misfires, and trauma-bonded comrades they entail, and watching him gradually become the last, best hope of a subjugated humanity who just so happens to have a retroengineered xenotech shotgun that can punch a hole clean through whatever is the closest approximation the Advent have for God.
The mods are good, too.
Fraser Brown: Still the best tactics game, hands down. This year I grew to appreciate it even more thanks to Zero Company. It has all of the ingredients of XCOM 2, but it just did nothing for me. That's because Firaxis worked some real magic with this one. It's properly special. I have nothing bad to say about it, which is incredibly rare for me.
Harvey Randall: You know how people will often take their roombas in for repairs, rather than exchanging them for a new model, because they've become attached to them? That's how I feel about my XCOM soldiers. Ostensibly, they're just lines of code and a 3D model, with no unique dialogue to back them up. But I care about them, damnit. The emergent stories that crop up in the game's many missions is a magic trick of anthropomorphism that I'll never stop being fascinated by.
6. Stardew Valley
Released: February 26, 2016 | Top 100 Score: 252.83
(Image credit: Future) Lauren Morton : The game that invented farm sims—just kidding, but "the game that reminded us how good Harvest Moon was" doesn't really roll off the tongue. Stardew Valley led a renaissance for a niche subgenre to flourish and to this day has not been usurped by any of the hundreds of Stardew-likes it inspired. It's still the platonic ideal of waking up at 6am to water tomatoes, go fishing, and save the town from stagnation. Apparently it won't ever stop being updated by its incorrigible creator either.
Issy van der Velde: My girlfriend and her sister run our farm with the iron fist of a sweatshop owner. It's not always a cosy game.
Harvey Randall: I, like Issy's girlfriend, have never been able to engage with Stardew Valley as a cosy game. I always get too concerned with being efficient. Is there something fundamentally broken with me? Always chasing optimisation even when I have an idyllic and peaceful life? Is my fear that the years will flee from me, paradoxically, the only thing that ensures they will?
Music's pretty good. I like that bit.
Shaun Prescott: My kids have played Stardew Valley for most of their childhood, so its soundtrack has flooded my house on Saturday and Sunday afternoons for years. It's genuinely gorgeous stuff. That Eric Barone composed it all on his lonesome is endlessly impressive.
5. Minecraft
Released: November 18, 2011 | Top 100 Score: 253.90
(Image credit: Future) Elie Gould: I frickin love this little blocky game. I only get the urge to play Minecraft every six months or so now, but those few weeks are always full of the best times—whether that be working on my expanding underground dwarven city or in my friend's Skyblock server where I'm forced to farm dirt.
Rory Norris: While Minecraft is already a very competent, incredibly cosy sandbox—my only ask is furniture in a game about building things—it's a totally different beast with mods. Eclipsing Skyrim, I'd say Minecraft is the most modded, transformable game ever. You can add furniture because Mojang oddly refuses too (I'm not mad), turn it into a Souls-inspired RPG, or make it a factory automation game. It's timeless. Like Skyrim, I'll always get the annual urge to return to it.
Harvey Randall: I somehow always become the guy who goes and mines stuff in my multiplayer servers. This probably says something about the nature of my soul.
Shaun Prescott: Creative mode is one of the best cosy, meditative experiences on PC.
4. Elden Ring
Released: February 24, 2022 | Top 100 Score: 254.90
(Image credit: Future) Sean Martin: What if Dark Souls embraced the open world formula? It's a simple concept, but Elden Ring stands testament to how successfully it was realised. Take FromSoft's iconic combat, boss fights, and quests, then explode them into an enigmatic world you slowly explore and unravel. I have over 800 hours in Elden Ring (plus 500 in Nightreign) and I still started a new playthrough when Tarnished Edition released.
Andy Chalk: I don't like Souls games but I loved Elden Ring, because it let me avoid the whole Souls thing: Instead of all that dodge-parry-slash nonsense (and no offense if that's what you're into, but brother, I am not), I just gave myself a big brain with a big stick, and melted everything. Some fans of the genre might say I deprived myself of the 'real' Souls experience, but I got to enjoy one of the most stunning fantasy worlds I've ever explored—something I'd have missed if the game hadn't been willing to let me play it on my own terms.
Harvey Randall: I have played Elden Ring (and its expansion) exactly once, and I will admit, I've not had the stomach to do so a second time—the scope of these games is a touch overwhelming to me. But that one playthrough did utterly enthral and capture me, so I can't complain too much. Besides, Sean plays enough Elden Ring for all of us.
Issy van der Velde: Elden Ring is the antithesis of the focus found in Sekiro, and it still rules. I love that Andy could have fun melting everyone while I got to enjoy shredding them with a big spikey wheel axe.
3. The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt
Released: May 18, 2015 | Top 100 Score: 258.38
(Image credit: Future) Ted Litchfield: I was late to the party (maybe not so much in the grand scheme) getting The Witcher 3 for Christmas in 2015. Velen is great, but things really clicked for me in Novigrad. One of my fondest gaming memories remains sitting on a beanbag in my parents' basement over the break, my chunky, already-aging laptop plugged into the TV with its fans screaming. I was rocking a first gen, owl-faced Steam Controller, and I was so invested in the search for Sigi Reuven's treasure that I pulled an all-nighter by accident.
11 years on, The Witcher 3 is still, somehow, one of the best-looking videogames out there, its balance of art direction and photorealism gracefully aging like a DILF-y Hollywood leading man. I think CDPR has managed to at least match the achievement of The Witcher 3 with Cyberpunk, but that's hardly a universal opinion, and Geralt's final(?) outing remains a triumph.
Jody Macregor: I do think The Witcher 3 has a magic Cyberpunk 2077 didn't match. The way it's structured incentivises pushing on in your search for Yennefer and then Ciri without feeling like you have such limited time you can't engage with whichever of its many excellent sidequests catches your interest. There's just enough impetus to keep up the momentum without making you feel like it's out-of-character to have a little fun. And if you crank the difficulty up Geralt's combat style (prep-heavy research-based battle herbalism) is actually great.
Andy Chalk: One of my favorite things about The Witcher 3 (and spoiler here, but it's been a decade) is that when all is said and done—if you played your cards reasonably right—Geralt gets a happy ending. I like happy endings, and if any videogame guy deserves one, it's Geralt. That dude powered through some shit , and as much as I'd like his adventures to continue, the send-off CD Projekt gave him with Blood and Wine left me far happier to call it done.
Joshua Wolens: Geralt of Rivia will return in The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt – Songs of the Past, and so help me CDPR if you do anything bad to him I'm picketing your offices.
Andy Chalk: Yeah, just a little follow-up to my previous comment here: If CD Projekt does a Vesemir to Geralt, I am gonna be setting shit on fire.
2. Disco Elysium
Released: October 15, 2019 | Top 100 Score: 259.74
(Image credit: Future) Ted Litchfield: Disco Elysium was the game that made me get serious about a career in games. It's now one of the biggest bummers I have to deal with professionally. The IP ownership and financial allegations? Byzantine. The interpersonal strife among its developers? Distressing. The layoffs and lives upended in its wake? To quote my man Geralt of Rivia, Poland's most soulful white boy from the previous entry on this list: It's "the last bitter drop in a chalice of sorrow."
And yet . Cut to the game underneath it all, and you'll still find a potentially life-changing work of baffling, miraculous provenance. Punks don't know how to make each other do the dishes without a struggle session. How the fuck did they make a game?
Six years on, it's easy to take Disco's design innovations for granted: Strip the so-so combat out of Planescape: Torment and replace it with a union of RPG and point 'n click adventure. Dialogue windows in the bottom-center of the screen with walls of text suck, so hammer it into a much more parsable, right-oriented vertical feed instead. Have the skills you invest in not only open opportunities, but shift the tone of the experience with their distinctive, hallucinatory personalities.
Disco tells a story with heart and characters that feel real, set in a tiny slice of a world that blends alternate history with pure fantasy like the best 20th century sci-fi writers, your Le Guins, Herberts, and Dicks. Its authors were people of strong social and political conviction who nevertheless trusted players enough to let them disagree and take the story in wildly different directions without it feeling like a failure state.
As I grow older, I've become more partial to stories that end. But we didn't get our fill of Elysium, and I still hope we can go back, someday.
Fraser Brown: A lot of the writing around Disco focuses on how weird it is, or how wonderful it is to have a videogame that's actually funny, and all of those things are true. But what really sticks with me is how heartbreaking it is. It's one of the only videogames to ever make my eyes get a bit leaky. Underneath all the high concept weirdness and political orienteering, it's an incredibly human game that hits like a fucking truck. We'll never see its like again.
Phil Savage: Heartbreaking, yes, but also hopeful. That's the thing that I wasn't expecting when I finally played it earlier this year. Not hopeful in an "everything's going to be OK" kind of way, Disco's optimism is both smaller and grander than that. Everything is not going to be OK, and maybe that's OK. Maybe, if you work on yourself, you can find some meaning in that. Maybe the arthropods are in silent and meaningless awe of you.
Harvey Randall: While you're distracted thinking about everything said above, I'm going to take this chance to go on record and say that I want to marry Kim Kitsuragi. That is all.
Issy van der Velde: I went into Disco Elysium with high expectations, but what I didn't anticipate was the mirror it would hold up to me. It made me realise I'll always be an addict at heart, but it also reaffirmed my desire to overcome that. I didn't let Harry relapse even though he's only pixels and words. I'm flesh and bone, so surely I deserve even better?
1. Baldur's Gate 3
Released: August 3, 2023 | Top 100 Score: 270.30
(Image credit: Future) Fraser Brown: Here we are again. Baldur's Gate 3 is our number one game for another year, and let's face it—it's probably going to be taking this spot again in 2027. It's just so damn impressive. There are few games I can say this about, but if you don't get on with BG3, I don't think we can be friends (just don't tell my partner, who doesn't remotely understand the hype). This is one of the best ever RPG studios firing on all cylinders, building on decades of experience and experiments. I hope RPGs haven't peaked with BG3, but I'm struggling to imagine a future where this doesn't continue to be my favourite game of all time.
Sean Martin: I don't even like Dungeons & Dragons that much, and yet I'm one of only 3% of players who've completed the game in Honour Mode. I'm not even sure how that happened? Baldur's Gate 3 is just so damn enchanting . The prospect of adventure, the wonderfully written characters, and the endless twists and turns your journey takes amount to a truly unique gaming experience. I still consider myself blessed that I got to see the orchestral concert in London where Andrew Wincott appeared and sang Raphael's Final Act, because that song is an all-timer.
Jody Macgregor: The Forgotten Realms isn't always an interesting backdrop for roleplaying, and I say that as someone who has run multiple campaigns there. Larian turned it into one by making the obligatory Realms stuff a delight—Volo the travelling disaster, Elminster the cheese freak—and pulling in cool bits from other D&D settings like githyanki and illithids so the world feels slightly alien and part of a larger cosmology. BG3 is a fantasy RPG through and through, but one that restores some of the genre's sense of wonder.
The thing that really makes it special is the reactivity. Act 3 is constantly referencing stuff you did in Act 1, and I only just found out if you take over the newspaper you can print your own stories, changing the city folk's ambient dialogue. Everything you do feels like it matters.
Ted Litchfield: 2023, '24, and much of '25 were dominated by BG3 for me, and it's been a second since I fired it up. I've been on a real Owlcat kick (we'll get Wrath of the Righteous or Rogue Trader on this list next year, prayer warriors), and when my favorite game is no longer right in front of me, my feckless heart can drift. Was it really that good?
Yes. Unequivocally. Universal heavyweight champion of the world. Just thinking about it for this write up has me wanting to roll a new guy⁠—I've never uninstalled, and I don't think I ever will barring force majeure. Larian simultaneously raised the bar on cinematic RPG storytelling while matching the crunchiest classics in depth and complexity. Common sense previously dictated that the two were mutually exclusive, and it feels like CRPGs can finally look forward, not back.
Harvey Randall: I have about 380 hours in this thing. I've completed it twice, once on honour mode, and I got another two extra honour mode playthroughs to Act 3 before I got distracted and left them in the dirt.
I can confidently call it one of the best RPGs that will perhaps ever be made. There's something about the sheer scope of it, the mixture of immersive sim style branching narratives and CRPG goodness that mashes up with professional, glossy production value and fully motion-captured cutscenes.
And while the TTRPG rules lover in me balks at Larian's irreverently-designed magic items which, let's be clear, grab D&D 5e's intended balance and snap it mercilessly over its knee… I'm still very glad they're there. They make the game a min-maxxer's delight.
Currently, I've been roped into an Honor Mode playthrough with Josh, Sean, and Ted, and my Cleric has stumbled onto a build that debuffs everybody just by standing around her. They can attest that I have made some utterly disgusting laugh-noises whenever I knock someone prone with Reverberation just for looking at me funny.
Personal Picks
Surprise! There are more than 100 good videogames. Below you'll find a selection of individual recommendations—each a game that a member of the PC Gamer team thinks you should play.
Rocket League
Tyler Wilde, US Editor-in-Chief: Rocket League hasn't evolved much since 2015, but that's because it was already a perfectly-designed competitive team game which no one has yet improved upon. Playing soccer with rocket-powered cars has a high skill ceiling, but great teamwork can trump individual skill, which has led to some of the most exciting underdog wins of my gaming career. I'll be playing when I'm 80 if they don't turn the servers off before then.
Thank Goodness You’re Here!
John Strike, Senior Art Editor: Big pies. Flat beer. Crazy northeners. Drunk cows. Thank Goodness You’re Here! has it all and then some. This beautiful cartoon-style slapstick romp around the fictional and truly bizarre Yorkshire town of Barnsworth is a must-play for anyone with a soft spot for northern ways. Put your trousers on, grab your net and go and catch those spirit level bubbles!
Silent Hill f
Elie Gould, News Writer: Oh my god, I forgot to put Silent Hill f on the voting list. This is unforgivable considering how amazing it is and how well it managed to pave the way for the new kind of Silent Hill we're now seeing unfold. Its setting is chilling, mysterious, and cool as all hell, it gives us the best female protagonist I've seen in years, and we're tested with some seriously tricky puzzles and grotesque monsters. It's the whole package.
Sea of Thieves
Christopher Livingston, Senior Editor: After a long absence I finally returned to Rare's open world ocean sandbox this year, and yep, there's still really no other game like it. The beauty of its world and water is still unmatched and there's nowhere else I've found that shares its blend of chill hangout vibes (90%) and humbling PvP nightmare (10%). All you can bring into each session are your skills because there's nothing else to give any pirate an advantage over another. One of a kind.
The Elder Scrolls Online
Rory Norris, Guides Writer: TESO is my most played game of all time, sitting at well over 2,000 hours in the decade since launch. It's an Elder Scrolls game but multiplayer, and it's been carrying the torch while the mainline series has been radio silent since Skyrim. You can explore almost all of Tamriel at this point, questing, doing world bosses, dungeons, and whatnot. And while it's technically a bit of a mess, the large-scale PvP is truly a sight to behold.
Esoteric Ebb
Ted Litchfield, Associate Editor: This one was supposed to be on the list proper, sorry everyone. Deadlock, I love you sweetie, but you're not finished. Step aside for what will be PCG's 2025 RPG of the year barring a coup and my execution. Esoteric Ebb riffs on Disco Elysium, but meaningfully pushes the evolving subgenre forward with smart changes like 6 attributes instead of 24 skills, potentially even greater reactivity⁠—especially in its handwritten turn-based battles⁠—and a comedic, hopeful, tone to set its excellent story apart.
Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War – Definitive Edition
Jody Macgregor, Weekend Editor: I may be a turn-based lover who sometimes thinks we should add Jagged Alliance to the Top 100, but even I know there have been a couple of classic RTSes, chief among them Dawn of War . It's got the best sense of scale of any game in the genre, a real feeling of ants versus bison as you build up to tanks and daemons, and the Definitive Edition lets you pull the camera back to appreciate it. Good luck, ants.
1000xResist
Joshua Wolens, News Writer: A 2024 narrative adventure that's more or less a visual novel, 1000xResist is one of those games that make you realise how narratively unambitious most other videogames are. It's about killing god, doing a revolution, inheriting trauma, inflicting trauma, the immigrant experience, the Hong Kong protests, original sin, noodles, and a lot else. It's like a modern Planescape: Torment, in that it's so tenderly and confidently written that it just makes all the other guys look bad.
Jagged Alliance 3
Evan Lahti, Strategic Director: If you're an XCOM person with any affection for '80s/'90s action movies, JA3 should be your next game. It's campy, it's tropical, and your mercenaries (through story or tactical decisions) can find themselves in no-win scenarios. But my favorite detail is the simmy ballistics: bullets aren't just particle effects, they're physical objects that can scatter randomly and catch collateral hits against enemies, friendlies, civs, or scenery. The campaign itself is delightfully tabletop in its combo of scripted stuff and freedom.
Transistor
Issy van der Velde, Deputy Editor, PC Gaming Show: Transistor has the best sci-fi love story I've ever experienced, and the combat is endlessly satisfying. Each ability can be used on its own, added to another to create a secondary effect, or held as a passive buff. It's easy to see how Supergiant built on this to create the boons in Hades. Everyone should play this masterpiece for Ashley Barrett and Darren Korb's soundtrack alone. There's even a dedicated button that lets you hum along to the music.
Lorelei and the Laser Eyes
Phil Savage, Global Editor-in-Chief: If you like the idea of Blue Prince, but don't like the roguelike elements, then I have two things to tell you: 1) You are weak and need to fix yourself, and 2) you should play Lorelei and the Laser Eyes. Simogo's mystery box adventure is an absolute treat of puzzle design, cleverly laying out its challenges in cascading threads of discovery. It's deeply satisfying to solve both the individual puzzles and the building mystery of its story. A genuine treat.
Plants vs. Zombies
Andy Chalk, US News Lead: The Plants vs. Zombies remaster that dropped in 2025 took some heat for technical shortcomings and allegations of AI art, but EA's addressed most of the complaints and these days it stands as a really good remaster of an all-time classic. The original is still available too, and much cheaper, and it holds up remarkably well for its age. Either way, Plants vs. Zombies is a short, snappy, incredibly cute and easy-to-engage tower defense game that remains as great—and essential—as ever.
Total War: Three Kingdoms
Sean Martin, Senior Guides Writer: I'm unsure why my compatriots turned on Total War this year, but I'm here to remind you that Three Kingdoms is still incredible. Its quality is often overshadowed by its early demise, but it's quite unlike anything Creative Assembly ever made, or will likely make again. It channels the courageous characters, political machinations, and endless scheming of China's most culturally iconic period into a top-tier strategy game, achieving a harmonious balance between history and romance.
Enshrouded
Andrea Shearon, Evergreen Writer: I've been enjoying the survival crafting renaissance, and by that I mean playing the hell out of Abiotic Factor and Enshrouded. The unbelievably detailed, massive high-fantasy RPG has one of the best building systems I've ever seen, and I love rescuing new villagers and crafters to slowly grow my own town. My only complaint is that Embervale is so pretty that I spend dozens of hours whispering, "Oh, maybe I'll settle down here," without getting anything done.
Exo Rally Championship
Morgan Park, Staff Writer: A gritty, unforgiving rally racing sim set in outer space. Exo Rally takes an already challenging rally format and adds gravity and thrusters into the mix. You'll tear your hair out trying to complete a singular turn on the moon, then ride the high of circumventing most of a track through well-timed thruster use. I haven't played enough yet to make my case for on the list, but it's turning me into a racing fan. A brilliant 2026 indie that's flying too low under the radar.
Project Zomboid
Mollie Taylor, Features Producer: I'm 13 years late to the party, but Project Zomboid's brutal, complex, and ridiculously moreish take on zombie survival has gripped me this year. It's one of the most customisable sandbox games I've ever tinkered with, meaning you can go for an unforgiving post-apocalyptic landscape or fine-tune it into a cosy (if not slightly gritty and terrifying) zombified The Sims 1. One of the few games I've been happy to sink hundreds of hours into learning.
Valheim
Jacob Ridley, Managing Editor, Hardware: There are some games you can sink hour after hour into and not even realise it's already morning. Valheim is one of those games. Jump in with a couple of friends and build a new homestead, trying to one-up each other with ever more elaborate creations (our Sistine Chapel are two rival towers on top of massive rocks). Or just go exploring and hunt for new lands, hoping to survive the treacherous ocean journey. Yeah, it's a comfort game for me.
Crimson Desert
Andy Edser, Hardware Writer: Crimson Desert is not the ultimate action RPG, despite wearing the ambition proudly on its sleeve. But it's also the most fun I've had in a fantasy open world in years. The map is gigantic, and stuffed with bizarre details to explore. The combat is fiddly, yet satisfying to master. It's a game with obvious passion running underneath it, and a brilliant, bat-swinging attempt to make something with real scope and fresh ideas. More of this sort of thing, please.
Mina the Hollower
Harvey Randall, Staff Writer: Perhaps a bit of a late entrant to catch PC Gamer's eye—which means I don't resent its absence from our Top 100 list—but I absolutely loved Mina the Hollower. It's a sprawling, satisfying Zelda-like with a bumping soundtrack and some of the best exploration I've had in a videogame. I was particularly impressed by how intuitive this game was. My experimentation-loving brain was constantly rewarded for putting its control scheme together in novel ways. Cute little mouse versus the eldritch horrors, what's not to love.
Big Walk
Fraser Brown, Online Editor: Big Walk launched after we created the magazine version of the Top 100 this year, otherwise I know it would have been in the list. This is simply the perfect co-op game. A simple, joyful puzzler absent a single flaw. Some of the antics its puzzles inspired genuinely left my crying with laughter, and that ending? Wow. It's a pure delight, start to finish. It's easily going to be my GOTY for 2026.
html:
Welcome to the PC Gamer Top 100—our annual list of the best games you can play right now. Every year, we look at the hundreds of thousands of PC games that are available to buy, and think, "yes, we can whittle this down into a numbered list". Hubris? Yes. A months-long crucible of heated arguments and impassioned pleas? Also yes.

More than anything, the Top 100 is designed to capture a moment in time. It's a place where the 'canon' classics of the past rub shoulders against the fresh new hotness. Where being a game that a significant portion of the team currently loves is as important as being a game that is recognised worldwide for its contributions to the medium.

It is a deeply subjective process—a way for PC Gamer's editorial team to advocate for the games they're passionate about. One member of our team has spent years attempting to get Overwatch back on the list, taking every opportunity to persuade their fellow editors to give it a chance. Not every entry required that level of dedication to earn its spot, but every pick is a game that at least a handful of our staff cares deeply about.

How we make the list

Ahead of the vote, the PC Gamer team is free to nominate any PC game for voting, giving us a longlist of over 300 games. Each member of the team is then asked to rate those games subjectively across three weighted categories:

  • Quality: Is it good? A rating of the game's calibre. (60% of the Top 100 Score)
  • Importance: Is it noteworthy? A rating of the game's influence. (20% of the Top 100 Score)
  • Freshness: Is it unique? A rating of the game's originality. (20% of the Top 100 Score)

The weightings are designed around the Top 100's function as an annual, ever-changing list. Too much weight to Importance, and the list stagnates. Too much to Freshness, and there's no consistency year-to-year. Quality is the most important category because, ultimately, if we don't think a game is actually very good, it doesn't make the list.

The sum of each game's ratings is divided by its number of voters, and then run through a few special formulae—including a penalty for games that receive too few votes—to produce the final Top 100 Score for each game.

We then make some manual adjustments. In the interest of variety we mostly restrict the list to one game per series—only including multiple if we think the games are different enough from each other to be worth mentioning, as with Baldur's Gate 2 and Baldur's Gate 3. Otherwise, the lower scoring game in a series is removed. We also let editors pitch for a change to the list—each of which is voted on by the wider team, and only ratified if it gets majority approval.

What's left is the 100 games you find below. Some might claim it folly—attempting to wrestle the varied tastes of our editorial team into a list of games we wholeheartedly recommend. Nevertheless, we're sure that within these entries, you'll find something new to love.

And yet. Cut to the game underneath it all, and you'll still find a potentially life-changing work of baffling, miraculous provenance. Punks don't know how to make each other do the dishes without a struggle session. How the fuck did they make a game?

Six years on, it's easy to take Disco's design innovations for granted: Strip the so-so combat out of Planescape: Torment and replace it with a union of RPG and point 'n click adventure. Dialogue windows in the bottom-center of the screen with walls of text suck, so hammer it into a much more parsable, right-oriented vertical feed instead. Have the skills you invest in not only open opportunities, but shift the tone of the experience with their distinctive, hallucinatory personalities.

Disco tells a story with heart and characters that feel real, set in a tiny slice of a world that blends alternate history with pure fantasy like the best 20th century sci-fi writers, your Le Guins, Herberts, and Dicks. Its authors were people of strong social and political conviction who nevertheless trusted players enough to let them disagree and take the story in wildly different directions without it feeling like a failure state.
